41: Slack Web API
42: The Slack Web API is an interface for querying information from and enacting change in a Slack workspace.
43: Use it for individual queries, or as part of a more complex tapestry of platform features in a Slack app.
44: Web API methods
45: Basic overview​
46: The Web API is a collection of HTTP RPC-style methods, all with URLs in the form https://slack.com/api/METHOD_FAMILY.method.
47: While it's not a REST API, those familiar with REST should be at home with its foundations in HTTP.
48: Use HTTPS, SSL, and TLS v1.2 or above when calling all methods. Learn more about our SSL and TLS requirements.
49: Each method has a series of arguments informing the execution of your intentions.
50: Pass arguments as:
51: GET querystring parameters,
52: POST parameters presented as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, or
53: a mix of both GET and POST parameters
54: Don't send a request body with GET or HEAD requests. Starting February 17th, 2027, these requests return an HTTP 400 error (HTTP 403 once enforced at the CloudFront edge). Learn more in the changelog entry.
55: Most write methods allow arguments with application/json attributes.
56: Some methods, such as chat.postMessage and dialog.open, feature arguments that accept an associative JSON array. However, these methods can be difficult to properly construct when using a application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-type, so we strongly recommend using JSON-encoded bodies instead.
57: POST bodies​
58: When sending a HTTP POST, you may present your arguments as either standard POST parameters, or you may use JSON instead.
59: URL-encoded bodies​
60: When sending URL-encoded data, set your HTTP Content-type header to application/x-www-form-urlencoded and present your key/value pairs according to RFC-3986.
61: For example, a POST request to the conversations.create method might look something like this:
62: POST /api/conversations.create
63: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
64: token=xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx&name=something-urgent
65: JSON-encoded bodies​
66: For write methods that support JSON, you may alternatively send your HTTP POST data as Content-type: application/json.
67: There are some ground rules:
68: You must explicitly set the Content-type HTTP header to application/json. We won't interpret your POST body as such without it.
69: You must transmit your token as a bearer token in the Authorization HTTP header.
70: You cannot send your token as part of the query string or as an attribute in your posted JSON.
71: Do not mix arguments between query string, URL-encoded POST body, and JSON attributes. Choose one approach per request.
72: Providing an explicitly null value for an attribute will result in whichever default behavior is assigned to it.
73: For example, to send the same request above to the conversations.create method with a JSON POST body, send something like this:
74: POST /api/conversations.create
75: Content-type: application/json
76: Authorization: Bearer xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx
77: {"name":"something-urgent"}
78: Note how we present the token with the string Bearer pre-pended to it, indicating the OAuth 2.0 authentication scheme. Consult your favorite HTTP tool or library's manual for further detail on setting HTTP headers.
79: Here's a more complicated example — posting a message with menus using chat.postMessage:
80: POST /api/chat.postMessage
81: Content-type: application/json
82: Authorization: Bearer xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx
83: {"channel":"C123ABC456","text":"I hope the tour went well, Mr. Wonka.","attachments":[{"text":"Who wins the lifetime supply of chocolate?","fallback":"You could be telling the computer exactly what it can do with a lifetime supply of chocolate.","color":"#3AA3E3","attachment_type":"default","callback_id":"select_simple_1234","actions":[{"name":"winners_list","text":"Who should win?","type":"select","data_source":"users"}]}]}
84: The attachments argument is sent a straightforward JSON array.
85: Here's how to do that with cURL:
86: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer xoxb-1234-56789abcdefghijklmnop' \
87: -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
88: --data '{"channel":"C123ABC456","text":"I hope the tour went well, Mr. Wonka.","attachments": [{"text":"Who wins the lifetime supply of chocolate?","fallback":"You could be telling the computer exactly what it can do with a lifetime supply of chocolate.","color":"#3AA3E3","attachment_type":"default","callback_id":"select_simple_1234","actions":[{"name":"winners_list","text":"Who should win?","type":"select","data_source":"users"}]}]}' \
89: https://slack.com/api/chat.postMessage<
90: Errors specific to passing JSON​
91: If the posted JSON is invalid, you'll receive one of the following errors in response:
92: invalid_json: The JSON you've included in your POST body cannot be parsed. This might be because it's actually not JSON, or perhaps you did not correctly set your HTTP Content-type header. Ensure your JSON attribute keys are strings wrapped with double-quote (") characters.
93: json_not_object: We could understand that your code was JSON-like enough to parse it, but it's not actually a JSON hash of attribute key/value pairs. Perhaps you sent us an array, or just a string or a number.
94: In both cases, you'll need to revise your JSON or how you're transmitting your data to resolve the error condition.
95: Evaluating responses​
96: All Web API responses contain a JSON object, which will always contain a top-level boolean property ok that indicates success or failure.
97: For failure results, the error property will contain a short machine-readable error code. In the case of problematic calls that could still be completed successfully, ok will be true and the warning property will contain a short machine-readable warning code (or comma-separated list of them, in the case of multiple warnings). See the following examples:
98: {
99: "ok": true,
100: "stuff": "This is good"
101: }
102: {
103: "ok": false,
104: "error": "something_bad"
105: }
106: {
107: "ok": true,
108: "warning": "something_problematic",
109: "stuff": "Your requested information"
110: }
111: Other properties are defined in the documentation for each relevant method. There's a lot of "stuff" to unpack, including these types and other method or domain-specific curiosities.
112: Authentication​
113: Authenticate your Web API requests by providing a bearer token, which identifies a single user or bot user relationship.
114: Register your application with Slack to obtain credentials for use with our OAuth 2.0 implementation, which allows you to negotiate tokens on behalf of users and workspaces.
115: We prefer tokens to be sent in the Authorization HTTP header of your outbound requests. However, you may also pass tokens in all Web API calls as a POST body parameter called token. Tokens cannot be sent as a query parameter.
116: Treat tokens with care
117: Never share tokens with other users or applications. Do not publish tokens in public code repositories. Review token safety tips.
118: HTTPS, SSL, and TLS​
119: Slack requires HTTPS, SSL, and TLS v1.2 or above. The platform and the Web API are governed by the same rules. Learn more about our deprecation of early TLS versions. Stay safe and secure.
120: All TLS connections must use the SNI extension. Lastly, TLS connections must support at least one of the following cipher suites:
121: TLS 1.2:
122: ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256
123: ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305
124: ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384
125: TLS 1.3:
126: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
127: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
128: TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256
129: Slack uses certificates issued by publicly trusted certificate authorities, including DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, and Amazon Trust Services. These certificates can be rotated or reissued by a different authority at any time without notice, and Slack doesn't support pinning certificates, intermediates, or certificate authorities. Rely on the default system trust store instead, so that a certificate rotation doesn't interrupt your app.
130: Methods​
131: With over 200 methods, surely there's one right for you. You can find them all in the reference, where you can filter by method family.

40: Installing via OAuth authorization code flow
41: Slack apps are installed with a v2 OAuth 2.0 flow. Your app can act with its own identity instead of acting on behalf of users, without requesting excessive permissions that could cause installations to be rejected.
42: OAuth 2.0 refers to the 2.0 version of the OAuth spec, and this is our second version of OAuth 2.0. For the rest of this guide, we'll just refer to it as "OAuth".
43: How it works: a high-level overview​
44: OAuth allows a user in any Slack workspace to install your app. At the end of the OAuth flow, your app gains an access token. Your app's access token allows your app to open doors to the Slack platform. During the OAuth flow, you specify which scopes your app needs. Those scopes determine exactly which doors your app can open.
45: Implementing an OAuth flow can feel hard because there are a lot of steps, but your app really only has to worry about three steps to make OAuth work: requesting scopes, waiting for a user to give their approval, and exchanging a temporary authorization code for an access token. Redirecting a user to Slack can be done with a single link. For example:
46: [Add to Slack](https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&client_id=33336676.569200954261)
47: Replace the client_id with your app's client ID, and add the scopes you'd like. Bot scopes should be added as scope=<bot_scope>, and user scopes should be added as user_scope=<user_scope>.
48: For example, if your app only has one bot scope and it is incoming-webhook, the redirect would look like that shown above. If your app has a user scope, it might look like this instead:
49: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261
50: If your app has both a bot and a user scope, it might look like this:
51: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261
52: Obtaining access tokens with OAuth​
53: Your app obtains an access token in three steps:
54: Requesting scopes.
55: Waiting for a user to approve your requested scopes.
56: Exchanging a temporary authorization code for an access token.
57: Why is there a third exchanging step in OAuth at all? Why doesn't Slack send your app an access token directly after the user okays your app? The reason is two-factor authentication. You have to prove both that you have the right temporary authorization code, and that you have your app's client secret.
58: 1. Request scopes​
59: While developing your app, you'll determine a minimum list of scopes that your app requires to work. When a user installs your app in their workspace, you'll request those scopes.
60: To request scopes, redirect Slack users to https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize. If you're developing a GovSlack app for use by public sector customers, redirect users to https://slack-gov.com/oauth/v2/authorize.
61: A scope conflict occurs when attempting to combine Sign in with Slack (SIWS) user scopes with non-Sign in with Slack scopes in the same OAuth flow
62: Each set of scopes must be requested in a separate OAuth flow.
63: Include both your app's client ID, which is found in the App Management page, and a comma-separated list of scopes, such as: scope=incoming-webhook,commands. The full redirect URL will look something like this:
64: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook,commands&client_id=3336676.569200954261
65: The scope list requests scopes for your app's bot user. If you have specific need for a user token (for example, so that you can act on behalf of a user), provide a user_scope parameter with requested user scopes instead of, or in addition to, the scope parameter.
66: Also note that each installation can result in additive scopes. For example, if a user installs your app in a workspace where you request channels:history and then installs your app again where you request channels:read, both channels:history and channels:read will be assigned to the token. There is no way to remove scopes from an existing token without revoking it entirely.
67: When requesting scopes, you also need to tell Slack where to send your temporary authorization code afterward. Include a redirect_uri parameter in the URL above. The redirect_uri is where Slack will send the user back to, along with the temporary authorization code, once the user okays your app. The redirect_uri must use HTTPS. Alternatively, you can configure a Redirect URL in the App Management page under OAuth & Permissions. A Redirect URL must also use HTTPS.
68: When there are multiple Redirect URL values configured, the redirect_url parameter must be sent in both the Authorize and Access steps described below, and the parameter value must be the same for both steps — otherwise, you will encounter a bad_redirect_uri error:
69: Authorize: You direct the user to the corresponding /oauth/v2/authorize path (this can be done with a link or button, for example). Send the redirect_uri in this step.
70: Redirect: Slack redirects the user to what was specified as the redirect_uri in the previous step, and adds a verification code to that URL.
71: Access: Your server retrieves the verification code from the previous step and sends it to the oauth.v2.access API endpoint to exchange that code for an access token. If you sent a redirect_uri field in the first step, you must send that same field with the same value in this step.
72: If there are multiple Redirect URL values configured, but no redirect_uri parameter is sent, the OAuth flow will use the first Redirect URL listed on the App Management page. You can use the redirect_uri parameter in your oauth/v2/authorize redirect as mentioned above and configure a Redirect URL in the App Management page. Your redirect_uri must match or be a subdirectory of a Redirect URL configured under App Management. A Redirect URL can not contain an anchor (#).
73: REDIRECT_URL: https://example.com/path
74: GOOD redirect_uri: https://example.com/path
75: GOOD: https://example.com/path/subdir/other
76: BAD: http://example.com/bar
77: BAD: http://example.com/
78: BAD: http://example.com:8080/path
79: BAD: http://oauth.example.com:8080/path
80: BAD: http://example.org
81: The team parameter​
82: The optional team parameter tells Slack which workspace you'd like the user to authorize against. Treat team as a hint rather than a guarantee. Slack honors it when it can, and falls back to another workspace when it can't.
83: If you omit team entirely, Slack selects a compatible organization or workspace from the user's existing sessions, or asks them to sign in if they have none. Either way, the user can switch install targets from the authorization screen before approving.
84: Passing an organization ID (E0123456789) requests an org-level installation rather than a single-workspace one. When the app is already installed on individual workspaces in that org, upgrading to an org-level installation may require an Org Owner or Org Admin: other members are either directed to a workspace where they can install the app, or shown an error asking them to contact an admin.
85: How the team parameter is treated for an app not publicly distributed depends on whether it can be installed at the org-level:
86: SituationResult
87: Your app does not support org-wide installation.Your app can only be installed on the workspace that owns it. Slack asks the user to sign in to that workspace if they aren't already, so team can't send the installation anywhere else.
88: Your app is created inside an Enterprise org that supports org-wide installation.Your app can be installed on any workspace in the same org, and team can select among them. See the immediate table below for more info, noting that any fallback stays inside that org.
89: How the team parameter is treated for an app that can be installed on more than one workspace depends on the user's current session:
90: SituationResult
91: The user is already signed in to the workspace you named.They're taken straight there, and they authorize against that workspace.
92: The user is signed in to Slack, but not to the workspace you named.team is dropped without an error, and the user authorizes against a workspace they already have a session on. Your app isn't told that this happened, so confirm the result in the oauth.v2.access response, as described below.
93: The user isn't signed in anywhere.They're asked to sign in, and team is carried through that step. If they sign in to the workspace you named, team is honored. If they sign in to a different one, the behavior then follows the The user is signed in to Slack, but not to the workspace you named situation described above.
94: Both of the last two situations can end with the team parameter being dropped, so don't assume the value you sent is where the app ended up. The oauth.v2.access response is the source of truth:
95: For individual workspace installations, use the team.id field to see the workspace the app was installed on. The team property will be null for org-level installations where "is_enterprise_install": true.
96: For org-level installations, use the enterprise.id and is_enterprise_install fields.
97: Optional scopes​
98: Optional scopes allow you to mark certain permissions as optional during app configuration, giving users more control over what data your app can access while reducing installation abandonment.
99: You can designate scopes as optional in two ways: via the app settings or the app manifest.
100: App settings: In the app settings, uncheck the checkbox next to any scope you want to mark as optional.
101: App manifest: Add optional scopes to the bot_optional or user_optional fields within the oauth_config.scopes object. Optional scopes must also be listed in the corresponding bot or user fields.
102: JSON
103: YAML
104: "oauth_config": {
105: "scopes": {
106: "bot": [
107: "commands",
108: "chat:write",
109: "chat:write.public",
110: "metadata.message:read",
111: "links:read",
112: "assistant:write",
113: "im:history",
114: "reactions:write"
115: ],
116: "bot_optional": [
117: "chat:write"
118: ],
119: "user": [
120: "channels:history",
121: "reactions:read",
122: "reactions:write"
123: ],
124: "user_optional": [
125: "reactions:write"
126: ]
127: },
128: "redirect_urls": [
129: "https://example.com/slack/auth"
130: ],
131: "token_management_enabled": true
132: },
133: oauth_config:
134: scopes:
135: bot:
136: - commands
137: - chat:write
138: - chat:write.public
139: - metadata.message:read
140: - links:read
141: - assistant:write
142: - im:history
143: - reactions:write
144: bot_optional:
145: - chat:write
146: user:
147: - channels:history
148: - reactions:read
149: - reactions:write
150: user_optional:
151: - reactions:write
152: redirect_urls:
153: - https://example.com/slack/auth
154: token_management_enabled: true
155: 2. Wait for a user to approve your requested scopes​
156: Good news! Your app doesn't really have to do anything.
157: Prepare for the return of a user by listening for HTTP requests at whatever Redirect URL you specified.
158: Optional scopes give end users visibility and control over what data an app can access from their account. During installation, users are presented with the optional scopes the admin has pre-approved and can choose which ones to grant. Apps should respect users' scope selections and handle the absence of ungranted scopes gracefully. Refer to the Handling optional scopes in your app section below for guidance.
159: 3. Exchange a temporary authorization code for an access token​
160: If all goes well, a user goes through the Slack app installation and okays your app with all the scopes it requests. Then, Slack redirects the user back to your specified Redirect URL.
161: Parse the HTTP request that lands at your Redirect URL for a code field. That's your temporary authorization code, which expires after ten minutes. Check the state parameter if you sent one along with your initial user redirect. If it doesn't match what you sent, consider the authorization a forgery.
162: Now, you just need to exchange the code for an access token. You'll do this by calling the oauth.v2.access method as follows:
163: curl -F code=1234 -F client_id=3336676.569200954261 -F client_secret=ABCDEFGH https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.access
164: Once you complete your access call, Slack sends you an HTTP request response containing an access token. It looks something like this:
165: {
166: "ok": true,
167: "access_token": "xoxb-17653672481-19874698323-pdFZKVeTuE8sk7oOcBrzbqgy",
168: "token_type": "bot",
169: "scope": "commands,incoming-webhook",
170: "bot_user_id": "U0KRQLJ9H",
171: "app_id": "A0KRD7HC3",
172: "team": {
173: "name": "Slack Pickleball Team",
174: "id": "T9TK3CUKW"
175: },
176: "enterprise": {
177: "name": "slack-pickleball",
178: "id": "E12345678"
179: },
180: "authed_user": {
181: "id": "U1234",
182: "scope": "chat:write",
183: "access_token": "xoxp-1234",
184: "token_type": "user"
185: }
186: }
187: If you requested scopes for a user token, you'll find them with a user access token under the authed_user property.
188: One more suggestion: show the user a nice message once they are redirected and you successfully gain an access token — or, if there's been an error, report that error to the user. The reason the user is redirected back to your app at the end of OAuth is for transparency purposes: the user deserves to know the end of the story, whether your app was installed successfully or not.
189: Handling optional scopes in your app​
190: Apps must demonstrate usage of all scopes (both required and optional) and handle the absence of optional scopes gracefully. When a user doesn't grant an optional scope, your app should still function for features that don't require it.
191: Graceful degradation: Handle missing_scope API errors when optional scopes aren't granted.
192: Token scope storage: Store the granted scopes from the oauth.v2.access response to proactively show or hide features based on what the user has authorized.
193: Feature gating: Check token scopes before displaying functionality that requires optional permissions.
194: The user-centric flow: the oauth.v2.user.access method​
195: In addition to the standard workspace installation flow, Slack provides a dedicated flow for obtaining user-specific access tokens. To initiate a user-specific flow, redirect users to the v2_user authorization endpoint:
196: https://slack.com/oauth/v2_user/authorize?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&scope=chat:write,channels:history
197: Unlike the the standard v2/authorize endpoint, this flow focuses exclusively on the user's identity and personal permissions. After approval, Slack redirects back to your redirect_uri with a temporary code, just like the standard flow.
198: Exchanging the code with oauth.v2.user.access​
199: Once you have the temporary authorization code, you must exchange it using the oauth.v2.user.access API method. This method is compliant to the OAuth 2.0 RFC.
200: Comparing oauth.v2.access and oauth.v2.user.access endpoints​
201: The oauth.v2.access API method supports generating either a bot token or user token or both.
202: The oauth.v2.user.access API method generates a user token by default following the standard OAuth spec and works out-of-the-box with MCP authorization flows.
203: The oauth.v2.user.access endpoint should be used in scenarios where:
204: You only need user tokens, not bot tokens
205: You're building MCP integrations with desktop IDE clients like Cursor or Claude Code
206: Use the oauth.v2.access API method unless your client cannot support passing scope and scope_user in the same request.
207: Appending scopes​
208: When you initially send a user through the OAuth flow, you receive a token that has the set of scopes you requested. Any subsequent time(s) you send that same user through the OAuth flow, any new scopes you request will be added to that initial set.
209: For example, if you initially request channels:read and channels:write from a user, the initial token will only be scoped to channels:read channels:write (plus identify, which is automatically included in any OAuth grant for a classic app). If you send that same user through a second OAuth flow, this time requesting files:write, the resulting token will have the new scope added to the previous set: channels:read channels:write files:write identify.
210: This process can be repeated any number of times, and each scope you request is additive to the scopes you've already been awarded. It is not possible to downgrade an access token's scopes.
211: As you make Web API requests, a x-oauth-scopes HTTP header will be returned with every response indicating which scopes the calling token currently has:
212: x-oauth-scopes: identity.basic,reactions:read
213: Securing OAuth connections for enterprise customers​
214: When your app completes the OAuth flow with a Slack workspace, we strongly recommend verifying that the connecting user's account matches the enterprise customer's expected domain.
215: After exchanging the authorization code for an access token:
216: Call the team.info and users.info API methods to retrieve the workspace's domain configuration.
217: Compare the domain on your side against the workspace's domain to ensure the user is connecting with their corporate account rather than a personal one.
218: This prevents a scenario where an employee authenticates with a personal account and inadvertently links corporate Slack data to an unmanaged instance outside their organization's control.
219: Enterprise administrators expect that when they install your app on their workspace, employees will connect using corporate-managed accounts. Implementing this check at the end of your OAuth flow helps protect your enterprise customers' data and demonstrates that your integration meets the security expectations of organizations using Slack.
220: More about tokens​
221: Using tokens​
222: The best way to communicate your access tokens — also known as bearer tokens — to Slack is by presenting them in a request's Authorization HTTP header where the full value, including "Bearer", is case-sensitive. This approach is required when using application/json with a write method.
223: GET /api/conversations.list?limit=50
224: Authorization: Bearer xoxb-1234-abcdefgh
225: Alternatively, you may send the token as a POST body attribute of the application/x-www-form-urlencoded variety.
226: POST body:
227: POST /api/conversations.list
228: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
229: token=xoxb-1234-abcdefgh&limit=50
230: Revoking tokens​
231: OAuth tokens do not expire. If they are no longer needed, they can be revoked. Revocation of an OAuth token happens if a workspace owner fully uninstalls the app, a user individually removes their configurations, or the account of the user who initially authenticated the Slack app is deactivated.
232: API access tokens are revoked via the auth.revoke method. After that happens:
233: The bot token no longer works.
234: The bot user is removed from the workspace.
235: Slash commands associated with the bot token will be removed from the workspace if no user tokens for the same app exist and carry the commands scope.
236: Incoming webhooks that were installed and associated with the bot token will be removed.
237: If no user tokens for the same app exist, the app will appear to be uninstalled from the workspace.
238: Additionally, for Slack apps using granular permissions, you can exchange your access token for a refresh token and an expiring access token with token rotation.
239: Storing tokens securely​
240: Store your application's credentials and user tokens with care. Restrict Web API access to only IP addresses you trust by allowlisting specific IP addresses. Read up on best practices for security.
241: Errors​
242: Below are some errors you may encounter and reasons for encountering them:
243: bad_redirect_uri: Occurs when there are multiple redirect_url parameter values configured and they do not match.
244: invalid_scope: Occurs if requesting a non-existent scope or requesting a set of scopes that are in conflict with each other (e.g. SIWS user scopes cannot be combined with non-SIWS user scopes).
245: invalid_team_for_non_distributed_app: Occurs when attempting to install/authorize an undistributed Slack API app on a team where the app was not created.
246: scope_not_allowed_on_enterprise: Occurs when attempting to install an app in an Enterprise org containing scopes that are not org-compatible. See below for more details.
247: unapproved_scope: Occurs if attempting to install a published app for which the requested scopes aren't approved either because they're still in review for that app, or they weren't yet submitted for review by the app developer.
248: Non-Enterprise scopes​
249: The following is a list of scopes that are not org-compatible:
250: bot

43: Slack MCP server overview
44: With the Slack MCP server, your integrated apps can search channels, send messages, and perform other Slack actions through MCP clients. Workspace admins can approve and manage all MCP client integrations, keeping your Slack data safe. This guide discusses the MCP server offerings from Slack and how to develop with the Slack MCP server.
45: Slack MCP server features​
46: The Slack MCP server provides tools for searching through Slack, retrieving and sending messages, managing canvases, managing users, uploading files, and working with lists. Each of these tools provides useful functionality for interacting with Slack; combine them for comprehensive integrations that grasp your team's context and history.
47: Searching throughout Slack​
48: The MCP server can search for a variety of information found throughout a Slack workspace:
49: Messages and files — filter by date, user, and content type. Retrieve metadata and content.
50: Users in a workspace — filter by name (with partial name matching), email, and user ID. Retrieve user details and statuses.
51: Private and public channels — filter by channel name and description. Retrieve channel metadata.
52: List user channels — list the channels you're a member of, filterable by type (public, private, DMs, group DMs), name prefix, and workspace. Supports pagination and can return full details, names only, or IDs only. Archived channels are included by default.
53: Emoji — returns the list of custom emoji available in the workspace.
54: Retrieving and sending messages​
55: The MCP server can retrieve and send messages throughout a Slack workspace:
56: Send messages — send messages to any type of conversation in Slack.
57: Schedule messages — schedule a message to be sent to a conversation at a future time.
58: Draft messages — draft, format, and preview messages directly within AI clients.
59: Read channels — grab the complete message history of channels.
60: Read threads — grab complete message thread conversations.
61: Create a conversation/channel — creates a new Slack channel, group DM, or IM conversation on behalf of the authenticated user.
62: Add reactions — adds an emoji reaction to a Slack message on behalf of the authenticated user.
63: Get reactions — retrieve the emoji reactions on a Slack message.
64: Managing canvases​
65: The MCP server can interact and modify Slack canvases:
66: Create/update a canvas — create and share rich, formatted documents.
67: Read a canvas — export canvases as markdown files.
68: Managing users​
69: Fetch user info — access complete user profile info, including custom profile fields and statuses.
70: List channel members — retrieve a list of user IDs for members of a given Slack channel or conversation.
71: Managing files​
72: Upload files — upload files to Slack via a two-step process. The file isn't visible until the second step completes.
73: Call the slack_get_file_upload_url tool to get a signed upload URL and file ID, then POST your file bytes to that URL.
74: Call the slack_complete_file_upload tool with the file ID to finalize it, optionally sharing the file to a channel with a message.
75: Working with lists​
76: The MCP server can work with Slack lists, which hold structured tabular data with typed columns (text, date, select, user, and more):
77: Create and read lists — create lists with custom schemas and read their contents.
78: Update lists and records — update list metadata and columns, and add or update individual records (rows). Columns are addressed by display name or internal key. Column types include select/multi_select with color-coded options.
79: Example use cases​
80: There are many possibilities with the Slack MCP server. Here are just a few ideas:
81: Create an AI assistant in Slack that can search through your team's Slack history to answer questions, find past decisions, and provide context for current projects.
82: Bring content from outside Slack into Slack via messages and canvases for discussion with coworkers.
83: Bring content from Slack to AI agents, providing them full context of projects that exist across multiple products.
84: Rate limits​
85: Like all Slack Web API methods, the Slack MCP server is subject to rate limits. Limits are enforced per tool or action type. Whether an action is performed via an MCP tool or directly through Slack Web API methods, the same rate limits apply. Here is the full list of MCP tools and their associated rate limit:
86: MCP ToolRate Limit
87: Search messages & filesSpecial rate limits apply; consult method page documentation
88: Read filesTier 4: 100+ per minute
89: Search emojiTier 2: 20+ per minute
90: Search usersTier 2: 20+ per minute
91: Search channelsTier 2: 20+ per minute
92: Send messageSpecial rate limits apply; consult method page documentation
93: Schedule messageTier 3: 50+ per minute
94: Read a channelTier 3: 50+ per minute
95: Read a threadTier 3: 50+ per minute
96: Create conversation/channelTier 2: 20+ per minute
97: Add reactionsTier 3: 50+ per minute
98: Get reactionsTier 3: 50+ per minute
99: Create a canvasTier 2: 20+ per minute
100: Update a canvasTier 3: 50+ per minute
101: Read a canvasTier 3: 50+ per minute / Tier 4: 100+ per minute
102: Read a user profileTier 4: 100+ per minute
103: List channel membersTier 4: 100+ per minute
104: List user channelsTier 2: 20+ per minute
105: Upload a fileTier 4: 100+ per minute
106: Create/read/update a listTier 2: 20+ per minute / Tier 3: 50+ per minute
107: Transport protocol and endpoint​
108: Slack supports JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP. All requests should be sent to:
109: https://mcp.slack.com/mcp
110: We do not support SSE-based connections or Dynamic Client Registration at this time.
111: App Identity​
112: MCP clients must be backed by a registered Slack app with a fixed app ID and hardcode that app ID. This allows Slack to:
113: Let admins manage and approve your app/MCP client app using standard Slack app approval process.
114: Associate requests with your app for logging, rate limits, and access control.
115: Provide better support and visibility into usage.
116: If you're already using a Slack app for your integration, you can reuse it for MCP access.
117: Only directory-published apps or internal apps may use MCP.
118: Security concerns​
119: When using the Slack MCP server, please be mindful about connecting to or utilizing other MCP servers at the same time. Different servers may have their own security, stability, and usage characteristics, so think carefully before mixing them together. Use judgment when evaluating what to connect and share across environments. Using these clients means giving them access to your Slack data so you can use it as context while interacting with those apps.
120: Audit MCP activity with the associated audit logs.
121: Only apps published in the Slack Marketplace and internal apps can use MCP at this time; unlisted apps are prohibited from using MCP.
122: IP allowlist​
123: If your app has allowed IP address ranges configured, requests to the Slack MCP server are subject to the same restrictions. API calls originating from IP addresses not on your allowlist will be rejected. Ensure that the IP addresses your MCP client uses are included in your app's allowed list.
124: Authentication and Token Handling​
125: Slack supports confidential OAuth for MCP clients. You'll need to use your app's client_id and client_secret for Slack OAuth.
126: If your MCP client supports OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) per MCP spec, you can rely on that. Users go through OAuth consent and authorize the app. You can initiate this OAuth request from your UX following standard MCP metadata discovery files:
127: https://mcp.slack.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
128: https://mcp.slack.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
129: OAuth URL and endpoints​
130: Authorization endpoint for Slack user tokens: https://slack.com/oauth/v2_user/authorize
131: Token endpoint for Slack user tokens: https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.user.access (method docs here)
132: If you also want to generate bot tokens (for in-Slack experience), follow instructions here.
133: OAuth scopes needed on user token for different tools​
134: ToolScopes needed
135: Search messages/channelssearch:read.public, search:read.private, search:read.mpim, search:read.im
136: Search filessearch:read.files
137: Read filesfiles:read
138: Search emojiemoji:read
139: Search userssearch:read.users
140: Send messagechat:write
141: Schedule messagechat:write
142: Read a channel/threadchannels:history, groups:history, mpim:history, im:history
143: Create conversation/channelchannels:write for public channels, groups:write for private channels, im:write for direct messages, mpim:write for multi-party DMs
144: Add reactionsreactions:write
145: Get reactionsreactions:read
146: Canvas create/updatecanvases:read, canvases:write
147: User profile/emailusers:read, users:read.email
148: List channel memberschannels:read for public channels, groups:read for private channels, mpim:read for multi-party DMs
149: List user channelschannels:read, groups:read, im:read, mpim:read
150: Listslists:read, lists:write
151: Upload a filefiles:write
152: Consider using PKCE
153: Looking to use desktop clients? PKCE support is now available! Read more here.
154: Using the Slack MCP server with partner apps​
155: If you'd rather not build a Slack app, you can use the Slack MCP server through a partner-built client, no coding needed. For the current list of partner apps and how to connect them, see the Guide to MCP in Slack in the Slack Help Center.
156: Related content​
157: ✨ Check out our documentation on Developing agents here.
158: ✨ To search Slack data without connecting it to an AI, see documentation for the Real Time Search API here. The Real Time Search (RTS) API offers access to Slack data via API call.

697: Frequently asked questions
698: How does Slack protect the security of my data when using AI features?
699: AI in Slack runs in Slack’s trusted infrastructure, and upholds the security practices and compliance standards that customers expect from Slack itself. Slack does not share customer data with large language model (LLM) providers and does not use customer data to train LLMs. Visit our Help Centre for more details.
700: Our large language models are hosted directly within Slack’s AWS virtual private cloud, ensuring that your data remains in-house.
701: How can I pay for Slack? Can I pay by credit card, or can you invoice me?
702: You can use a credit card to pay for any subscription. If you choose to pay annually, you may be eligible to be invoiced and pay by ACH or bank transfer. Visit our Help Centre for more details, or contact us to start the process.
703: If you choose to pay by credit card, you’ll see the first credit card charge from Slack on the day that you purchase a paid subscription. Here are some other times when you’ll see charges:
704: On your monthly renewal date if you pay monthly.
705: On your annual renewal date if you pay annually.
706: On the last day of the month if you pay annually and there’s an outstanding balance for adding new members.
707: You can change billing cycles or switch to invoicing at any time. Learn more about managing billing details here.
708: Our team has several accounts which are not being actively used, but which we don’t want to disable. Do we still have to pay for them?
709: At Slack, we believe that you should only be billed for what you use. Members who take an action in Slack at any time within a 28-day period will be considered active for billing purposes. If someone that you’ve already paid for becomes inactive, we’ll add a prorated credit to your account for the unused time.
710: We want to add new users to our workspace. How will that be billed?
711: You’ll be charged a prorated amount for new team members for the remainder of the current billing period. For a detailed overview of our billing model and how your subscription term affects when you will be billed, visit the Help Centre.
712: Which subscription do I need to use Slackbot?
713: Soon, Slack users across every subscription will be able to try Slackbot. Demand has been extraordinary, and we are opening access so that every team can experience an agent built directly into their workflow. Slack Free and Pro users will have the chance to explore Slackbot’s capabilities first-hand through a limited trial experience. Ongoing Slackbot access will continue to be available to Business+ and Enterprise+ customers, and coming soon, Salesforce CRM customers who connect their accounts to Slack will also receive ongoing access to Slackbot!
714: Do you offer discounts for charities/not-for-profit organisations or educational institutions?
715: We do! Slack wants to support people doing good in the world, which is why we offer special discount pricing for qualified charities and educational institutions.
716: How can I get more access to Slackbot?
717: Existing Salesforce customers on Slack Free and Pro invoice subscriptions can get access to Slackbot, and Slack Business+ customers on invoice subscriptions can unlock higher message limits by purchasing Flex Credits through Salesforce.
718: Please get in touch with your sales executive to buy Flex Credits.

77: Twilio API overview
78: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
79: The Twilio APIs are organized around REST. Behind these APIs is a software layer connecting and optimizing communications networks around the world. With the Twilio APIs, you can build applications that help your users send messages, make phone calls, look up phone numbers, and more.
80: In Twilio's ecosystem, each product corresponds to an API. For example, Twilio Messaging corresponds to the Messaging API. Although each API has its own unique features, they all share a common set of principles and practices. This consistency lets you work with different Twilio APIs in a similar way. You can use the APIs directly over HTTPS or through Twilio SDKs available for several programming languages.
81: This section covers how to work with the Twilio APIs:
82: Make requests to the Twilio APIs, including authenticating your requests, choosing the right content type, and handling webhooks.

75: API keys overview
76: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
77: API keys are the preferred way to authenticate with Twilio's REST APIs. With API keys, you control which users and applications have access to your Twilio Account's API resources, and you can revoke access at your discretion.
78: If your Twilio application uses one of the client-side SDKs, then you need to use API keys to create Access Tokens.
79: (information)
80: Info
81: Twilio API credentials are a Region-specific resource. If your Account uses Twilio Regions, refer to Manage Regional API Credentials.
82: When using the Twilio CLI to create regional profiles, you must specify both --region and --edge flags together. See Regional CLI usage for details.
83: Why you should use API keys
84: why-you-should-use-api-keys page anchor
85: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
86: API keys are a powerful and flexible way to manage access to Twilio resources.
87: Create individual API keys for specific purposes and individuals. You have complete control of the lifecycle of the API credentials for your Twilio Account. For example, you can issue separate API keys to different developers or subsystems within your application. If a key is compromised or no longer used, revoke it to prevent unauthorized access.
88: You can further reduce security risks by using Restricted API keys to provide minimum and specific levels of access.
89: Types of API keys
90: types-of-api-keys page anchor
91: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
92: (information)
93: Best practices for working with API keys
94: For guidance on securing your API credentials and configuring your environment:
95: Learn how to safely store your API keys in environment variables in the How to Set Environment Variables blog post(link takes you to an external page).
96: Learn more about general API security best practices in the Guide to Basic API Security Best Practices blog post(link takes you to an external page).
97: The API key types are Main, Standard, and Restricted (Key resource v1 only). The following table describes each type:
98: Key typeAccess permissionsCreate in ConsoleCreate with REST API
99: MainFull access to all Twilio API resources. Equivalent to using your Account SID and Auth Token for API requests.YesNo
100: StandardAccess to all Twilio API resources, except for Accounts (/Accounts) or Keys (/Accounts/{SID}/Keys, /v1/Keys) resources.YesYes
101: RestrictedCustomized, fine-grained access to specific Twilio API resources. Learn more about Restricted API keys.YesYes (v1 only)

106: Create and manage API keys using the REST API.
107: Create and manage API Keys using CLI profiles for regional authentication.
108: Create Access Tokens if you plan on using a client-side SDK with Twilio. Learn more about Access Tokens.
109: Need some help?
110: We all do sometimes; code is hard. Get help now from our support team(link takes you to an external page), or lean on the wisdom of the crowd by browsing the Twilio tag(link takes you to an external page) on Stack Overflow.

113: Get started with your Twilio free trial account
114: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
115: You can sign up for a Twilio free trial account without a credit card. After you sign up, explore the solutions for your use case in the Twilio Console.
116: What you get with your Twilio trial account
117: what-you-get-with-your-twilio-trial-account page anchor
118: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
119: Your trial includes product-specific free units — such as 100 SMS messages, 100 WhatsApp messages, 3,000 emails, and 75 voice minutes — instead of a shared dollar balance. Trial accounts expire after 30 days.
120: You can track your consumption at any time using the Free units tracker in the Console. Click it to see a summary of your current usage and the percentage of units remaining.
121: For full details on free units, restrictions, and supported countries, see Twilio trial account.
122: Sign up for your Twilio trial account
123: sign-up-for-your-twilio-trial-account page anchor
124: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
125: Sign up for your Twilio account(link takes you to an external page).
126: The sign-up process includes the following steps:
127: Verify your email address.
128: Verify your personal phone number.
129: Customize your account by providing information about your project.
130: After signing up, the Twilio Console(link takes you to an external page) opens so you can find your Twilio credentials, check your usage, and use Twilio products.
131: Explore Twilio from your Console home page
132: explore-twilio-from-your-console-home-page page anchor
133: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
134: After signing up, your Console home page shows options based on the product you selected during signup.
135: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
136: From the Twilio Console home page(link takes you to an external page), you can do the following:
137: Continue building with your selected product.
138: View your Account SID and Auth Token for API authentication.
139: Navigate to other Twilio products using the sidebar.
140: Click Upgrade when you're ready to move to a paid account.
141: In the legacy Console, you can still explore products from your Console home page(link takes you to an external page). The setup steps are similar, but URLs and navigation paths differ from the Twilio Console steps.
142: (information)
143: Try out products for faster setup
144: The fastest way to get started is to use the Try out flows directly from the Console home page. Each product trial walks you through setup in minutes and shows you real API requests and responses as you build:
145: Try out SMS Messaging
146: Try out Voice
147: Try out Email
148: Try out WhatsApp
149: Work with phone numbers
150: work-with-phone-numbers page anchor
151: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
152: If you're using SMS or Voice, you'll be working with phone numbers.
153: Use phone numbers during your trial
154: use-phone-numbers-during-your-trial page anchor
155: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
156: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
157: In the Twilio Console, product trials guide you through the trial setup for SMS, Voice, WhatsApp, and Email. For SMS, Voice, and WhatsApp trials, the Try out flow provides the trial resources needed to send messages or make calls. You don't choose a trial phone number during sign-up.
158: To start with SMS, Voice, or WhatsApp, use one of the product trial flows:
159: Try out SMS Messaging
160: Try out Voice
161: Try out WhatsApp Messaging
162: In the legacy Console, go to the Console home page(link takes you to an external page) and click Get phone number. If you don't see this option, you can purchase a number from the Buy a number(link takes you to an external page) page using your preloaded trial balance.
163: Learn about phone number types
164: learn-about-phone-number-types page anchor
165: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
166: Twilio offers the following types of phone numbers for purchase:
167: Local
168: Mobile
169: Toll-free
170: National
171: For an overview of the capabilities of each type, see Twilio Phone Number Types and Their Capabilities(link takes you to an external page) in the Twilio Help Center.
172: Understand phone number regulatory requirements
173: understand-phone-number-regulatory-requirements page anchor
174: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
175: Countries have different regulatory requirements for each type of number and method of communication.
176: Learn about country-specific guidelines(link takes you to an external page) for phone numbers, SMS, Voice, porting, and short codes.
177: For messaging to the US and Canada, see Differences between long codes (A2P 10DLC), short codes (paid accounts only), and toll-free numbers(link takes you to an external page) in the Twilio Help Center.
178: Toll-free verification (US and Canada only)
179: toll-free-verification-us-and-canada-only page anchor
180: Toll-free numbers must be verified before you can use them to send messages to the United States or Canada. Toll-free verification is an industry-wide regulatory requirement to help protect message recipients. Toll-free verification is free to complete.
181: If your trial setup includes a verified toll-free number, you can message up to five pre-designated phone numbers across the mobile network. Legacy Console trial users can also message the Twilio Virtual Phone.
182: Learn more about toll-free verification and see Trial Limits and US Toll-Free Number Restrictions(link takes you to an external page) in the Twilio Help Center.
183: A2P 10DLC (US only)
184: a2p-10dlc-us-only page anchor
185: (warning)
186: Requires a paid account
187: To complete A2P 10DLC registration, you must have a paid Twilio account.
188: US and Canadian 10-digit long code (10DLC) phone numbers must be registered before you can use them to send messages from your application to US-based recipients. A2P (Application-to-Person) 10DLC is the standard enforced by telecom carriers in the United States to ensure that SMS traffic through long code phone numbers to US recipients is verified and consensual.
189: Regulatory compliance bundles (worldwide)
190: regulatory-compliance-bundles-worldwide page anchor
191: Regulatory compliance (RC) bundles help you organize and submit the information and documentation you need to meet regulatory requirements for individual countries.
192: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
193: In the Twilio Console(link takes you to an external page), you can create RC bundles from Phone numbers > Regulatory compliance > Bundles. You can also use the Regulatory Compliance API.
194: In the legacy Console, you can create RC bundles from the Regulatory Compliance Bundles(link takes you to an external page) page or by using the Regulatory Compliance API.
195: For detailed phone number requirements for each country, see Phone Number Regulations Guidelines(link takes you to an external page).
196: Use additional verified recipients
197: use-additional-verified-recipients page anchor
198: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
199: You can call or message only verified recipients from a trial account. Twilio removes this security restriction when you upgrade your account.
200: When you signed up, you verified a personal phone number. While you have a trial account, you must verify each non-Twilio phone number that you want to use to do the following:
201: Receive SMS or MMS messages from Twilio numbers.
202: Receive phone calls from Twilio numbers.
203: Call Twilio numbers.
204: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
205: To verify additional recipient phone numbers, use the Try out page for the product you're testing, then add and verify recipients from that page.
206: Try out SMS Messaging
207: Try out Voice
208: Try out WhatsApp Messaging
209: In the legacy Console, go to the Verified Caller IDs(link takes you to an external page) page to verify additional numbers for your trial.
210: (warning)
211: Warning
212: You must select SMS as the verification method and have access to the device to receive the text with your verification code.
213: Test SMS with the Twilio Virtual Phone in the legacy Console
214: test-sms-with-the-twilio-virtual-phone-in-the-legacy-console page anchor
215: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
216: The Twilio Virtual Phone is available in the legacy Console trial experience. You can use it to test sending and receiving messages. The Virtual Phone is a simulated mobile device that uses a phone number owned by Twilio.
217: To send your first SMS message using the Twilio Virtual Phone in the legacy Console, follow our SMS developer quickstart or SMS no-code quickstart. To test SMS in Twilio Console, use Try out SMS Messaging.
218: Format phone numbers
219: format-phone-numbers page anchor
220: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
221: When your application sends messages or makes phone calls, the phone numbers must be in E.164 format. E.164 is an international standard for phone number formatting that includes the country code and omits any leading zeros or special characters.
222: For more information, see What is E.164? in the Twilio glossary.
223: Learn how Voice uses TwiML
224: learn-how-voice-uses-twiml page anchor
225: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
226: TwiML is Twilio's XML-based instruction language for controlling call behavior. For example, TwiML can specify how to read text aloud, gather speech or keypad input, play audio, route a call, or end a call. To see TwiML in action during your trial, try Twilio Voice. For more information, see Voice TwiML docs.
227: Monitor your trial activity
228: monitor-your-trial-activity page anchor
229: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
230: As you build, you can monitor your trial activity and consumption:
231: Free units tracker: Shows your current usage and remaining units for each product. Available from the Console home page or within each product's trial page.
232: Logs: View detailed logs for SMS, Voice, Email, and WhatsApp activity. View logs from each product's page in the Console to see delivery status, errors, and requests/responses.
233: Use your Twilio credentials for the API
234: use-your-twilio-credentials-for-the-api page anchor
235: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
236: Your Twilio trial account uses the same account credentials (Account SID and Auth Token) that you use after you upgrade. There are no separate trial-only credentials. Trial restrictions are enforced by your account status, not by different credentials.
237: You can view your credentials directly from your Console home page to start using the API immediately, or access them from the API Keys & Tokens page to manage additional API keys.
238: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
239: View your Account SID and Auth Token on the Console home page(link takes you to an external page).
240: Manage credentials and create API keys from the API Keys & Tokens(link takes you to an external page) page.
241: In the legacy Console, go to the API Keys & Tokens(link takes you to an external page) page to manage your credentials and API keys.
242: Send messages internationally
243: send-messages-internationally page anchor
244: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
245: During your trial, SMS messages and voice calls are restricted to your sign-up country, determined by the phone number you used during registration.
246: After you upgrade your account, you can send messages to other countries and regions when you meet the following general conditions:
247: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
248: Your number is SMS-enabled and not restricted to sending or receiving messages and calls from only local numbers. Check your phone number's capabilities on the Active Numbers(link takes you to an external page) page in the Console.
249: The target country you're sending messages to is enabled in your Messaging Geographic Permissions(link takes you to an external page).
250: You own the phone numbers you're sending to.
251: If you're using the legacy Console, you can send messages to other countries and regions from your trial account when your verified trial number is SMS-enabled, the target country is enabled in Messaging Geographic Permissions(link takes you to an external page), and you own and have verified the destination phone numbers. See Verified Caller IDs(link takes you to an external page) in the legacy Console.
252: For a list of countries where trials are available, see Supported countries.
253: Trial account restrictions and limitations
254: trial-account-restrictions-and-limitations page anchor
255: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
256: Trial accounts expire after 30 days and include product-specific free units instead of a dollar balance.
257: Restrictions include:
258: 30-day expiration: Trial ends 30 days after sign-up. Upgrade before expiration to continue building.
259: Geographic restrictions: SMS and voice are limited to your sign-up country. Email is restricted to your sign-up email address.
260: Verified recipients: You can only send to verified phone numbers (up to 5 per account). Your sign-up number is automatically verified.
261: Pre-defined content: You must use Twilio-provided templates. Custom message bodies, email content, and WhatsApp templates aren't available during trial.
262: Trial numbers: Product trials can use Twilio-provided trial phone numbers. You don't choose these numbers during the Twilio Console trial experience, and trial numbers can vary by product and by recipient. After upgrading, you use numbers you've purchased.
263: For the full list of restrictions and product-specific limitations, see Trial restrictions.
264: Upgrade your account
265: upgrade-your-account page anchor
266: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
267: When your project is ready for production or you need more resources than a trial account allows, upgrade to a paid account.
268: Twilio ConsoleLegacy Console
269: To get started, click the Trial banner or Upgrade your account in the Console. You can also search for Upgrade in the Console search bar. You'll create a profile, add your address, load a starting balance, and add payment details.
270: In the legacy Console, click Upgrade at the top of the page. You'll create a profile, add your address, load a starting balance, and add payment details.
271: When you upgrade, you automatically receive a fresh set of post-upgrade free units for eligible products, regardless of what you used during your trial. Twilio deducts these units before charging any usage to your account.
272: (information)
273: Info
274: After you upgrade, Twilio refreshes free units for eligible products. These post-upgrade free units help you continue building your proof of concept into a production application, or try another Twilio product without additional upfront cost.
275: For full details on upgrade benefits, post-upgrade free unit allocations, and trial restrictions, see Twilio trial account.
276: Take the next steps
277: take-the-next-steps page anchor
278: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback

164: Twilio MCP Monorepo
165: This is a monorepo for the Model Context Protocol server that exposes all of Twilio APIs.
166: What is MCP?
167: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a protocol for exchanging model context information between AI tools and services. This implementation allows you to expose Twilio's APIs to AI assistants and other tools that support the MCP protocol.
168: Packages
169: This monorepo contains two main packages:
170: mcp - MCP Server for all of Twilio's Public API
171: openapi-mcp-server - An MCP server that serves the given OpenAPI spec
172: Each package has its own comprehensive README with detailed documentation:
173: MCP Package Documentation
174: OpenAPI MCP Server Documentation
175: Quick Start
176: The easiest way to get started is by using npx:
177: {
178: "mcpServers": {
179: "twilio": {
180: "command": "npx",
181: "args": [
182: "-y",
183: "@twilio-alpha/mcp",
184: "YOUR_ACCOUNT_SID/YOUR_API_KEY:YOUR_API_SECRET"
185: ]
186: }
187: }
188: }
189: Visit Twilio API Keys docs for information on how to find/create your API Key and Secret.
190: Security Recommendations
191: To guard against injection attacks that may allow untrusted systems access to your Twilio data, the ETI team advises users of Twilio MCP servers to avoid installing or running any community MCP servers alongside our official ones. Doing so helps ensure that only trusted MCP servers have access to tools interacting with your Twilio account, reducing the risk of unauthorized data access.
192: Basic Configuration Options
193: Both packages accept configuration parameters. Here's a brief overview:
194: MCP Server: Use --services and --tags to filter which APIs to expose
195: OpenAPI MCP Server: Use --apiPath to specify OpenAPI spec files location
196: For complete configuration details, refer to the package-specific documentation linked above.
197: Development
198: # Run tests
199: npm test
200: # Run linting
201: npm run lint
202: # Fix linting issues
203: npm run lint:fix
204: Troubleshooting Common Issues
205: Context Size Limitations: Due to LLM context limits, load specific APIs using --services or --tags
206: Authentication Issues: Verify your Twilio API credentials format and permissions
207: API Versioning: Check you're using the correct API version (v1, v2, v3) for your needs
208: For detailed troubleshooting guidance, see the package-specific documentation.

210: Contributions are welcome! Please feel free to submit a Pull Request.

211: About Cliq REST API
212: REST is a kind of web-service architecture used for communication between two applications. REST API is
213: organized around HTTP protocols, making it simple to use.
214: API Root Endpoint
215: API Root End Point
216: https://cliq.zoho.com
217: Cliq API is standardized around REST, allowing you to perform read and write operations that you do with
218: our
219: web client.
220: The relative path prefix /v2/ means that we are currently using version 2 of our API.
221: This API follows HTTP rules, identifies Cliq users using OAuth and provides response as a JSON Object.
222: Every resource URL is recognised as a resource identifier. The URL of each resource can be obtained by
223: accessing the API Root Endpoint.
224: Networks
225: API Root Endpoint for Networks
226: https://cliq.zoho.com/network/{NETWORK_UNIQUE_NAME}
227: https://cliq.zoho.com/network/{NETWORK_ID}
228: Cliq network is a dedicated space for collaborating with external business stakeholders such as partners, vendors, agencies, consultants, volunteers, and more. It equips you with an extensive set of configurable permissions to facilitate controlled, secure, and full-fledged external collaboration.
229: In the case of networks, the API Root endpoint differs.
230: All the network endpoints should have the prefix as /network/{NETWORK_UNIQUE_NAME} or /network/{NETWORK_ID}
231: For example , the API Root endpoints to call information from a Cliq network named 'Zylker Clients' would be :
232: https://cliq.zoho.com/network/zylkerclients
233: zylkerclients is the unique name of the network.
234: Multiple data centers
235: Zoho Cliq is hosted at multiple data centers, and therefore available on different domains.
236: There are 6 different domains for Zoho Cliq's APIs, so you can use the one that is applicable to you.
237: Data centerDomainBase API URI
238: United States.comhttps://cliq.zoho.com/
239: Europe.euhttps://cliq.zoho.eu/
240: India.inhttps://cliq.zoho.in/
241: Australia.auhttps://cliq.zoho.com.au/
242: China.cnhttps://cliq.zoho.com.cn/
243: Japan.jphttps://cliq.zoho.jp/
244: Saudi Arabia.sahttps://cliq.zoho.sa
245: United Kingdom.ukhttps://cliq.zoho.uk
246: Canada.zohocloud.cahttps://cliq.zohocloud.ca
247: The APIs on this page are for organizations hosted on the .com domain. If your organization is on a
248: different domain, replace ".com" with the appropriate domain for the API endpoints on this page
249: before using them
250: Note: You can find out which domain you're accessing Zoho Cliq by checking the URL while
251: accessing Zoho Cliq
252: Authentication
253: Zoho Cliq's Rest API's follows the OAuth 2.0 protocol to authorize and authenticate requests. Each API
254: request
255: must include an OAuth token in order to receive a success response. All API requests must be made over
256: HTTPS.
257: Calls made over plain HTTP and using API without authentication will also fail.
258: Note: You must use domain specific Zoho Cliq URL to generate and refresh tokens.
259: OAuth Token Generation
260: The steps to generate an OAuth token are as folllows:
261: Generate Client ID and Client Secret
262: Authorization by generating the grant token
263: Generating Access and Refresh Token
264: Generate Access Token from Refresh Token
265: Step 1: Generate Client ID and Client Secret
266: Register your application as a new client by accessing this website:
267: https://accounts.zoho.com/developerconsole
268: Note: Make sure to use domain specific Zoho Accounts URL while registering
269: 1.Click on Add Client IDand give the following :
270: Client Name
271: Client Domain
272: Authorized redirect URIs
273: 2.Click Create.
274: Upon providing the necessary details for registering, you will be given a set of OAuth credentials known
275: as the
276: client id and client secret exclusive for your application. These credentials
277: will be
278: known to both Zoho and your application.
279: Sample request to generate grant token
280: Step 2: Authorization by generating grant token
281: Request URL
282: GET oauth/v2/auth
283: Host: https://accounts.zoho.com
284: Query String:
285: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/auth?scope=ZohoCliq.Channels.CREATE,ZohoCliq.Channels.READ,ZohoCliq.Channels.UPDATE,ZohoCliq.Channels.DELETE&client_id=1000.0SRSZSY37WMZ69405H3K3TMYI2239V&state=5466400890088961855&response_type=code&redirect_uri=http://application_name.com/&access_type=offline
286: Redirect the user to the authorization URL, authorization will be done when the user grants access in the
287: "user
288: consent" page. The authorization URL is: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/auth and below
289: are the
290: mandatory case sensitive parameters to be passed with the authorization URL.
291: Sample response on generating grant token
292: http://accounts.zoho.com/oauth2callback?state=5466400890088961855&code=1000.dd7e47321d48b8a7e312e3d6eb1a9bb8.b6c07ac766ec11da98bf6a261e24dca4
293: ParameterDescription
294: scopeThe scope required for your extension.
295: The scopes vary for each endpoint. Hence, Refer to the APIs and identify the necessary scopes based on your use case.
296: Example : ZohoCliq.Messages.READ
297: client_idClient id obtained during client registration.
298: stateA generated value that correlates the callback with its associated authorization request.
299: response_type"code"
300: redirect_uriThe redirect URL mentioned during client registration.
301: access_typeAccess type will be either online or offline.
302: Sample request to generate access token
303: Step 3: Generating Access and Refresh Token
304: Request URL
305: POST oauth/v2/token
306: Host: https://accounts.zoho.com
307: Query String:
308: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token?code=1000.dd7e47321d48b8a7e312e3d6eb1a9bb8.b6c07ac766ec11da98bf6a261e24dca4&grant_type=authorization_code&scope=ZohoCliq.Channels.CREATE,ZohoCliq.Channels.READ,ZohoCliq.Channels.UPDATE,ZohoCliq.Channels.DELETE&client_id=1000.0SRSZSY37WMZ69405H3K3TMYI2239V&client_secret=39c689de68c712fa5f1f06c3b1319ab98f59fa921b&redirect_uri=http://application_name.com/
309: Sample response on generating the access token
310: {
311: "access_token": "1000.70d737e7cc1d8869123f796363f55345.830d0dc7ea80c404ace4a261d1b710d4",
312: "refresh_token": "1000.8ecd474019e31d52d2f94aad659c5cb7.4638677ebc14f2f2ee410b6dfb6cebdc",
313: "token_type": "Bearer",
314: "expires_in": 3600000
315: }
316: Example for using the access token
317: Request URL
318: GET
319: https://cliq.zoho.com/api/v2/channels
320: Request Header:
321: Authorization: Zoho-oauthtoken dd7e47321d48b8a7e312e3d6eb1a9bb8.b6c07ac766ec11da98bf6a261e24dca4
322: The value for code parameter obtained in the response of Step 2 should be used to generate
323: the
324: access and refresh token.
325: Make a POST request to the following URL:
326: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token
327: along with the below given parameters.
328: ParameterDescription
329: codeAuthorization code obtained during grant token generation.
330: client_idClient id obtained during client registration.
331: client_secretClient secret obtained during client registration.
332: redirect_uriRedirect uri mentioned during client registration.
333: grant_typeauthorization_code
334: scopeSpecify the scope allowed for your extension.
335: stateA generated value that correlates the callback with its associated authorization request.Has
336: to be
337: maintained the same during the entire process for authenticity.
338: On making a successful request along with the authorization code, Zoho will issue a response to your
339: application with the following information.
340: expires_in - Time in milliseconds that the token remains valid.
341: token_type - Type of token. It is bearer in this case.
342: access_token - Access token for the user. This token can be used for the final API calls and will be
343: valid
344: only for an hour.
345: refresh_token - Refresh token to use when the token has timed out. This token is permanent and can
346: be used
347: multiple times (limit - 20) to refresh the app and get a new access token.
348: Example for generating the access token using refresh token
349: Step 4: Generating the access token from refresh token
350: Request URL
351: POST oauth/v2/token
352: Host: https://accounts.zoho.com
353: Query String :
354: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token?refresh_token=1000.dd7e47321d48b8a7e312e3d6eb1a9bb8.b6c07ac766ec11da98bf6a261e24dca4&grant_type=refresh_token&scope=ZohoCliq.Channels.CREATE,ZohoCliq.Channels.READ,ZohoCliq.Channels.UPDATE,ZohoCliq.Channels.DELETE&client_id=1000.0SRSZSY37WMZ69405H3K3TMYI2239V&client_secret=39c689de68c712fa5f1f06c3b1319ab98f59fa921b&redirect_uri=http://application_name.com/
355: You can request for a refresh token to be generated along with the access token. To request for a
356: refresh
357: token, add access_type=offline in the request for generating the grant token. (Refer Step
358: 2).
359: The refresh token will always be generated by giving the parameters prompt=consent
360: In most general cases the access tokens expire in one hour. Until then, the access token has unlimited
361: usage.
362: Once the access token expires the refresh token can be used to generate a new access token.
363: Make a POST request to https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token along with the
364: below
365: given parameters
366: ParameterDescription
367: client_idClient id obtained during client registration.
368: client_secretClient secret obtained during client registration.
369: redirect_uriRedirect uri mentioned during client registration.
370: grant_typerefresh_token
371: refresh_tokenThe refresh token obtained during access token generation.(Step 3)
372: scopeSpecify the scope allowed for your extension.
373: Sample request using the OAuth token
374: Sample request using the OAuth token
375: Request Header:
376: Authorization:Zoho-oauthtoken dd7e47321d48b8a7e312e3d6eb1a9bb8.b6c07ac766ec11da98bf
377: Content-Type: application/json
378: Request URL
379: GET
380: https://cliq.zoho.com/api/v2/channels
381: The access token should be passed as a header when you call any Cliq REST API. Please note that the
382: access
383: token can be passed only as a request header and not as a request parameter.
384: The list of mandatory headers are:
385: Header NameHeader Value
386: AuthorizationZoho-oauthtoken {{access token}}
387: contentTypeapplication/json
388: Revoking the Refresh Token
389: Revoking the Refresh Token
390: Request URL
391: POST oauth/v2/token/revoke
392: Host: https://accounts.zoho.com
393: Query String :
394: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token/revoke?token=1000.dd7e47321d48b8a7e312e3d6eb1a9bb8.b6c07ac766ec11da98bf6a261e24dca4

396: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token/revoke with the below given parameter
397: OpenAPI Specification (OAS) for Zoho Cliq APIs
398: An OpenAPI Specification (OAS) is a standardized method for describing RESTful APIs. It outlines the API's structure, authentication methods, endpoints, and request and response formats in either JSON or YAML. You can download the OpenAPI specification file below, which can be used to interact with various API elements.
399: Why Use the OpenAPI Specification?
400: The OpenAPI Specification is designed to provide the following:
401: API Endpoints: It specifies the request URL and HTTP methods, detailing optional and mandatory parameters for making API calls. Additionally, it lists the response formats for all possible HTTP response codes.
402: Authorization: The specification supports OAuth 2.0 authentication, ensuring secure access to the API.
403: Request and Response Formats: It offers standardized request formats for GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE operations. Detailed response schemas describe the data structures returned and error handling guidelines to assist developers in debugging API requests.
404: Swagger API Hub
405: The Swagger UI tool allows users to visualize and interact with the API in a format that's easy to read and understand. The Swagger Hub and Swagger Editor are the de facto editor tools for designing and working with APIs using the OpenAPI Specification. Here, we have used Swagger's API hub to demonstrate how to use the OpenAPI Specification version 3.0.0 specification for Zoho Cliq APIs.

458: How to Use the Zoho Cliq OpenAPI Specification 3.0.0
459: All Zoho Cliq APIs' functionalities, structures, and syntax are documented in standardized formats using the OpenAPI Specification (OAS). As indicated above, the OAS files can be downloaded as a complete zip file or module by module.
460: Choose any API resource/module that suits your business case and download the YAML by clicking.
461: Go to Swagger's API Hub >Design >Import API (Import your existing API definitions to API Hub for Designs).
462: Under Path or URL, choose the downloaded YAML file by clicking browse.
463: Upon successfully importing the YAML file, you will be directed to the API Design Editor or API Definition page, where you can view, define, edit, and document your API using the OpenAPI Specification (OAS).
464: Note :
465: Zoho Cliq's OAS files are designed generically to illustrate standard API endpoints, request and response structures, and HTTP methods. They do not include any specific unique business logic.
466: For instance, each module may require different input data in specific cases, which, due to their generic design, may not fully address your application's particular business needs. Developers must plan for and manually address gaps based on their use cases and integrate them with their applications.

9996: Buttons
9997: A button can be attached as a component in the message object.
9998: The key parts of a button in a message are explained below:
9999: Label: The display value of the button in the message.
10000: Button Type: A simple color indication to differentiate if the button action is intended to
10001: be
10002: positive, negative or neutral.
10003: Button Action Types: The types of action entries that can be triggered on clicking a button.

10005: Invoke
10006: Function
10007: Open
10008: URL

10012: Instant Buttons
10013: Message Card Buttons
10014: The functionality behind instant buttons and message card buttons is the same and the only difference
10015: between
10016: them is the ease of use. The format for instant buttons is deceptively simple making it quick to use.

10027: Start Chat
10028: Contact Invite.
