404: Can I get a demo of Zoho Cliq?
405: Yes, we would be happy to demonstrate Zoho Cliq through a web-conference at your convenience. To schedule your personal session, please fill in your details and let us know your preferred time by clicking here. We will get back to you on your time!
406: What happens after my trial ends?
407: After your 14-day trial expires you will need to purchase a subscription to convert your trial account into a permanent account with all your data, and integrations and advanced features squarely intact. If you choose to not subscribe to Zoho Cliq after your trial ends, your account will be downgraded to our free plan, where you can continue to communicate and collaborate with your colleagues.
408: How can I pay?
409: We accept payment via Visa, MasterCard, American Express and PayPal. We also accept payments via bank transfer or check transfer for yearly subscriptions.
410: What features of Cliq are available as a part of Zoho Workplace and People Plus suites?
411: The Zoho Workplace Suite offers a complete set of tools for communication and collaboration, and the People Plus Suite offers a complete set of tools to empower the workforce and HR Teams. The Standard version of Cliq with unlimited message search is available as a part of Zoho Workplace Standard plan and People Plus, and the Professional version of Cliq is available as a part of Zoho Workplace Professional Plan. The admin console of both suites allows you to set up and manage Cliq users.
412: Additionally, support for up to 20,000 users within a single channel is applicable for the Zoho Workplace suite.
413: What features of Cliq are available as a part of Zoho One?
414: Zoho One gives you one suite of more than 40 integrated business and productivity applications for your entire organization. Cliq's Enterprise plan with all the features is available as a part of the Zoho One bundle.
415: What is Networks and when should I use them?
416: Organizations can use Networks to communicate with external agents, partners, and other people who aren't part of your organization. If you want to set up a permanent external collaboration platform, you can use Networks. Learn more

154: Cliq-MCP: AI WorkBuddy for Zoho Cliq
155: AI WorkBuddy is an intelligent assistant for Zoho Cliq that provides smart automation and productivity features through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It combines the power of modern AI with seamless Cliq integration to enhance team collaboration and productivity.
156: 🎯 Key Features
157: 🤖 AI-Powered Capabilities
158: Smart Summarization: Automatically summarize channel conversations with key insights
159: Task Extraction: Identify and extract action items from discussions
160: Meeting Minutes: Generate structured meeting minutes from conversations
161: Issue Classification: Intelligent categorization and prioritization of support tickets
162: Context-Aware Responses: AI understanding of workplace communication patterns
163: 🔧 Technical Excellence
164: MCP Protocol: Built on the Model Context Protocol for seamless AI integration
165: Multi-Provider Support: Compatible with OpenAI GPT and Anthropic Claude
166: Professional Architecture: Clean, scalable, and maintainable codebase
167: Comprehensive Testing: 48% test coverage with unit and integration tests
168: Docker Ready: Full containerization support for easy deployment
169: ⚡ Cliq Integration
170: Webhook Support: Real-time event processing from Zoho Cliq
171: Rich Card Responses: Beautiful, interactive responses in channels
172: Command Interface: Intuitive slash commands for AI features
173: Error Handling: Graceful error handling with user-friendly messages
174: 🚀 Quick Start
175: Prerequisites
176: Python 3.11+
177: Zoho Cliq account with bot permissions
178: OpenAI API key or Anthropic API key
179: Installation
180: Clone the repository
181: git clone https://github.com/rohansen856/cliq-mcp
182: cd cliq-mcp
183: Set up environment
184: # Copy environment template
185: cp .env.example .env
186: # Edit .env with your configuration
187: nano .env
188: Install dependencies
189: python -m venv venv
190: source venv/bin/activate # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
191: pip install -r requirements.txt
192: Start the application
193: # Using the start script (recommended)
194: ./scripts/start.sh
195: # Or manually
196: python -m src.main run
197: Docker Deployment
198: # Build and run with Docker Compose
199: docker-compose up -d
200: # Check status
201: docker-compose ps
202: # View logs
203: docker-compose logs -f cliq-mcp

175: Official Document
176: Trouble Shooting
177: ⚠️ Beta Version Notice: This tool is currently in Beta stage. Features and APIs may change, so please stay updated with version releases.
178: This is the Feishu/Lark official OpenAPI MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool designed to help users quickly connect to the Feishu/Lark platform and enable efficient collaboration between AI Agents and Feishu/Lark. The tool encapsulates Feishu/Lark Open Platform API interfaces as MCP tools, allowing AI assistants to directly call these interfaces and implement various automation scenarios such as document processing, conversation management, calendar scheduling, and more.
179: Preparation
180: Creating a Feishu/Lark Application
181: Before using the lark-mcp tool, you need to create a Feishu/Lark application:
182: Visit the Feishu Open Platform or Lark Open Platform and log in
183: Click "Console" and create a new application
184: Obtain the App ID and App Secret, which will be used for API authentication
185: Add the necessary permissions for your application based on your usage scenario
186: If you need to call APIs as a user, set the OAuth 2.0 redirect URL to http://localhost:3000/callback
187: For detailed application creation and configuration guidelines, please refer to the Feishu Open Platform Documentation - Creating an Application.
188: Installing Node.js
189: Before using the lark-mcp tool, you need to install the Node.js environment.
190: Using the Official Installer (Recommended):
191: Visit the Node.js website
192: Download and install the LTS version
193: After installation, verify in the terminal:
194: node -v
195: npm -v
196: Quick Start
197: Using with Trae/Cursor/Claude
198: To integrate Feishu/Lark functionality in AI tools like Trae, Cursor or Claude, install using the button below.
199: or add the following to your configuration file:
200: {
201: "mcpServers": {
202: "lark-mcp": {
203: "command": "npx",
204: "args": [
205: "-y",
206: "@larksuiteoapi/lark-mcp",
207: "mcp",
208: "-a",
209: "<your_app_id>",
210: "-s",
211: "<your_app_secret>"
212: ]
213: }
214: }
215: }
216: If you need to access APIs with user identity, you need to login first using the login command in the terminal. Note that you need to configure the application's redirect URL in the developer console first, default is http://localhost:3000/callback
217: # Login and get user access token
218: npx -y @larksuiteoapi/lark-mcp login -a cli_xxxx -s yyyyy
219: # Or optionally, login with specific OAuth scope - if not specified, all permissions will be authorized by default
220: npx -y @larksuiteoapi/lark-mcp login -a cli_xxxx -s yyyyy --scope offline_access docx:document
221: Then add the following to your configuration file:
222: {
223: "mcpServers": {
224: "lark-mcp": {
225: "command": "npx",
226: "args": [
227: "-y",
228: "@larksuiteoapi/lark-mcp",
229: "mcp",
230: "-a",
231: "<your_app_id>",
232: "-s",
233: "<your_app_secret>",
234: "--oauth",
235: "--token-mode", "user_access_token"
236: ]
237: }
238: }
239: }
240: Note: When enabling --oauth, it's recommended to explicitly set --token-mode to user_access_token, which means calling APIs with user access tokens, suitable for accessing user resources or scenarios requiring user authorization (such as reading personal documents, sending IM messages). If you keep the default auto, some APIs AI may fallback to tenant_access_token, which could result in insufficient permissions or inability to access user private data.
241: Domain Configuration
242: Based on your usage scenario, lark-mcp supports configuring different domain environments:
243: Feishu (China Version):
244: Default uses https://open.feishu.cn domain
245: Suitable for users in China
246: Lark (International Version):
247: Uses https://open.larksuite.com domain
248: Suitable for overseas users or international version of Lark
249: To switch to the international version of Lark, add the --domain parameter in your configuration:
250: {
251: "mcpServers": {
252: "lark-mcp": {
253: "command": "npx",
254: "args": [
255: "-y",
256: "@larksuiteoapi/lark-mcp",
257: "mcp",
258: "-a",
259: "<your_app_id>",
260: "-s",
261: "<your_app_secret>",
262: "--domain",
263: "https://open.larksuite.com"
264: ]
265: }
266: }
267: }
268: 💡 Tip: Ensure your application is created in the corresponding domain environment's open platform. International version applications cannot be used with Feishu China version, and vice versa.
269: Custom API Configuration
270: ⚠️ File Upload/Download: File upload and download operations are not yet supported
271: ⚠️ Document Editing: Direct editing of Feishu cloud documents is not supported (only importing and reading are available)
272: By default, the MCP service enables common APIs. To enable other tools or only specific APIs or presets, you can specify them using the -t parameter in the MCP Client configuration (JSON):
273: {
274: "mcpServers": {
275: "lark-mcp": {
276: "command": "npx",
277: "args": [
278: "-y",
279: "@larksuiteoapi/lark-mcp",
280: "mcp",
281: "-a", "<your_app_id>",
282: "-s", "<your_app_secret>",
283: "-t", "im.v1.message.create,im.v1.message.list,im.v1.chat.create,preset.calendar.default"
284: ]
285: }
286: }
287: }
288: For detailed information about all preset tool collections and which tools are included in each preset, please refer to the Preset Tool Collections Reference.
289: A complete list of all supported Feishu/Lark tools can be found in tools.md.
290: ⚠️ Notice：Non-preset APIs have not undergone compatibility testing, and the AI may not perform optimally during the process of understanding and using them.
291: Development Integration
292: Developers can refer to the minimal example for integrating with Agent: lark-samples/mcp_quick_demo.
293: You can also refer to the Lark bot integration example: lark-samples/mcp_larkbot_demo/nodejs.
294: This example demonstrates how to integrate MCP capabilities into Feishu/Lark bots, triggering tool calls and message sending through bot conversations, suitable for scenarios that integrate existing tools into Bot.
295: Advanced Configuration
296: For detailed configuration options and deployment scenarios, please refer to our Configuration Guide.
297: For detailed information about all available command line parameters and their usage, please refer to the Command Line Reference.

56: Pumble API Overview
57: 2 min read
58: isidora.komaromi@cake.com
59: Who can use this feature?
60: Owner, Admin, Member
61: Available on all plans
62: By using the Pumble API addon, you can interact with Pumble’s API documentation without using any complex authentication processes. This addon lets you generate an API key that allows you to send messages, reactions, and more via simple HTTP requests.
63: Info
64: The rate limit is up to 1000 requests per minute per user.
65: Install API addon #
66: Before you can create an API key, you need to install the API addon on your Pumble workspace.
67: Here’s how to do this:
68: Click on + Add apps in the left sidebar
69: Click on Install in the API section
70: Allow permissions
71: Generate an API key #
72: Once your API addon is installed, you can generate API keys directly in Pumble.
73: Here’s how:
74: Click on API in the left sidebar
75: Select Add API key
76: Enter API key name
77: Click Generate to complete the action
78: You’ll receive an ephemeral message containing the generated API key. This message is not visible to other users. Copy this key for future use. The generated key enables interaction with the Addon’s public API, allowing users to send requests and execute various actions within Pumble, including:
79: Sending messages
80: Leaving a reply to a message
81: Message deletion
82: Adding a reaction to a message
83: Channel creation
84: Listing the messages in a channel (if the channel is private, Addon Bot needs to be a member of that channel)
85: Listing the channels and DMs that belong to the user who created the key
86: The full list of available actions is available in the Swagger documentation. You can also use the documentation in Swagger, just enter your API key in the Authorize part.
87: Delete API key #
88: You can remove an API key by following these steps:
89: Click on API in the left sidebar
90: Select Delete API key
91: Choose a key from the list
92: Click Delete to confirm the action
93: Valid commands #
94: There are a few specific actions for interacting with the Pumble API addon. You can use these commands directly in messages:
95: /api-keys generate – addon will generate API keys for that particular user and store it in their database. Users can generate as much API keys as they want to.
96: /api-keys list – addon will list all user’s API keys
97: /api-keys help – to list all valid commands you can use

When you create an incoming webhook, you receive a unique URL by which you can send a JSON payload with the message text. 59: Creating an incoming webhook # 60: To create a new incoming webhook: 61: Click on your Workspace name at the top left corner 62: Navigate to the Workspace settings 63: Select General settings from the dropdown 64: Click on the Incoming Webhooks section in the sidebar 65: Click on the New Webhook button at the top right corner 66: Choose the channel where your webhook will post messages 67: Click on the Add incoming Webhook button to complete the process 68: When you create your webhook, the editor opens up automatically. There, you’ll be able to customize its name, change the channel, add a descriptive label, customize the icon, and most importantly, copy or regenerate your unique URL. 69: Info 70: The rate limit on incoming webhooks on Pumble is 1 second per webhook. 71: Info 72: The maximum number of characters in a webhook is 10000. 73: Using incoming webhook to send a message # 74: To send a message using the incoming webhooks you just created, simply make an HTTP POST request to the unique URL you copied from the webhook editor. 75: The request payload should contain the text property and that text will be posted into a specified channel. Currently supported content types are: 76: application/json 77: application/x-www-form-urlencoded 78: Here is a sample curl request for posting to a channel using an incoming webhook using the application/x-www-form-urlencoded content type: 79: Copy 80: curl -X POST \ --location "https://api.pumble.com/workspaces/WORKSPACE-ID/incomingWebhooks/postMessage/WEBHOOK-CODE" \ --data-urlencode "payload={ \"text\": \"This is posted to general and comes from a bot named MyNewWebhook.\" }" 81: Here is a sample JSON curl request for posting to a channel using an incoming webhook: 82: Copy 83: curl -X POST \ --location 84: "https://api.pumble.com/workspaces/WORKSPACE-ID/incomingWebhooks/postMessage/WEBHOOK-CODE" \ 85: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 86: -d '{"text":"This is posted to general and comes from a bot named MyNewWebhook."}' 87: Info 88: You can use rich text formatting for webhook messages. Here are some payload examples: 89: User mention: 90: Copy 91: { 92: "text": "User mention: <<@{{userId}}>>, channel mention: <<#{{channelId}}>>, user group mention: <<&{{userGroupId}}>> and @here @channel" 93: } 94: Attachment: 95: Copy 96: { 97: "attachments": [ 98: { 99: "pretext": "Pretext of Pumble webhooks article", 100: "title": "Pumble webhooks", 101: "title_link": "https://pumble.com/help/integrations/add-pumble-apps/incoming-webhooks-for-pumble", 102: "text": "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris nisi ut aliquip ex ea commodo consequat. Duis aute irure dolor in reprehenderit in voluptate velit esse cillum dolore eu fugiat nulla pariatur. Excepteur sint occaecat cupidatat non proident, sunt in culpa qui officia deserunt mollit anim id est laborum.", 103: "author_name": "Pumble", 104: "author_link": "https://pumble.com", 105: "footer": "Lorem ipsum v1.0.0", 106: "footer_icon": "https://files.pumble.com/avatars/default/pumble-logo", 107: "color": "green", // or hex RGB 108: "ts": 1759479334 109: } 110: ] 111: } 112: This attachment example will send a message that looks like this: 113: Hyperlinks: 114: Copy 115: { 116: "text": "[Markdown Hyperlink](https://pumble.com) | Html hyperlink | " 117: } 118: Emojis: 119: Copy 120: { 121: "text": "Emojis :raised_hands: :heart:" 122: } 123: Code block: 124: Copy 125: { 126: "text": "`Inline code` and ```Code block\n hello \nEnd of code block```" 127: } 128: Here’s an example message that incorporates different types of rich text formatting: 129: Copy 130: { 131: "text": "Hello team! :wave: :tada:\n\n**Quick Update**:\n- Feature deployed successfully! :rocket:\n- Bugs resolved: `5`\n\n*Styling Reference:*\n- Markdown **bold**, *italic*\n- HTML bold, italic, inline code\n\n🔗 Useful Links:\n- [Pumble Website](https://pumble.com)\n- Pumble via HTML\n- \n\n:busts_in_silhouette: Mentions:\n- Channel: <<#{{68e3a383ce5f2c8d95ff46a6}}>> \nNotifications: @here @channel \n\n:computer: Code snippet:```function greet() {\n console.log(\"Hello, Pumble!\");\n}```" 132: } 133: This webhook message would look like this: 134: Error handling # 135: If everything is set up correctly, you’ll receive an HTTP 200 status to indicate that your incoming webhook was successful. This might not always be the case, and this action can fail for numerous reasons. 136: Use the following table to troubleshoot common webhook errors. 137: Error codeError messageCause 138: 400440Channel is archived.The channel where the webhook is sending messages is archived. 139: 400700Incoming webhook is disabled.The webhook was disabled by the Workspace Admin. 140: 400702Incoming webhook is deleted.The webhook was deleted by the Workspace Admin. 141: 400703Invalid payload format.The request payload is not in a supported format. 142: 403200You cannot perform this operation.You don’t have permission to post in the specified channel. 143: 404100Not found.The unique URL was not found and most likely regenerated by a Workspace Admin. 144: Related Articles # 145: Guide to Pumble Integrations 146: Related Articles 147: Connect Zoom to Pumble with Zapier and Webhooks 148: Changelog 149: Receive GitLab Notifications on Pumble via Webhooks 150: Was this article helpful? 151: Submit 152: Cancel 153: Thank you! 154: @infralayers/pumble-mcp
155: Universal, production-ready Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Pumble. It connects autonomous AI agents and LLMs to your Pumble workspace with 100% official REST API coverage (26 tools), sub-millisecond in-memory entity resolution, affirmative execution receipts, and built-in anti-loop security guardrails.
156: Works seamlessly across Cursor, Cline / Roo Code, Windsurf, Claude Desktop, Claude Code CLI, Google Antigravity, Zed, and any custom agent framework.
157: Security note: the Pumble API key you configure grants broad,
158: workspace-wide access. Read the Security / Permissions
159: section before installing.
160: ⚡ Highlights & Performance
161: 100% Official REST API Coverage: 26 autonomous tools covering messaging, threads, scheduling, reactions, channel operations, user directories, and status updates.
162: Ultra-Low Latency (~0.05ms Resolution): Standard API calls take ~1,500ms to resolve user and channel identifiers over the network. Our in-memory RAM cache reduces steady-state lookups to ~0.05ms (30,000x faster), completely eliminating network penalties.
163: Boot-Time Prefetching: Users and channels are prefetched in parallel during server startup without blocking the client MCP handshake.
164: Write-Through In-Place Updates: Channel creation, member additions/removals, and custom status updates sync directly to the local RAM cache in 0ms.
165: Affirmative Execution Receipts: Mutation tools return structured receipts (ok: true, delivered: true, status: "Verification complete") that eliminate compulsive post-action read loops (e.g. list_messages spam).
166: Loop-Prevention Circuit Breaker: Finite State Machine (FSM) guardrail locks out speculative reconnaissance and fast-fails missing entities with actionable guidance.
167: Security Challenge Gate (AUTH-XXXX): Destructive actions (deleting messages, removing members) require single-use, time-limited confirmation codes, stopping accidental deletions.
168: 💾 Memory Footprint: Scaling in Large Workspaces
169: A common concern with in-memory caching is memory consumption in large organizations. This server uses an optimized, lean data model that retains only essential routing identifiers (id, name, email for users; id, name, channelType, userIds for channels):
170: Workspace Scale
171: Entities Cached
172: Estimated RAM Footprint
173: Memory Impact
174: Small Team
175: 50 users, 20 channels
176: ~15 KB
177: Negligible
178: Mid-Size Company
179: 1,000 users, 100 channels
180: ~230 KB
181: < 0.25 MB
182: Enterprise Workspace

184: ~1.1 MB

190: Takeaway: Even in an enterprise workspace with thousands of users and hundreds of channels, the cache consumes less than 5 MB of RAM—a microscopic fraction of Node.js's standard baseline memory (~30 MB). The cache operates with a 60-second TTL, ensuring fresh data without memory leaks or bloat.
191: 🚀 Quick Start (Zero-Install via npx)
192: Run directly with npx in any MCP-compliant client without cloning or manual building:
193: Standard MCP Configuration
194: Works out of the box in Cursor, Cline / Roo Code, Windsurf, Claude Desktop, and Antigravity.
195: Add this block to your client's MCP configuration file (e.g. claude_desktop_config.json, .cursor/mcp.json, or Cline MCP settings):
196: {
197: "mcpServers": {
198: "pumble": {
199: "command": "npx",
200: "args": ["-y", "@infralayers/pumble-mcp"],
201: "env": {
202: "PUMBLE_API_KEY": "<your-pumble-api-key>"
203: }
204: }
205: }
206: }
207: CLI Agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Terminal)
208: Register directly from your shell:
209: # Claude Code CLI
210: claude mcp add pumble --env PUMBLE_API_KEY="<your-pumble-api-key>" -- npx -y @infralayers/pumble-mcp
211: Verify your registered tools:
212: claude mcp list
213: 🔑 Getting Your Pumble API Key
214: In your Pumble workspace, install the API Key addon (Apps & Integrations).
215: Generate a key from the addon's settings. Pumble shows it once as an ephemeral message — copy it immediately.
216: Pass the key in your client's env configuration as PUMBLE_API_KEY.
217: 🛠️ Complete 26-Tool Reference
218: Architecture Note: All tools natively accept human-readable fuzzy names, emails, and exact IDs, automatically resolving them via the backend to prevent the AI from wasting context tokens on manual lookups. Ambiguous names will safely throw an error requesting clarification.
219: 1. Messages & Threads (8 Tools)
220: Tool
221: Pumble Endpoint
222: Notes & Parameters
223: send_message_via_channel_name_or_id
224: POST /sendMessage
225: Send a message to any channel or DM. Takes channelIdentifier (name or ID), text, optional asBot. Returns affirmative delivery receipt.
226: list_messages_via_channel_name_or_id
227: GET /listMessages
228: List messages in a channel or DM. Takes channelIdentifier, optional limit (default: 10, max: 50), and cursor.
229: get_message_via_id
230: GET /fetchMessage
231: Fetch a single message by ID. Takes channelIdentifier and messageId.
232: edit_message
233: POST /editMessage
234: Edit an existing message. Takes channelIdentifier, messageId, and updated text.
235: delete_message
236: DELETE /deleteMessage
237: Delete a message. Takes channelIdentifier, messageId, and confirm: true (destructive).
238: reply_message_via_channel_name_or_id
239: POST /sendReply
240: Reply to a message to start or continue a thread. Takes channelIdentifier, messageId, text, optional asBot.
241: list_thread_replies_via_channel_name_or_id
242: GET /fetchThreadReplies
243: Fetch replies in a thread. Takes channelIdentifier, messageId, optional limit, cursor. Returns replies newest first.
244: search_messages
245: POST /searchMessages
246: Search messages across the workspace by text, fromUser, or inChannel. User and channel names resolve automatically.
247: 2. Scheduled Messages (5 Tools)
248: Tool
249: Pumble Endpoint
250: Notes & Parameters
251: create_scheduled_message_via_name_or_id
252: POST /createScheduledMessage
253: Schedule a future message. Takes channelIdentifier OR userIdentifier, text, and sendAt (ISO string or epoch ms, min 30s in future).
254: list_scheduled_messages
255: GET /fetchScheduledMessages
256: List queued scheduled messages. Supports optional destination filters, limit, and cursor.
257: get_scheduled_message_via_name_or_id
258: GET /getScheduledMessage
259: Inspect a scheduled message by its scheduledMessageId.
260: edit_scheduled_message_via_name_or_id
261: POST /editScheduledMessage
262: Modify a scheduled message's text, sendAt, or move it to a new channel/DM destination.
263: delete_scheduled_message_via_name_or_id
264: DELETE /deleteScheduledMessage
265: Cancel and delete a queued scheduled message. Takes scheduledMessageId and confirm: true (destructive).
266: 3. Reactions (2 Tools)
267: Tool
268: Pumble Endpoint
269: Notes & Parameters
270: add_reaction
271: POST /addReaction
272: Add an emoji reaction to a message. Takes channelIdentifier, messageId, and reaction code (e.g. :thumbsup:).
273: remove_reaction
274: POST /removeReaction
275: Remove an emoji reaction from a message. Takes channelIdentifier, messageId, and reaction code.
276: 4. Channels & Membership (5 Tools)
277: Tool
278: Pumble Endpoint
279: Notes & Parameters
280: list_channels_only_when_user_calls
281: GET /listChannels
282: List all visible channels (public, private, and direct). Guarded against unnecessary agent discovery loops.
283: get_channel_detail_via_channel_name_or_id
284: GET /getChannel
285: Hydrate full channel details, including resolved member lists with names and emails.
286: create_channel
287: POST /createChannel
288: Create a new channel. Takes name and type (PUBLIC or PRIVATE). Updates cache immediately.
289: add_users_to_channel_via_name_or_id
290: POST /addUsersToChannel
291: Add workspace members to a channel. Takes channelIdentifier and an array of userIdentifiers (names, emails, or IDs). Blocks DM additions.
292: remove_user_from_channel_via_name_or_id
293: POST /removeUserFromChannel
294: Remove a member from a channel. Takes channelIdentifier, userIdentifier, and confirm: true (destructive). Blocks DM removals.
295: 5. Workspace, Users & Status (6 Tools)
296: Tool
297: Pumble Endpoint
298: Notes & Parameters
299: send_dm_via_name_email_or_id
300: POST /dmUser
301: Send a 1-on-1 direct message. Takes userIdentifier (name, email, or ID) and text.
302: send_group_dm_via_names_emails_or_ids
303: POST /groupDm
304: Send a multi-person group direct message. Takes userIdentifiers (array of names/emails/IDs) and text.
305: list_users_not_for_id_lookup
306: GET /listUsers
307: List workspace users. Guarded against speculative agent reconnaissance.
308: get_my_info
309: GET /myInfo
310: Get account and profile details of the authenticated bot / API key owner.
311: list_user_groups
312: GET /listUserGroups
313: List all user groups configured in the Pumble workspace.
314: update_my_custom_status
315: POST /updateCustomStatus
316: Set or clear custom status text, emoji, and expiration duration. Write-through to cache in 0ms.
317: 🛡️ Security / Permissions
318: This server hands a single static Pumble API key to an MCP server that any connected client or LLM session can invoke. Understand the blast radius before installing:
319: Blast Radius & Capabilities
320: The API key inherits the full visibility and privileges of the Pumble user who generated it. It is a password-equivalent secret.
321: With these twenty-six tools, anyone able to invoke this server can, as you:
322: Messages: Read, send, edit, delete, and reply to messages in any channel or DM the key can access.
323: Scheduled Messages: Queue messages to post later in any channel or DM, and read, rewrite, redirect, or delete anything already queued.
324: Workspace Search: Search across workspace history by text, author, or channel.
325: Direct Messages: Send 1-on-1 and group DMs to any user in the workspace.
326: User Directory: Enumerate every workspace member's name and email address.
327: Channel Membership: Create channels, add users to channels, or remove users from channels.
328: Reactions & Status: Add/remove emoji reactions and modify your profile's custom status.
329: Built-in Agent Defenses
330: Destructive Challenge Gates (AUTH-XXXX):
331: Destructive operations (remove_user_from_channel, delete_scheduled_message, delete_message) cannot be executed speculatively by autonomous agents. If called without human authorization, the server intercepts execution and issues a dynamic 60-second runtime confirmation token challenge requiring human verification.
332: Missing Entity Fast-Fail:
333: Missing users or channels fail immediately with a strict directive stopping partial batches or hallucinations.
334: Recommendations & Best Practices
335: Never commit .env: .env is gitignored by default. Never paste your API key into logs, commit messages, or chat transcripts.
336: Key Rotation: If a key is ever exposed, rotate it immediately in Pumble (Apps & Integrations > API Key Addon), update your environment, and revoke the old key.
337: Dedicated Service Account: If your Pumble workspace allows it, generate the key from a dedicated service account rather than an individual admin user's personal account.
338: 💻 Local Development
339: 1. Clone & Install
340: git clone https://github.com/infralayers/pumble-mcp.git
341: cd pumble-mcp
342: npm install
343: 2. Configure Environment
344: The server reads PUMBLE_API_KEY from its environment. It does not load a .env file on its own.
345: For development, export it in your shell (or add to ~/.bashrc):
346: export PUMBLE_API_KEY="<your-pumble-api-key>"
347: 3. Development Scripts
348: npm run dev # Watch mode via tsx
349: npm run typecheck # Typecheck without emitting (tsc --noEmit)
350: npm test # Run unit tests via vitest
351: npm run build # Compile TypeScript to dist/
352: npm start # Run compiled server (node dist/index.js)
353: To run your local build directly in an MCP client:
354: {
355: "command": "node",
356: "args": ["/absolute/path/to/pumble-mcp/dist/index.js"],
357: "env": {
358: "PUMBLE_API_KEY": "<your-pumble-api-key>"
359: }
360: }

104: The Discord API is a REST API that allows you to interact with Discord data from your own applications. It’s the primary way to interact with Discord from your own code.
105: Copy pageCopy page
106: Base URL
107: https://discord.com/api
108: API Versioning
109: Some API and Gateway versions are now non-functioning, and are labeled as discontinued in the table below for posterity. Trying to use these versions will fail and return 400 Bad Request.
110: Discord exposes different versions of our API. You should specify which version to use by including it in the request path like https://discord.com/api/v{version_number}. Omitting the version number from the route will route requests to the current default version (marked below). You can find the change log for the newest API version here.
111: API Versions

178: Authentication
179: Authenticating with the Discord API can be done in one of three ways:
180: Using a bot token found on the Bot page within your app’s settings. For more information on bots see bots vs user accounts.
181: Using an OAuth2 bearer token gained through the OAuth2 API.
182: Using basic authentication with credentials as the client ID and client secret found on the OAuth2 page of your app’s settings in the format client_id:client_secret as a Base64 encoded string. Only applicable for OAuth2 API token endpoints.
183: For all authentication types, authentication is performed with the Authorization HTTP header in the format Authorization: TOKEN_TYPE TOKEN.
184: Example Bot Token Authorization Header
185: Authorization: Bot MTk4NjIyNDgzNDcxOTI1MjQ4.Cl2FMQ.ZnCjm1XVW7vRze4b7Cq4se7kKWs
186: Example Bearer Token Authorization Header
187: Authorization: Bearer CZhtkLDpNYXgPH9Ml6shqh2OwykChw
188: Example Basic Token Authorization Header
189: Authorization: Basic MTk4NjIyNDgzNDcxOTI1MjQ4OlEzS052N0NSRW5DYS1nS0xMajFEOGV1ZFl1SmZ1Nm96
190: Encryption
191: All HTTP-layer services and protocols (e.g. HTTP, WebSocket) within the Discord API are using TLS 1.2.
192: Snowflakes
193: Discord utilizes Twitter’s snowflake format for uniquely identifiable descriptors (IDs). These IDs are guaranteed to be unique across all of Discord, except in some unique scenarios in which child objects share their parent’s ID. Because Snowflake IDs are up to 64 bits in size (e.g. a uint64), they are always returned as strings in the HTTP API to prevent integer overflows in some languages. See Gateway ETF/JSON for more information regarding Gateway encoding.
194: Snowflake ID Broken Down in Binary
195: 111111111111111111111111111111111111111111 11111 11111 111111111111
196: 64 22 17 12 0
197: Snowflake ID Format Structure (Left to Right)
198: FieldBitsNumber of bitsDescriptionRetrieval
199: Timestamp63 to 2242 bitsMilliseconds since Discord Epoch, the first second of 2015 or 1420070400000.(snowflake >> 22) + 1420070400000
200: Internal worker ID21 to 175 bits(snowflake & 0x3E0000) >> 17
201: Internal process ID16 to 125 bits(snowflake & 0x1F000) >> 12
202: Increment11 to 012 bitsFor every ID that is generated on that process, this number is incrementedsnowflake & 0xFFF
203: Convert Snowflake to DateTime
204: Snowflake IDs in Pagination
205: We typically use snowflake IDs in many of our API routes for pagination. The standardized pagination paradigm we utilize is one in which you can specify IDs before and after in combination with limit to retrieve a desired page of results. You will want to refer to the specific endpoint documentation for details.
206: It is useful to note that snowflake IDs are just numbers with a timestamp, so when dealing with pagination where you want results from the beginning of time (in Discord Epoch, but 0 works here too) or before/after a specific time you can generate a snowflake ID for that time.
207: Generating a snowflake ID from a Timestamp Example
208: (timestamp_ms - DISCORD_EPOCH) << 22
209: ID Serialization
210: There are some cases in which our API and Gateway may return IDs in an unexpected format. Internally, Discord stores IDs as integer snowflakes. When we serialize IDs to JSON, we transform bigints into strings. Given that all Discord IDs are snowflakes, you should always expect a string.
211: However, there are cases in which passing something to our API will instead return IDs serialized as an integer; this is the case when you send our API or Gateway a value in an id field that is not bigint size. For example, when requesting GUILD_MEMBERS_CHUNK from our gateway:
212: // Send
213: {
214: op: 8,
215: d: {
216: guild_id: '308994132968210433',
217: user_ids: [ '123123' ]
218: }
219: }
220: // Receive
221: {
222: t: 'GUILD_MEMBERS_CHUNK',
223: s: 3,
224: op: 0,
225: d: {
226: not_found: [ 123123 ],
227: members: [],
228: guild_id: '308994132968210433'
229: }
230: }
231: You can see in this case that the sent user_id is not a bigint; therefore, when it is serialized back to JSON by Discord, it is not transformed into a string. This will never happen with IDs that come from Discord. But, this can happen if you send malformed data in your requests.
232: ISO8601 Date/Time
233: Discord utilizes the ISO8601 format for most Date/Times returned in our models. This format is referred to as type ISO8601 within tables in this documentation.
234: Nullable and Optional Resource Fields
235: Resource fields that may contain a null value have types that are prefixed with a question mark. Resource fields that are optional have names that are suffixed with a question mark.
236: Example Nullable and Optional Fields
237: FieldType
238: optional_field?string
239: nullable_field?string
240: optional_and_nullable_field??string
241: Consistency
242: Discord operates at a scale where true consistency is impossible. Because of this, lots of operations in our API and in-between our services are eventually consistent. Due to this, client actions can never be serialized and may be executed in any order (if executed at all). Along with these constraints, events in Discord may:
243: Never be sent to a client
244: Be sent exactly one time to the client
245: Be sent up to N times per client
246: Clients should operate on events and results from the API in as much of an idempotent behavior as possible.
247: HTTP API
248: User Agent
249: Clients using the HTTP API must provide a valid User Agent which specifies information about the client library and version in the following format:
250: User Agent Example
251: User-Agent: DiscordBot ($url, $versionNumber)
252: Clients may append more information and metadata to the end of this string as they wish.
253: Client requests that do not have a valid User Agent specified may be blocked and return a Cloudflare error.
254: Content Type
255: Clients using the HTTP API must provide a valid Content-Type header, either application/json, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, or multipart/form-data, except where specified. Failing to do so will result in a 50035 “Invalid form body” error.
256: Rate Limiting
257: The HTTP API implements a process for limiting and preventing excessive requests in accordance with RFC 6585. API users that regularly hit and ignore rate limits will have their API keys revoked, and be blocked from the platform. For more information on rate limiting of requests, please see the Rate Limits section.
258: Boolean Query Strings
259: Certain endpoints in the API are documented to accept booleans for their query string parameters. While there is no standard system for boolean representation in query string parameters, Discord represents such cases using True, true, or 1 for true and False, false or 0 for false.
260: Array Query Strings
261: Certain endpoints in the API are documented to accept arrays for their query string parameters. Unless otherwise specified, Discord represents such cases using multiple instances of the same query string parameter. For example, ?id=123&id=456 for ["123", "456"].
262: Gateway (WebSocket) API
263: Discord’s Gateway API is used for maintaining persistent, stateful websocket connections between your client and our servers. These connections are used for sending and receiving real-time events your client can use to track and update local state. The Gateway API uses secure websocket connections as specified in RFC 6455. For information on opening Gateway connections, please see the Gateway API section.
264: Message Formatting
265: Discord utilizes a subset of markdown for rendering message content on its clients, while also adding some custom functionality to enable things like mentioning users and channels. This functionality uses the following formats:
266: Formats
267: TypeStructureExample
268: User<@USER_ID><@80351110224678912>
269: User *<@!USER_ID><@!80351110224678912>
270: Channel<#CHANNEL_ID><#103735883630395392>
271: Role<@&ROLE_ID><@&165511591545143296>
272: Game profile<@$GAME_ID><@$1402418491272986635>
273: Slash command</NAME:COMMAND_ID></airhorn:816437322781949972>
274: Slash command with subcommand</NAME SUBCOMMAND:ID></foo bar:123456789012345678>
275: Slash command with subcommand group</NAME SUBCOMMAND_GROUP SUBCOMMAND:ID></foo group bar:123456789012345678>
276: Standard emojiUnicode characters🪴
277: Custom emoji<:NAME:ID><:mmLol:216154654256398347>
278: Animated custom emoji<a:NAME:ID><a:b1nzy:392938283556143104>
279: Unix timestamp<t:TIMESTAMP><t:1618953630>
280: Styled unix timestamp<t:TIMESTAMP:STYLE><t:1618953630:d>
281: Guild navigation<id:TYPE>See below
282: Using the markdown for users or roles will mention the target(s), and notify them depending on the sender’s permissions as well as the value of the allowed_mentions field when creating a message.
283: Standard emoji are currently rendered using Twemoji for Desktop and Android while iOS devices use Apple’s native emoji set.
284: Timestamps are expressed in seconds and display the given timestamp in the user’s timezone and locale.
285: * User mentions with an exclamation point are deprecated and should be handled like any other user mention.
286: Timestamp Styles
287: StyleExample OutputDescription
288: t16:20Short Time
289: T16:20:30Medium Time
290: d20/04/2021Short Date
291: DApril 20, 2021Long Date
292: f *April 20, 2021 at 16:20Long Date, Short Time
293: FTuesday, April 20, 2021 at 16:20Full Date, Short Time
294: s20/04/2021, 16:20Short Date, Short Time
295: S20/04/2021, 16:20:30Short Date, Medium Time
296: R4 years agoRelative Time
297: *default
298: Guild Navigation Types
299: Guild navigation types link to the corresponding resource in the current server.
300: Full SyntaxLinked Resource
301: <id:customize>Channel & Roles tab with Onboarding prompts
302: <id:browse>Browse Channels tab
303: <id:guide>Server Guide tab
304: <id:linked-roles>Linked Roles tab
305: <id:linked-roles:id>Specific linked role, opening the connection modal on click (the second id is the role id)
306: Image Formatting
307: Image Base URL
308: https://cdn.discordapp.com/
309: Discord uses ids and hashes to render images in the client. These hashes can be retrieved through various API requests, like Get User. Below are the formats, size limitations, and CDN endpoints for images in Discord. The returned format can be changed by changing the extension name at the end of the URL. The returned size can be changed by appending a querystring of ?size=desired_size to the URL. Image size can be any power of two between 16 and 4096.
310: Animated images uploaded as WebP or AVIF do not convert cleanly to GIF. Apps should request animated images as WebP for maximum compatibility, as this works regardless of the original upload format.
311: Image Formats
312: NameExtension
313: JPEG.jpg, .jpeg
314: PNG.png
315: WebP.webp
316: GIF.gif
317: Lottie.json

342: * In the case of endpoints that support GIFs, the hash will begin with a_ if it is available in an animated format (example: a_1269e74af4df7417b13759eae50c83dc). These images can be retrieved as animated WebP using the .webp file extension and ?animated=true querystring parameter.
343: ** In the case of the Default User Avatar endpoint, the value for index depends on whether the user is migrated to the new username system. For users on the new username system, index will be (user_id >> 22) % 6. For users on the legacy username system, index will be discriminator % 5.
344: *** In the case of the Default User Avatar and Sticker endpoints, the size of images returned is constant with the “size” querystring parameter being ignored.
345: **** In the case of the Sticker endpoint, the sticker will be available as PNG if its format_type is PNG or APNG, GIF if its format_type is GIF, and as Lottie if its format_type is LOTTIE.
346: ***** For Custom Emoji, we highly recommend requesting emojis as WebP for maximum performance and compatibility. Emojis can be uploaded as JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, and AVIF formats. WebP and AVIF formats must be requested as WebP since they don’t convert well to other formats. The Discord client uses WebP for all emojis displayed in-app. See the Emoji Resource page for more details.
347: Sticker GIFs do not use the CDN base URL, and can be accessed at https://media.discordapp.net/stickers/<sticker_id>.gif.
348: Image Data
349: Image data is a Data URI scheme that supports JPG, GIF, and PNG formats. An example Data URI format is:
350: data:image/jpeg;base64,BASE64_ENCODED_JPEG_IMAGE_DATA
351: Ensure you use the proper content type (image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif) that matches the image data being provided.
352: Signed Attachment CDN URLs
353: Attachments uploaded to Discord’s CDN (like user and bot-uploaded images) have signed URLs with a preset expiry time. Discord automatically refreshes attachment CDN URLs that appear within the client, so when your app receives a payload with a signed URL (like when you fetch a message), it will be valid.
354: When passing CDN URLs into API fields, like url in an embed image object and avatar_url for webhooks, your app can pass the CDN URL without any parameters as the value and Discord will automatically render and refresh the URL.
355: The standard CDN endpoints listed above are not signed, so they will not expire.
356: Example Attachment CDN URL
357: https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1012345678900020080/1234567891233211234/my_image.png?ex=65d903de&is=65c68ede&hm=2481f30dd67f503f54d020ae3b5533b9987fae4e55f2b4e3926e08a3fa3ee24f&
358: Attachment CDN URL Parameters
359: ParameterDescription
360: exHex timestamp indicating when an attachment CDN URL will expire
361: isHex timestamp indicating when the URL was issued
362: hmUnique signature that remains valid until the URL’s expiration
363: Uploading Files
364: The file upload size limit applies to each file in a request. The default limit is 20 MiB for all users, but may be higher for users depending on their Nitro status or by the server’s Boost Tier. The attachment_size_limit value provided when working with interactions is calculated as the maximum of these values.
365: Endpoints that support file uploads use a multipart/form-data request body. The file field name varies by endpoint and is shown in its parameter table. Non-file parameters can be sent as individual form fields or collectively as JSON in the payload_json form field.
366: Some endpoints use files[n] to upload files as attachments. All files[n] parameters must include a valid Content-Disposition subpart header with a filename and unique name parameter. Each file parameter must be uniquely named in the format files[n] such as files[0], files[1], or files[42]. The suffixed index n is the snowflake placeholder that can be used in the attachments field, which can be passed to the payload_json parameter (or Callback Data Payloads).
367: Images can also be referenced in embeds using the attachment://filename URL. An example payload is provided below.
368: Editing Message Attachments
369: The attachments JSON parameter includes all files that will be appended to the message, including new files and their respective snowflake placeholders (referenced above). When making a PATCH request, only files listed in the attachments parameter will be appended to the message. Any previously-added files that aren’t included will be removed.
370: The description and is_spoiler fields of existing attachments can optionally be updated.
371: Example Request Bodies (multipart/form-data)
372: Note that these examples are small sections of an HTTP request to demonstrate behavior of this endpoint - client libraries will set their own form boundaries (boundary is just an example). For more information, refer to the multipart/form-data spec.
373: This example demonstrates usage of the endpoint without payload_json.
374: --boundary
375: Content-Disposition: form-data; name="content"
376: Hello, World!
377: --boundary
378: Content-Disposition: form-data; name="tts"
379: true
380: --boundary--
381: This example demonstrates usage of the endpoint with payload_json and all content fields (content, embeds, files[n]) set.
382: --boundary
383: Content-Disposition: form-data; name="payload_json"
384: Content-Type: application/json
385: {
386: "content": "Hello, World!",
387: "embeds": [{
388: "title": "Hello, Embed!",
389: "description": "This is an embedded message.",
390: "thumbnail": {
391: "url": "attachment://myfilename.png"
392: },
393: "image": {
394: "url": "attachment://mygif.gif"
395: }
396: }],
397: "message_reference": {
398: "message_id": "233648473390448641"
399: },
400: "attachments": [{
401: "id": 0,
402: "description": "Image of a cute little cat",
403: "filename": "myfilename.png"
404: }, {
405: "id": 1,
406: "description": "Rickroll gif",
407: "filename": "mygif.gif"
408: }]
409: }
410: --boundary
411: Content-Disposition: form-data; name="files[0]"; filename="myfilename.png"
412: Content-Type: image/png
413: [image bytes]
414: --boundary
415: Content-Disposition: form-data; name="files[1]"; filename="mygif.gif"
416: Content-Type: image/gif
417: [image bytes]
418: --boundary--
419: Using Attachments within Embeds
420: You can upload attachments when creating a message and use those attachments within your embed. To do this, you will want to upload files as part of your multipart/form-data body. Make sure that you’re uploading files which contain a filename, as you will need to reference it in your payload.
421: Only .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .webp, and .gif may be used at this time. Other file types are not supported.
422: Within an embed object, you can set an image to use an attachment as its URL with the attachment scheme syntax: attachment://filename.png
423: For example:
424: {
425: "embeds": [{
426: "image": {
427: "url": "attachment://screenshot.png"
428: }
429: }]
430: }
431: File Type Filtering
432: You can filter for up to 10 file types in File Upload components and Slash Command Options. Each value must be either one of the group names below, or a dot-prefixed file extension (e.g. .pdf). Extensions are case-insensitive and are normalized to
433: lowercase, so .PDF and .pdf are equivalent.
434: We recommend using the file groups rather than listing extensions individually. If you do list extensions
435: individually, include .jpg for image uploads and both .mp4 and .mov for video uploads, as some mobile clients
436: rely on those extensions.
437: This feature only checks the file extension against the filename and does not inspect the file contents. You are still responsible for validating the actual contents of the file.
438: The following preset groups are available:
439: Group NameExtensions
440: image.png, .gif, .jpg, .jpeg, .jfif, .webp, .avif
441: video.mp4, .mov, .qt, .webm
442: audio.mp3, .m4a, .wav, .ogg, .opus, .flac
443: Do not hardcode the extension lists above. They match the file types Discord natively supports and are subject to change.

93: OAuth2 enables application developers to build applications that utilize authentication and data from the Discord API. Within Discord, there are multiple types of OAuth2 authentication. We support the authorization code grant, the implicit grant, client credentials, and some modified special-for-Discord flows for Bots and Webhooks.
94: Shared Resources
95: The first step in implementing OAuth2 is registering a developer application and retrieving your client ID and client secret. Most people who will be implementing OAuth2 will want to find and utilize a library in the language of their choice. For those implementing OAuth2 from scratch, please see RFC 6749 for details. After you create your application with Discord, make sure that you have your client_id and client_secret handy. The next step is to figure out which OAuth2 flow is right for your purposes.

139: State and Security
140: Before we dive into the semantics of the different OAuth2 grants, we should stop and discuss security, specifically the use of the state parameter. Cross-site request forgery, or CSRF, and Clickjacking are security vulnerabilities that must be addressed by individuals implementing OAuth. This is typically accomplished using the state parameter. state is sent in the authorization request and returned back in the response and should be a value that binds the user’s request to their authenticated state. For example, state could be a hash of the user’s session cookie, or some other nonce that can be linked to the user’s session.
141: When a user begins an authorization flow on the client, a state is generated that is unique to that user’s request. This value is stored somewhere only accessible to the client and the user, i.e. protected by the same-origin policy. When the user is redirected, the state parameter is returned. The client validates the request by checking that the state returned matches the stored value. If they match, it is a valid authorization request. If they do not match, it’s possible that someone intercepted the request or otherwise falsely authorized themselves to another user’s resources, and the request should be denied.
142: While Discord does not require the use of the state parameter, we support it and highly recommend that you implement it for the security of your own applications and data.
143: Issuer Identification
144: Every authorization response that Discord redirects to your redirect_uri includes an iss parameter set to https://discord.com. This follows RFC 9207 and is a best practice for OAuth2 authorization servers.
145: If your app supports more than one OAuth2 provider, check that iss matches the issuer in Discord’s authorization server metadata before you exchange the code. If it doesn’t match, reject the response. This prevents authorization server mix-up attacks, where a malicious provider tricks your app into sending it an authorization code that Discord issued.
146: Authorization Code Grant
147: The authorization code grant is what most developers will recognize as “standard OAuth2” and involves retrieving an access code and exchanging it for a user’s access token. It allows the authorization server to act as an intermediary between the client and the resource owner, so the resource owner’s credentials are never shared directly with the client.
148: All calls to the OAuth2 endpoints require either HTTP Basic authentication or client_id and client_secret supplied in the form data body.
149: Authorization URL Example
150: https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=157730590492196864&scope=identify%20guilds.join&state=15773059ghq9183habn&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fnicememe.website&prompt=consent&integration_type=0
151: client_id is your application’s client_id. scope is a list of OAuth2 scopes separated by url encoded spaces (%20). redirect_uri is whatever URL you registered when creating your application, url-encoded. state is the unique string mentioned in State and Security.
152: When someone navigates to this URL, they will be prompted to authorize your application for the requested scopes. On acceptance, they will be redirected to your redirect_uri, which will contain an additional querystring parameter, code. state will also be returned if previously sent, and should be validated at this point. The redirect also includes iss, which identifies Discord as the authorization server.
153: prompt controls how the authorization flow handles existing authorizations. If a user has previously authorized your application with the requested scopes and prompt is set to consent, it will request them to reapprove their authorization. If set to none, it will skip the authorization screen and redirect them back to your redirect URI without requesting their authorization. For passthrough scopes, like bot and webhook.incoming, authorization is always required.
154: The integration_type parameter specifies the installation context for the authorization. The installation context determines where the application will be installed, and is only relevant when scope contains applications.commands. When set to 0 (GUILD_INSTALL) the application will be authorized for installation to a server, and when set to 1 (USER_INSTALL) the application will be authorized for installation to a user. The application must be configured in the Developer Portal to support the provided integration_type.
155: Redirect URL Example
156: https://nicememe.website/?code=NhhvTDYsFcdgNLnnLijcl7Ku7bEEeee&state=15773059ghq9183habn&iss=https%3A%2F%2Fdiscord.com
157: code is now exchanged for the user’s access token by making a POST request to the token URL with the following parameters:
158: grant_type - must be set to authorization_code
159: code - the code from the querystring
160: redirect_uri - the redirect_uri associated with this authorization, usually from your authorization URL
161: Access Token Exchange Example
162: import requests
163: API_ENDPOINT = 'https://discord.com/api/v10'
164: CLIENT_ID = '332269999912132097'
165: CLIENT_SECRET = '937it3ow87i4ery69876wqire'
166: REDIRECT_URI = 'https://nicememe.website'
167: def exchange_code(code):
168: data = {
169: 'grant_type': 'authorization_code',
170: 'code': code,
171: 'redirect_uri': REDIRECT_URI
172: }
173: headers = {
174: 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
175: }
176: r = requests.post('%s/oauth2/token' % API_ENDPOINT, data=data, headers=headers, auth=(CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET))
177: r.raise_for_status()
178: return r.json()
179: In response, you will receive:
180: Access Token Response
181: {
182: "access_token": "6qrZcUqja7812RVdnEKjpzOL4CvHBFG",
183: "token_type": "Bearer",
184: "expires_in": 604800,
185: "refresh_token": "D43f5y0ahjqew82jZ4NViEr2YafMKhue",
186: "scope": "identify"
187: }
188: Having the user’s access token allows your application to make certain requests to the API on their behalf, restricted to whatever scopes were requested. expires_in is how long, in seconds, until the returned access token expires, allowing you to anticipate the expiration and refresh the token. To refresh, make another POST request to the token URL with the following parameters:
189: grant_type - must be set to refresh_token
190: refresh_token - the user’s refresh token
191: Refresh Token Exchange Example
192: import requests
193: API_ENDPOINT = 'https://discord.com/api/v10'
194: CLIENT_ID = '332269999912132097'
195: CLIENT_SECRET = '937it3ow87i4ery69876wqire'
196: def refresh_token(refresh_token):
197: data = {
198: 'grant_type': 'refresh_token',
199: 'refresh_token': refresh_token
200: }
201: headers = {
202: 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
203: }
204: r = requests.post('%s/oauth2/token' % API_ENDPOINT, data=data, headers=headers, auth=(CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET))
205: r.raise_for_status()
206: return r.json()
207: Boom; fresh access token response!
208: Token Revocation Example
209: To disable an access or refresh token, you can revoke it by making a POST request to the token revocation URL with the following parameters:
210: token - the access token or refresh token to revoke
211: token_type_hint (optional) - the token parameter’s type—either access_token or refresh_token
212: When you revoke a token, any active access or refresh tokens associated with that authorization will be revoked, regardless of the token and token_type_hint values you pass in.
213: import requests
214: API_ENDPOINT = 'https://discord.com/api/v10'
215: CLIENT_ID = '332269999912132097'
216: CLIENT_SECRET = '937it3ow87i4ery69876wqire'
217: def revoke_access_token(access_token):
218: data = {
219: 'token': access_token,
220: 'token_type_hint': 'access_token'
221: }
222: headers = {
223: 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
224: }
225: requests.post('%s/oauth2/token/revoke' % API_ENDPOINT, data=data, headers=headers, auth=(CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET))
226: Boom; the tokens are safely revoked.
227: Implicit Grant
228: The implicit OAuth2 grant is a simplified flow optimized for in-browser clients. Instead of issuing the client an authorization code to be exchanged for an access token, the client is directly issued an access token.
229: The implicit grant is not recommended outside of quick prototypes. It returns the access token directly in the redirect URL, where it can leak through browser history, logs, and Referer headers, and it doesn’t provide a refresh token. For production apps, use the authorization code grant with PKCE instead.
230: The URL is formatted as follows:
231: Authorization URL Example
232: https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize?response_type=token&client_id=290926444748734499&state=15773059ghq9183habn&scope=identify
233: On redirect, your redirect URI will contain additional URI fragments: access_token, token_type, expires_in, scope, state (if specified), and iss. These are not querystring parameters. Be mindful of the ”#” character:
234: Redirect URL Example
235: https://findingfakeurlsisprettyhard.tv/#access_token=RTfP0OK99U3kbRtHOoKLmJbOn45PjL&token_type=Bearer&expires_in=604800&scope=identify&state=15773059ghq9183habn&iss=https%3A%2F%2Fdiscord.com
236: There are tradeoffs in using the implicit grant flow. It is both quicker and easier to implement, but rather than exchanging a code and getting a token returned in a secure HTTP body, the access token is returned in the URI fragment, which makes it possibly exposed to unauthorized parties. You also are not returned a refresh token, so the user must explicitly re-authorize once their token expires.
237: Client Credentials Grant
238: The client credential flow is a quick and easy way for bot developers to get their own bearer tokens for testing purposes. By making a POST request to the token URL with a grant type of client_credentials, using Basic authentication with your client id as the username and your client secret as the password, you will be returned an access token for the bot owner. Therefore, always be super-extra-very-we-are-not-kidding-like-really-be-secure-make-sure-your-info-is-not-in-your-source-code careful with your client_id and client_secret. We don’t take kindly to imposters around these parts.
239: You can specify scopes with the scope parameter, which is a list of OAuth2 scopes separated by spaces:
240: Team applications are limited to the identify and applications.commands.update scope, because teams are not bound to a specific user.

242: import requests
243: API_ENDPOINT = 'https://discord.com/api/v10'
244: CLIENT_ID = '332269999912132097'
245: CLIENT_SECRET = '937it3ow87i4ery69876wqire'
246: def get_token():
247: data = {
248: 'grant_type': 'client_credentials',
249: 'scope': 'identify connections'
250: }
251: headers = {
252: 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
253: }
254: r = requests.post('%s/oauth2/token' % API_ENDPOINT, data=data, headers=headers, auth=(CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET))
255: r.raise_for_status()
256: return r.json()
257: In return, you will receive an access token (without a refresh token):

261: "token_type": "Bearer",
262: "expires_in": 604800,
263: "scope": "identify connections"

265: Bot Users
266: Discord’s API provides bot users, which are a separate type of user dedicated to automation. Bot users are automatically added to all apps, and are authenticated using the bot token found in your app’s settings. Unlike the normal OAuth2 flow, bot users have full access to most API routes without using bearer tokens, and can connect to the Real Time Gateway.
267: Bot vs User Accounts
268: Developers must abide by the terms of service, which includes refraining from automating standard user accounts (generally called “self-bots”) outside of the OAuth2/bot API.
269: Bot users have a few differences compared to standard Discord users:
270: Bots are added to guilds through the OAuth2 API, and cannot accept normal invites.
271: Bots cannot have friends or be added to or join Group DMs.
272: Verified bots do not have a maximum number of guilds.
273: Bots have an entirely separate set of rate limits.
274: Bot Authorization Flow
275: Bot authorization is a special server-less and callback-less OAuth2 flow that makes it easy for users to add bots to guilds. The URL you create looks similar to what we use for full stack implementation:
276: Bot Auth Parameters
277: namedescription
278: client_idyour app’s client id
279: scope?needs to include bot for the bot flow
280: permissions?the permissions you’re requesting
281: guild_id?pre-fills the dropdown picker with a guild for the user
282: disable_guild_select?true or false—disallows the user from changing the guild dropdown
283: integration_type?the installation context for the authorization
284: URL Example
285: https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=157730590492196864&scope=bot&permissions=1
286: In the case of bots, the scope parameter should be set to bot. There’s also a new parameter, permissions, which is an integer corresponding to the permission calculations for the bot. You’ll also notice the absence of response_type and redirect_uri. Bot authorization does not require these parameters because there is no need to retrieve the user’s access token.
287: When the user navigates to this page, they’ll be prompted to add the bot to a guild in which they have proper permissions. On acceptance, the bot will be added. Super easy!
288: If you happen to already know the ID of the guild the user will add your bot to, you can provide this ID in the URL as a guild_id=GUILD_ID parameter.
289: When the authorization page loads, that guild will be preselected in the dialog if that user has permission to add the bot to that guild. You can use this in conjunction with the parameter disable_guild_select=true to disallow the user from picking a different guild.
290: If you only provide the client_id parameter (with optionally permissions, guild_id, or disable_guild_select), the authorization will use the default install settings configured in the developer portal. Specifying scope, integration_type, or redirect_uri will override this behavior.
291: If your bot is super specific to your private clubhouse, or you just don’t like sharing, you can leave the Public Bot option unchecked in your application’s settings. If unchecked, only you can add the bot to guilds. If marked as public, anyone with your bot’s URL can add it to guilds in which they have proper permissions.
292: Advanced Bot Authorization
293: Devs can extend the bot authorization functionality. You can request additional scopes outside of bot and applications.commands, which will prompt a continuation into a complete authorization code grant flow and add the ability to request the user’s access token. If you request any scopes outside of bot and applications.commands, response_type is again mandatory; we will also automatically redirect the user to the first URI in your application’s registered list unless redirect_uri is specified.
294: When receiving the access code on redirect, there will be additional querystring parameters of guild_id and permissions. The guild_id parameter should only be used as a hint as to the relationship between your bot and a guild. To be sure of the relationship between your bot and the guild, consider requiring the Oauth2 code grant in your bot’s settings. Enabling it requires anyone adding your bot to a server to go through a full OAuth2 authorization code grant flow. When you retrieve the user’s access token, you’ll also receive information about the guild to which your bot was added:

350: Two-Factor Authentication Requirement
351: For bots with elevated permissions (permissions with a * next to them), we enforce two-factor authentication on the owner’s account when added to guilds that have server-wide 2FA enabled.
352: Webhooks
353: Discord’s webhook flow is a specialized version of an authorization code implementation. In this case, the scope querystring parameter needs to be set to webhook.incoming:
354: URL Example
355: https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=157730590492196864&scope=webhook.incoming&state=15773059ghq9183habn&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fnicememe.website
356: When the user navigates to this URL, they will be prompted to select a channel in which to allow the webhook. When the webhook is executed, it will post its message into this channel. On acceptance, the user will be redirected to your redirect_uri. The URL will contain the code querystring parameter which should be exchanged for an access token. In return, you will receive a slightly modified token response:
357: Webhook Token Response Example
358: {
359: "token_type": "Bearer",
360: "access_token": "GNaVzEtATqdh173tNHEXY9ZYAuhiYxvy",
361: "scope": "webhook.incoming",
362: "expires_in": 604800,
363: "refresh_token": "PvPL7ELyMDc1836457XCDh1Y8jPbRm",
364: "webhook": {
365: "application_id": "310954232226357250",
366: "name": "testwebhook",
367: "url": "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/347114750880120863/kKDdjXa1g9tKNs0-_yOwLyALC9gydEWP6gr9sHabuK1vuofjhQDDnlOclJeRIvYK-pj_",
368: "channel_id": "345626669224982402",
369: "token": "kKDdjXa1g9tKNs0-_yOwLyALC9gydEWP6gr9sHabuK1vuofjhQDDnlOclJeRIvYK-pj_",
370: "type": 1,
371: "avatar": null,
372: "guild_id": "290926792226357250",
373: "id": "347114750880120863"

376: From this object, you should store the webhook.token and webhook.id. See the execute webhook documentation for how to send messages with the webhook.
377: Any user that wishes to add your webhook to their channel will need to go through the full OAuth2 flow. A new webhook is created each time, so you will need to save the token and id. If you wish to send a message to all your webhooks, you’ll need to iterate over each stored id:token combination and make POST requests to each one. Be mindful of our Rate Limits!

120: Message Object
121: Represents a message sent in a channel within Discord.
122: Message Structure
123: Fields specific to the MESSAGE_CREATE and MESSAGE_UPDATE events are listed in the Gateway documentation.
124: An app will receive empty values in the content, embeds, attachments, and components fields while poll will be omitted if they have not configured (or been approved for) the MESSAGE_CONTENT privileged intent (1 << 15).
125: FieldTypeDescription
126: idsnowflakeid of the message
127: channel_idsnowflakeid of the channel the message was sent in
128: author [1]user objectthe author of this message (not guaranteed to be a valid user, see below)
129: content [2]stringcontents of the message
130: timestampISO8601 timestampwhen this message was sent
131: edited_timestamp?ISO8601 timestampwhen this message was edited (or null if never)
132: ttsbooleanwhether this was a TTS message
133: mention_everyonebooleanwhether this message mentions everyone
134: mentionsarray of user objectsusers specifically mentioned in the message
135: mention_rolesarray of role object idsroles specifically mentioned in this message
136: mention_channels? [3]array of channel mention objectschannels specifically mentioned in this message
137: attachments [2]array of attachment objectsany attached files that are not referenced in embeds or components
138: embeds [2]array of embed objectsany embedded content
139: reactions?array of reaction objectsreactions to the message
140: nonce?integer or stringused for validating a message was sent
141: pinnedbooleanwhether this message is pinned
142: webhook_id?snowflakeif the message is generated by a webhook, this is the webhook’s id
143: typeintegertype of message
144: activity?message activity objectsent with Rich Presence-related chat embeds
145: application?partial application objectsent with Rich Presence-related chat embeds
146: application_id?snowflakeif the message is an Interaction or application-owned webhook, this is the id of the application
147: flags?integermessage flags combined as a bitfield
148: message_reference?message reference objectdata showing the source of a crosspost, channel follow add, pin, or reply message
149: message_snapshots? [5]array of message snapshot objectsthe message associated with the message_reference. This is a minimal subset of fields in a message (e.g. author is excluded.)
150: referenced_message? [4]?message objectthe message associated with the message_reference
151: interaction_metadata?message interaction metadata objectSent if the message is sent as a result of an interaction
152: interaction?message interaction objectDeprecated in favor of interaction_metadata; sent if the message is a response to an interaction
153: thread?channel objectthe thread that was started from this message, includes thread member object
154: components? [2]array of message componentssent if the message contains components like buttons, action rows, or other interactive components
155: sticker_items?array of message sticker item objectssent if the message contains stickers
156: stickers?array of sticker objectsDeprecated the stickers sent with the message
157: position?integerA generally increasing integer (there may be gaps or duplicates) that represents the approximate position of the message in a thread, it can be used to estimate the relative position of the message in a thread in company with total_message_sent on parent thread
158: role_subscription_data?role subscription data objectdata of the role subscription purchase or renewal that prompted this ROLE_SUBSCRIPTION_PURCHASE message
159: resolved?resolved datadata for users, members, channels, and roles referenced in this message
160: poll? [2]poll objectA poll!
161: call?message call objectthe call associated with the message
162: shared_client_theme?shared client theme objectthe custom client-side theme shared via the message
163: [1] The author object follows the structure of the user object, but is only a valid user in the case where the message is generated by a user or bot user. If the message is generated by a webhook, the author object corresponds to the webhook’s id, username, and avatar. You can tell if a message is generated by a webhook by checking for the webhook_id on the message object.
164: [2] An app will receive empty values in the content, embeds, attachments, and components fields while poll will be omitted if they have not configured (or been approved for) the MESSAGE_CONTENT privileged intent (1 << 15).
165: [3] Not all channel mentions in a message will appear in mention_channels. Only textual channels that are visible to everyone in a public guild will ever be included. Only crossposted messages (via Channel Following) currently include mention_channels at all. If no mentions in the message meet these requirements, this field will not be sent.
166: [4] This field is only returned for messages with a type of 19 (REPLY), 21 (THREAD_STARTER_MESSAGE), or 23 (CONTEXT_MENU_COMMAND). If the message is one of these but the referenced_message field is not present, the backend did not attempt to fetch the message that was being replied to, so its state is unknown. If the field exists but is null, the referenced message was deleted.
167: [5] See message reference types
168: Message Types
169: Type 19 and 20 are only available in API v8 and above. In v6, they are represented as type 0. Additionally, type 21 is only available in API v9 and above.

327: Message Interaction Metadata Object
328: Metadata about the interaction, including the source of the interaction and relevant server and user IDs.
329: One of Application Command Interaction Metadata, Message Component Interaction Metadata, or Modal Submit Interaction Metadata.
330: Application Command Interaction Metadata Structure

336: original_response_message_id?snowflakeID of the original response message, present only on follow-up messages
337: target_user?user objectThe user the command was run on, present only on user command interactions
338: target_message_id?snowflakeThe ID of the message the command was run on, present only on message command interactions. The original response message will also have message_reference and referenced_message pointing to this message.
339: Message Component Interaction Metadata Structure

345: original_response_message_id?snowflakeID of the original response message, present only on follow-up messages
346: interacted_message_idsnowflakeID of the message that contained the interactive component
347: Modal Submit Interaction Metadata Structure

354: triggering_interaction_metadataApplication Command Interaction Metadata or Message Component Interaction Metadata objectMetadata for the interaction that was used to open the modal
355: Message Call Object
356: Information about the call in a private channel.
357: Message Call Object Structure
