360: ended_timestamp??ISO8601 timestamptime when call ended
361: Message Reference Object
362: Message Reference Structure
363: FieldTypeDescription
364: type? *integertype of reference.
365: message_id?snowflakeid of the originating message
366: channel_id? **snowflakeid of the originating message’s channel
367: guild_id?snowflakeid of the originating message’s guild
368: fail_if_not_exists?booleanwhen sending, whether to error if the referenced message doesn’t exist instead of sending as a normal (non-reply) message, default true
369: * If type is unset, DEFAULT can be assumed in order to match the behavior before message reference had types.
370: In future API versions this will become a required field.
371: ** channel_id is optional when creating a reply, but will always be present when receiving an event/response that includes this data model. Required for forwards.
372: Message Reference Types
373: Determines how associated data is populated.
374: TypeValueCoupled Message FieldDescription
375: DEFAULT0referenced_messageA standard reference used by replies.
376: FORWARD1message_snapshotReference used to point to a message at a point in time.
377: FORWARD can only be used for basic messages; i.e. messages which do not have strong bindings to a non global entity.
378: Thus we support only messages with type DEFAULT, REPLY, CHAT_INPUT_COMMAND, or CONTEXT_MENU_COMMAND, and don’t support messages with a poll, call, or activity.
379: This is subject to change in the future.
380: Applications must be able to read a message’s content in order to forward it. An application attempting to forward a message it cannot read will receive error code 160014 with the message “You cannot forward a message whose content you cannot read.”
381: Message Reference Content Attribution
382: Message references are generic attribution on a message.
383: There are multiple message types that have a message_reference object.
384: Crosspost messages
385: These are messages that originated from another channel (IS_CROSSPOST flag).
386: These messages have all three fields, which point to the original message that was crossposted.
387: Channel Follow Add messages
388: These are automatic messages sent when a channel is followed into the current channel (type 12).
389: These messages have the channel_id and guild_id fields, which point to the followed announcement channel.
390: Pin messages
391: These are automatic messages sent when a message is pinned (type 6).
392: These messages have message_id and channel_id, and guild_id if it is in a guild, which point to the message that was pinned.
393: Forwards
394: These are messages which capture a snapshot of a message.
395: These messages have an array of message_snapshot objects containing a copy of the original message. This copy follows the same structure as a message, but has only the minimal set of fields returned required for context/rendering.
396: of note: author will be excluded
397: A forwarded message can be identified by looking at its message_reference.type field
398: message_snapshots will be the message data associated with the forward. Currently we support only 1 snapshot.
399: prevents spoofing forwarded data
400: message_snapshots are taken the moment a forward message is created, and are immutable; any mutations to the original message will not be propagated.
401: Forwards are created by including a message_reference with FORWARD type when sending a message.
402: Required fields: type, message_id, channel_id
403: the requestor must have VIEW_CHANNEL permissions
404: Replies
405: These are messages replying to a previous message (type 19).
406: These messages have message_id and channel_id, and guild_id if it is in a guild, which point to the message that was replied to. The channel_id and guild_id will be the same as the reply.
407: Replies are created by including a message_reference when sending a message. When sending, only message_id is required.
408: These messages can have the referenced message resolved in the referenced_message field.
409: Thread Created messages
410: These are automatic messages sent when a public thread is created from an old message or without a message (type 18).
411: These messages have the channel_id and guild_id fields, which point to the created thread channel.
412: Thread starter messages
413: These are the first message in public threads created from messages. They point back to the message in the parent channel from which the thread was started. (type 21)
414: These messages have message_id, channel_id, and guild_id.
415: These messages can have the referenced message resolved in the referenced_message field.
416: These messages will never have content, embeds, or attachments, mainly just the message_reference and referenced_message fields.
417: Poll result messages
418: These are automatic messages sent after a poll has ended and the results have been finalized. (type 46)
419: These messages have message_id and channel_id, which point to the original poll message. The channel_id will be the same as that of the poll.
420: The author will be the same as the author of the poll and will be mentioned.
421: These messages contain a poll_result embed
422: Context Menu Command messages
423: These are messages sent when a user uses a context menu Application Command. (type 23)
424: If the command was a message command, the message will have message_id and channel_id, and guild_id if it is in a guild, which point to the message that the command was used on. The channel_id and guild_id will be the same as the new message.
425: These messages can have the referenced message resolved in the referenced_message field.
426: Voice Messages
427: Voice messages are messages with the IS_VOICE_MESSAGE flag. They have the following properties.
428: They cannot be edited.
429: Only a single audio attachment is allowed. No content, stickers, etc…
430: The attachment has additional fields: duration_secs and waveform. The Content-Type of the attachment must begin with audio/ to respect these fields.
431: The waveform is intended to be a preview of the entire voice message, with 1 byte per datapoint encoded in base64. Clients sample the recording at most
432: once per 100 milliseconds, but will downsample so that no more than 256 datapoints are in the waveform.
433: As of 2023-04-14, clients upload a 1 channel, 48000 Hz, 32kbps Opus stream in an OGG container.
434: The encoding, and the waveform details, are an implementation detail and may change without warning or documentation.
435: Message Snapshot Object

441: While message snapshots are able to support nested snapshots, we currently limit the depth of nesting to 1.

485: Embed Flags

491: Content scanning can run after the message is sent, so the CONTAINS_* flags may not be present on the initial message and can be added later in a Message Update event.If your app reposts media from users, check the flags on the message you send and in any later Message Update event, and take action, like deleting the message, if the media was flagged.

537: Embed Limits
538: To facilitate showing rich content, rich embeds do not follow the traditional limits of message content. However, some limits are still in place to prevent excessively large embeds. The following table describes the limits:
539: All of the following limits are measured inclusively. Leading and trailing whitespace characters are not included (they are trimmed automatically).
540: FieldLimit
541: title256 characters
542: description4096 characters
543: fieldsUp to 25 field objects
544: field.name256 characters
545: field.value1024 characters
546: footer.text2048 characters
547: author.name256 characters
548: Additionally, the combined sum of characters in all title, description, field.name, field.value, footer.text, and author.name fields across all embeds attached to a message must not exceed 6000 characters. Violating any of these constraints will result in a Bad Request response.

615: Allowed Mentions Object
616: Setting the allowed_mentions field lets you determine whether users will receive notifications when you include mentions in the message content, or the content of components attached to that message. This field is always validated against your permissions and the presence of said mentions in the message, to avoid “phantom” pings where users receive a notification without a visible mention in the message. For example, if you want to ping everyone, including it in the allowed_mentions field is not enough, the mention format (@everyone) must also be present in the content of the message or its components. It is important to note that setting this field does not guarantee a push notification will be sent, as additional factors can influence this:
617: To mention roles and notify their members, the role’s mentionable field must be set to true, or the bot must have the MENTION_EVERYONE permission
618: To mention @everyone and @here, the bot must have the MENTION_EVERYONE permission
619: Setting the SUPPRESS_NOTIFICATIONS flag when sending a message will disable push notifications and only cause a notification badge
620: Users can customize their notification settings through the Discord app, which might cause them to only receive a notification badge and no push notification
621: Allowed Mention Types
622: TypeValueDescription
623: Role Mentions”roles”Controls role mentions
624: User Mentions”users”Controls user mentions
625: Everyone Mentions”everyone”Controls @everyone and @here mentions
626: Default Settings for Allowed Mentions
627: The default value for the allowed_mentions field, used when it is not passed in the body, varies depending on the context:
628: In regular messages, all mention types are parsed, which is equivalent to sending the following data:
629: {
630: "parse": ["users", "roles", "everyone"]
631: }
632: In interactions and webhooks, only user mentions are parsed, which corresponds to the following:
633: {
634: "parse": ["users"]
635: }
636: FieldTypeDescription
637: parse?array of allowed mention typesAn array of allowed mention types to parse from the content
638: roles?array of snowflakesArray of role ids to mention, max 100
639: users?array of snowflakesArray of user ids to mention, max 100
640: replied_user?booleanFor replies, whether to mention the author of the message being replied to, defaults to false
641: Allowed Mentions Examples
642: Because the behavior of the allowed_mentions field is more complex than it seems, here’s a set of examples:
643: In the following case, we are sending a regular message without configuring allowed_mentions. As a result, all included mentions will be parsed.
644: {
645: "content": "@here Hello <@&1234> and <@5678> 👋"
646: }
647: If you want to completely suppress all mentions in the message, you can configure the allowed_mentions field as we’ve documented above:
648: {
649: "content": "@here Hello <@&1234> and <@5678> 👋",
650: "allowed_mentions": {
651: "parse": []
652: }
653: }
654: It is important to note that the parse field is mutually exclusive with the other fields. In the example below, only the 1234 role and the 5678 user mentions would be parsed, but not the @here at the beginning. Passing a falsy value such as null or an empty array into the users field does not trigger a validation error.
655: {
656: "content": "@here Hello <@&1234> and <@5678> 👋",
657: "allowed_mentions": {
658: "parse": ["users", "roles"],
659: "users": []
660: }
661: }
662: In this next example, only @everyone would be parsed, as well as users 1234 and 5678 in case they suppressed @everyone mentions in their settings.
663: {
664: "content": "@everyone <@1234> <@5678> <@&789> 👋",
665: "allowed_mentions": {
666: "parse": ["everyone"],
667: "users": ["1234", "5678"]
668: }
669: }
670: Due to possible ambiguities, not all configurations are accepted. Here’s an example of an invalid configuration, because it includes both parse and users, despite those fields being mutually exclusive, causing a validation error.
671: {
672: "content": "@everyone <@1234> <@5678> <@9012> <@&200>",
673: "allowed_mentions": {
674: "parse": ["users"],
675: "users": ["1234", "5678"]
676: }
677: }
678: Any entities whose id is included can be mentioned. Do note the API will silently ignore entities whose id are present in the allowed_mentions field, but not in the content of the message or its components. For example, in the following configuration, the user 123 mention would be parsed because it is present in the content. However, since there is no mention of user 456 in the content, they would not be notified.
679: {
680: "content": "<@123> Time for some memes 🤠",
681: "allowed_mentions": {
682: "users": ["123", "456"]
683: }
684: }

721: Get Channel Messages
722: Retrieves the messages in a channel. Returns an array of message objects from newest to oldest on success.
723: If operating on a guild channel, this endpoint requires the current user to have the VIEW_CHANNEL permission. If the channel is a voice channel, they must also have the CONNECT permission.
724: If the current user is missing the READ_MESSAGE_HISTORY permission in the channel, then no messages will be returned.
725: The before, after, and around parameters are mutually exclusive, only one may be passed at a time.

732: Search Guild Messages
733: Returns a list of messages without the reactions key that match a search query in the guild. Requires the READ_MESSAGE_HISTORY permission.
734: This endpoint is restricted according to whether the MESSAGE_CONTENT Privileged Intent is enabled for your application.
735: If the entity you are searching is not yet indexed, the endpoint will return a 202 accepted response. The response body will not contain any search results, and will look similar to an error response:
736: {
737: "message": "Index not yet available. Try again later",
738: "code": 110000,
739: "documents_indexed": 0,
740: "retry_after": 2
741: }
742: You should retry the request after the timeframe specified in the retry_after field. If the retry_after field is 0, you should retry the request after a short delay.
743: Due to speed optimizations, search may return slightly fewer results than the limit specified when messages have not been accessed for a long time.
744: Clients should not rely on the length of the messages array to paginate results.Additionally, when messages are actively being created or deleted, the total_results field may not be accurate.

812: Get Channel Message
813: Retrieves a specific message in the channel. Returns a message object on success.
814: If operating on a guild channel, this endpoint requires the current user to have the VIEW_CHANNEL and READ_MESSAGE_HISTORY permissions. If the channel is a voice channel, they must also have the CONNECT permission.
815: Create Message
816: Discord may strip certain characters from message content, like invalid unicode characters or characters which cause unexpected message formatting. If you are passing user-generated strings into message content, consider sanitizing the data to prevent unexpected behavior and using allowed_mentions to prevent unexpected mentions.
817: Post a message to a guild text or DM channel. Returns a message object. Fires a Message Create Gateway event. See message formatting for more information on how to properly format messages.
818: To create a message as a reply or forward of another message, apps can include a message_reference.
819: Refer to the documentation for required fields.
820: Files must be attached using a multipart/form-data body as described in Uploading Files.
821: Limitations
822: When operating on a guild channel, the current user must have the SEND_MESSAGES permission.
823: When sending a message with tts (text-to-speech) set to true, the current user must have the SEND_TTS_MESSAGES permission.
824: When creating a message as a reply to another message, the current user must have the READ_MESSAGE_HISTORY permission.
825: The referenced message must exist and cannot be a system message.
826: The maximum request size when sending a message is 25 MiB
827: For the embed object, you can set every field except type (it will be rich regardless of if you try to set it), provider, video, and any height, width, or proxy_url values for images.

829: FieldTypeDescription
830: content?*stringMessage contents (up to 2000 characters)
831: nonce?integer or stringCan be used to verify a message was sent (up to 25 characters). Value will appear in the Message Create event.
832: tts?booleantrue if this is a TTS message
833: embeds?*array of embed objectsUp to 10 rich embeds (up to 6000 characters)
834: allowed_mentions?allowed mention objectAllowed mentions for the message
835: message_reference?*message referenceInclude to make your message a reply or a forward
836: components?*array of message component objectsComponents to include with the message
837: sticker_ids?*array of snowflakesIDs of up to 3 stickers in the server to send in the message
838: files[n]?*file contentsContents of the file being sent. See Uploading Files
839: payload_json?stringJSON-encoded body of non-file params, only for multipart/form-data requests. See Uploading Files
840: attachments?array of partial attachment request objectsMetadata for the attachments. See Uploading Files
841: flags?**integerMessage flags combined as a bitfield (only SUPPRESS_EMBEDS, SUPPRESS_NOTIFICATIONS, IS_VOICE_MESSAGE, and IS_COMPONENTS_V2 can be set)
842: enforce_nonce?booleanIf true and nonce is present, it will be checked for uniqueness in the past few minutes. If another message was created by the same author with the same nonce, that message will be returned and no new message will be created.
843: poll?poll request objectA poll!
844: shared_client_theme?shared client theme objectThe custom client-side theme to share via the message

886: Edit Message
887: Edit a previously sent message. The fields content, embeds, flags and components can be edited by the original message author. Other users can only edit flags and only if they have the MANAGE_MESSAGES permission in the corresponding channel. When specifying flags, ensure to include all previously set flags/bits in addition to ones that you are modifying. Only flags documented in the table below may be modified by users (unsupported flag changes are currently ignored without error).
888: When the content field is edited, the arrays mentions and mention_roles and the boolean mention_everyone in the message object will be reconstructed from scratch based on the new content. When the message flag IS_COMPONENTS_V2 is set, the reconstructed arrays and boolean are based on the edited content in the components array. The allowed_mentions field of the edit request controls how this happens. If there is no explicit allowed_mentions in the edit request, the content will be parsed with default allowances, that is, without regard to whether or not an allowed_mentions was present in the request that originally created the message.
889: Returns a message object. Fires a Message Update Gateway event.
890: Refer to Uploading Files for details on attachments and multipart/form-data requests.
891: Any provided files will be appended to the message. To remove or replace files you will have to supply the attachments field which specifies the files to retain on the message after edit.
892: Starting with API v10, the attachments array must contain all attachments that should be present after edit, including retained and new attachments provided in the request body.
893: All parameters to this endpoint are optional and nullable.

899: allowed_mentionsallowed mention objectAllowed mentions for the message
900: componentsarray of message componentComponents to include with the message
901: files[n]file contentsContents of the file being sent/edited. See Uploading Files
902: payload_jsonstringJSON-encoded body of non-file params (multipart/form-data only). See Uploading Files
903: attachmentsarray of attachment request objectsAttached files to keep and their metadata. See Uploading Files
904: * The SUPPRESS_EMBEDS flag can be both set and unset, while the IS_COMPONENTS_V2 flag can only be set. When the IS_COMPONENTS_V2 flag is set, any of the used content, embeds, sticker_ids, or poll fields must have their values reset to empty. For content and poll this is null. For embeds and sticker_ids this is []. Failing to do this will result in a 400 BAD REQUEST response.

10: Bots: An introduction for developers
11: Bots are small applications that run entirely within the Telegram app. Users interact with bots through flexible interfaces that can support any kind of task or service. For more information, see:
12: Detailed Guide to Bot Features
13: Full API Reference for Developers
14: Basic Tutorial: From @BotFather to 'Hello World'
15: The Telegram Bot Platform hosts more than 10 million bots and is free for both users and developers.
16: What Can You Do with Bots?
17: Replace Entire Websites
18: Natively Integrate AI Agents and Chatbots
19: Manage Your Business
20: Receive Payments
21: Create Custom Tools
22: Integrate with Services and Devices
23: Host Games
24: Build Social Networks
25: Monetize Your Service
26: Promote Your Project
27: Anything Else!
28: Replace Entire Websites
29: Telegram bots can host Mini Apps built with JavaScript. This allows for infinitely flexible interfaces that can power everything from online stores to arcade games. Unlike websites, bots support seamless authorization and notifications through Telegram out of the box.
30: Try @DurgerKingBot – or check out the dedicated guide to Mini Apps to build your own.
31: Natively Integrate AI Agents and Chatbots
32: On Telegram, AI bots can natively meet, chat and compete: users can summon assistants into the same chat, watch their responses stream in real time, coordinate multiple agents at once or have them manage their whole account.
33: Bots also support threaded conversations to manage several different topics in parallel — letting users easily access information from previous chats.
34: See here to check out more tools and integrations available for AI-powered bots on Telegram.
35: Manage Your Business
36: Telegram Business users can connect Telegram bots to process and answer messages on their behalf, via their personal account. This allows businesses to seamlessly integrate any existing tools and workflows, or add new AI assistants to increase productivity.
37: As we continue to expand the set of free tools available to bots through this integration, we encourage all developers to innovate and develop useful applications and services for businesses on Telegram.
38: Developers can turn on Business Mode in @BotFather if their bot supports integration with Telegram Business accounts.
39: Receive Payments
40: Bots can sell all kinds of goods and services on Telegram – to anyone in the world. Telegram Stars allow users to securely and effortlessly buy digital products via in-app purchases. In addition, physical products can be easily purchased through third-party providers that support integration with Mini Apps.
41: Try @ShopBot – or check out our dedicated guides for digital and physical products to build your own.
42: Create Custom Tools
43: Increase your productivity by creating bots for specific tasks – like converting files, managing chats or fetching today’s forecast. Users can chat directly with bots, or add them to groups and channels to introduce extra features.
44: Mini apps can generate media and files – that users can effortlessly share to other chats or a post as a story.
45: Integrate with Services and Devices
46: Mini apps can seamlessly integrate with third-party services, APIs and devices to instantly process and update information – like changing a user's emoji status when they start a game or get in a taxi .
47: By default, Mini Apps seamlessly integrate with Android and iOS, allowing users to add direct shortcuts to their device’s home screen.
48: Likewise, many popular platforms already have official Telegram bots, which allow users to comfortably access content in one app – or perform quick searches using inline mode.
49: Try @GMailBot, @GitHubBot, @Bing, @YouTube, @wiki and more.
50: Host Games
51: Developers can create both lightweight HTML5 Games and immersive full-screen modern games with support for detailed motion controls, location-based points of interest and dynamic hardware optimizations.
52: Try some of the games in the @Gamee library – or check out the HTML5 and Mini App manuals to build your own.
53: Build Social Networks
54: Bots can serve as an intermediary to connect users based on shared interests, location, and more. Coordinate meetups, show local services, or help people sell second-hand items.
55: Users can place direct shortcuts to specific mini apps on the home screen of their devices – accessing services in one tap.
56: Monetize Your Service
57: Telegram offers a robust ecosystem of monetization features, allowing any bot to support its development with multiple revenue streams. Popular bots can passively earn income through Revenue Sharing from Telegram Ads, implement subscription plans for users – or offer paid content and digital products for Telegram Stars.
58: Telegram Stars in your bot's balance can be used to increase message limits, send gifts to users or accept rewards in Toncoin.
59: Promote Your Project
60: Bots can host affiliate marketing programs – giving developers a transparent way to quickly scale with organic growth from user referrals.
61: Affiliate Programs support custom revenue sharing rates and variable commission periods, allowing you to customize your offers and update your campaign over time.
62: To learn more and get started in just a few taps, check out our dedicated guide.
63: Anything Else
64: The possibilities for bots are endless – from simple scripts to complex mini apps. Whether you’re a beginner or professional programmer, you can create personalized tools with the help of the Bot Platform.
65: All Mini Apps you build on Telegram can be highly customized to fit your brand identity, including by uploading high-quality media demos and setting a custom Loading Screen with your own logo and color palette
66: How Do Bots Work?
67: For a detailed explanation of Bot Features, see this guide
68: Telegram bots are special accounts that do not need a phone number to set up. Bots are connected to their owner’s server, which processes inputs and requests from users.
69: Telegram’s intermediary server handles all encryption and communication with the Telegram API. Developers communicate with this server via an easy HTTPS-interface with a simplified version of the Telegram API – known as the Bot API.
70: How Are Bots Different from Users?
71: Bots are able to process inputs and requests in ways that user accounts can’t, but there are several differences between a bot and a normal user.
72: Bots don’t have ‘last seen’ or online statuses – instead they show a ‘bot’ label in the chat.
73: Bots have limited cloud storage – older messages may be removed by the server shortly after they have been processed.
74: Bots can't start conversations with users. A user must either add them to a group or send them a message first. People can search for your bot’s username or start a chat via its unique t.me/bot_username link.
75: By default, bots added to groups only see relevant messages in the chat (see Privacy Mode).
76: Bots never eat, sleep or complain (unless expressly programmed otherwise).
77: Bot Links
78: Bot usernames normally require a ‘bot’ suffix, but some bots don’t have them – such as @stickers, @gif, @wiki or @bing.
79: Anyone can assign collectible usernames to bots, including those without the 'bot' suffix.
80: How Do I Create a Bot?
81: Creating Telegram bots is super-easy, but you will need at least some skills in computer programming.
82: Creating a bot is streamlined by Telegram’s Bot API, which gives the tools and framework required to integrate your code. To get started, message @BotFather on Telegram to register your bot and receive its authentication token.
83: Your bot token is its unique identifier – store it in a secure place, and only share it with people who need direct access to the bot. Everyone who has your token will have full control over your bot.
84: What Next?
85: We recommend that you check out our guide to Bot Features to see what you can teach your bot to do:

13: The Bot API is an HTTP-based interface created for developers keen on building bots for Telegram.

16: Subscribe to @BotNews to be the first to know about the latest updates and join the discussion in @BotTalk
17: November 22, 2026
18: Bot API 10.5
19: Bot Settings
20: Added the method setMySettings, allowing bots to change their settings, including inline mode settings, privacy mode, the ability to be added to groups, forum topic mode in private chats, and the mode of receiving callback queries.
21: Added the ability to receive callback queries from buttons in messages sent by the bot with the field inline_message_id instead of the field message in the class CallbackQuery, depending on the parameter callback_query_mode of the method setMySettings.
22: Added the ability for bots to show the list of topics in a sidebar in private chats with the bot using the parameter has_topic_sidebar of the method setMySettings.
23: Split out the class BotFullInfo from the class User and changed the return type of the method getMe to BotFullInfo. The fields that were returned only in getMe were removed from the class User.
24: Added the field active_usernames to the class BotFullInfo, allowing the bot to get the list of all its active usernames.
25: Added the field inline_query_placeholder to the class BotFullInfo, allowing the bot to get its placeholder for inline queries.
26: Added the field needs_inline_query_location to the class BotFullInfo, allowing the bot to check whether it requests the location of the user with every inline query.
27: Added the field has_topic_sidebar to the class BotFullInfo, allowing the bot to check whether topics in private chats with the bot are shown in a sidebar.
28: General
29: Added the ability for bot owners to invite up to 10 users at once to private chats with the bot by pressing the link https://t.me/botinvite/<bot_username>. The bot can send messages to the invited users.
30: Added the field inviter to the class WriteAccessAllowed for service messages about users invited to the private chat with the bot by the owner of the bot.
31: Replaced the field text with the field blocks in the classes RichBlockExpandableBlockQuotation and InputRichBlockExpandableBlockQuotation, allowing expandable block quotations to contain arbitrary blocks.

36: Added the method sendWidget, allowing bots to send messages with HTML widgets. Currently, in the production environment, widgets can be sent only to private chats, and sent widgets automatically have protected content and therefore can't be forwarded.
37: Added the method sendSharedWidget, allowing bots to send again shared widgets created by the bot.

40: Added the classes WidgetQueryType, WidgetQueryTypeData, WidgetQueryTypeSignData, WidgetQueryTypeSentTransaction and WidgetQueryWallet, describing the type of a query from a widget. A query can contain data for the bot together with the TON wallet card of the user, data signed by a TON wallet of the user, or a notification about a transaction sent from a TON wallet of the user.

52: Added the field quote_rich_texts to the class ReplyParameters, allowing bots to quote rich messages.

55: Added the class TonWalletTransfer and the field ton_wallet_transfer to the class Message for service messages about transfers with a TON wallet.

121: Added the class CommunityChatRemoved and the field community_chat_removed to the class Message.

123: General
124: Added updates about changes to a user payment subscription, represented by the class BotSubscriptionUpdated and the field subscription in the class Update.
125: Hardened the security of Mini Apps by disallowing the usage of Mini App methods from origins different from the original Mini App domain. The protection will be automatically enabled for all Mini Apps on July 20, 2026. You can opt-out from the protection through the @BotFather Mini App. If you do so, you acknowledge that it is the responsibility of the bot to ensure that the Mini App has no links to untrusted sites.
126: See earlier changes »
127: Authorizing your bot
128: Each bot is given a unique authentication token when it is created. The token looks something like 123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11, but we'll use simply <token> in this document instead. You can learn about obtaining tokens and generating new ones in this document.
129: Making requests
130: All queries to the Telegram Bot API must be served over HTTPS and need to be presented in this form: https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/METHOD_NAME. Like this for example:
131: https://api.telegram.org/bot123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11/getMe
132: We support GET and POST HTTP methods. We support four ways of passing parameters in Bot API requests:
133: URL query string
134: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
135: application/json (except for uploading files)
136: multipart/form-data (use to upload files)
137: The response contains a JSON object, which always has a Boolean field 'ok' and may have an optional String field 'description' with a human-readable description of the result. If 'ok' equals True, the request was successful and the result of the query can be found in the 'result' field. In case of an unsuccessful request, 'ok' equals False and the error is explained in the 'description'. An Integer 'error_code' field is also returned, but its contents are subject to change in the future. Some errors may also have an optional field 'parameters' of the type ResponseParameters, which can help to automatically handle the error.
138: All methods in the Bot API are case-insensitive.
139: All queries must be made using UTF-8.
140: Making requests when getting updates
141: If you're using webhooks, you can perform a request to the Bot API while sending an answer to the webhook. Use either application/json or application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data response content type for passing parameters. Specify the method to be invoked in the method parameter of the request. It's not possible to know that such a request was successful or get its result.
142: Please see our FAQ for examples.
143: Using a Local Bot API Server
144: The Bot API server source code is available at telegram-bot-api. You can run it locally and send the requests to your own server instead of https://api.telegram.org. If you switch to a local Bot API server, your bot will be able to:
145: Download files without a size limit.
146: Upload files up to 2000 MB.
147: Upload files using their local path and the file URI scheme.
148: Use an HTTP URL for the webhook.
149: Use any local IP address for the webhook.
150: Use any port for the webhook.
151: Set max_webhook_connections up to 100000.
152: Receive the absolute local path as a value of the file_path field without the need to download the file after a getFile request.
153: Do I need a Local Bot API Server
154: The majority of bots will be OK with the default configuration, running on our servers. But if you feel that you need one of these features, you're welcome to switch to your own at any time.
155: Getting updates
156: There are two mutually exclusive ways of receiving updates for your bot - the getUpdates method on one hand and webhooks on the other. Incoming updates are stored on the server until the bot receives them either way, but they will not be kept longer than 24 hours.
157: Regardless of which option you choose, you will receive JSON-serialized Update objects as a result.

254: getUpdates
255: Use this method to receive incoming updates using long polling (wiki). Returns an Array of Update objects.
256: Parameter
257: Type
258: Required
259: Description
260: offset
261: Integer
262: Optional
263: Identifier of the first update to be returned. Must be greater by one than the highest among the identifiers of previously received updates. By default, updates starting with the earliest unconfirmed update are returned. An update is considered confirmed as soon as getUpdates is called with an offset higher than its update_id. The negative offset can be specified to retrieve updates starting from -offset update from the end of the updates queue. All previous updates will be forgotten.
264: limit
265: Integer
266: Optional
267: Limits the number of updates to be retrieved. Values between 1-100 are accepted. Defaults to 100.
268: timeout
269: Integer
270: Optional
271: Timeout in seconds for long polling. Defaults to 0, i.e. usual short polling. Should be positive, short polling should be used for testing purposes only.
272: allowed_updates
273: Array of String
274: Optional
275: A JSON-serialized list of the update types you want your bot to receive. For example, specify ["message", "edited_channel_post", "callback_query"] to only receive updates of these types. See Update for a complete list of available update types. Specify an empty list to receive all update types except chat_member, message_reaction, and message_reaction_count (default). If not specified, the previous setting will be used.
276: Please note that this parameter doesn't affect updates created before the call to getUpdates, so unwanted updates may be received for a short period of time.
277: Notes
278: 1. This method will not work if an outgoing webhook is set up.
279: 2. In order to avoid getting duplicate updates, recalculate offset after each server response.
280: setWebhook
281: Use this method to specify a URL and receive incoming updates via an outgoing webhook. Whenever there is an update for the bot, we will send an HTTPS POST request to the specified URL, containing a JSON-serialized Update. In case of an unsuccessful request (a request with response HTTP status code different from 2XY), we will repeat the request and give up after a reasonable amount of attempts. Returns True on success.
282: If you'd like to make sure that the webhook was set by you, you can specify secret data in the parameter secret_token. If specified, the request will contain a header “X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token” with the secret token as content.

305: Optional

See Update for a complete list of available update types. Specify an empty list to receive all update types except chat_member, message_reaction, and message_reaction_count (default). If not specified, the previous setting will be used.

1195: Describes reply parameters for the message that is being sent.
1196: Field
1197: Type

1199: message_id

Not supported for messages sent on behalf of a business account, messages from channel direct messages chats and ephemeral messages.
1205: ephemeral_message_id
1206: Integer
1207: Optional. Identifier of the incoming ephemeral message that will be replied to in the current chat. A reply to an ephemeral message must itself be an ephemeral message. An ephemeral message may only be replied to within 15 seconds of being sent. Required if message_id isn't specified.
1208: allow_sending_without_reply
1209: Boolean
1210: Optional. Pass True if the message should be sent even if the specified message to be replied to is not found. Always False for replies in another chat or forum topic, and sent ephemeral messages. Always True for messages sent on behalf of a business account.
1211: quote
1212: String
1213: Optional. Quoted part of the message to be replied to; 0-1024 characters after entities parsing. The quote must be an exact substring of the message to be replied to, including bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, spoiler, custom_emoji, and date_time entities. The message will fail to send if the quote isn't found in the original message. Ignored for ephemeral messages.
1214: quote_parse_mode
1215: String
1216: Optional. Mode for parsing entities in the quote. See formatting options for more details.
1217: quote_entities
1218: Array of MessageEntity
1219: Optional. A JSON-serialized list of special entities that appear in the quote. It can be specified instead of quote_parse_mode.
1220: quote_rich_texts
1221: Array of RichText
1222: Optional. A JSON-serialized list of quoted parts of the rich message to be replied to. Must contain one element for each quoted text of the message in the order of their appearance. Each of the following is a separate quoted text: the text of a paragraph, a heading, a preformatted block, a footer, or a mathematical expression; the text and the credit of a block quotation or a pull quotation; the summary of a details block; the caption and each cell of a table; the text and the credit of a caption of a media block, a collage, a slideshow, or a map. Texts of blocks nested in lists, block quotations, details, collages, and slideshows are separate quoted texts too. The first and the last elements can contain only a part of the corresponding text; all other elements must contain the whole text. Formatting of the quoted parts must be kept, and rich texts must be nested in the same way as in the message received from the server. Mathematical expressions must be quoted entirely. Buttons in RichBlockButtons, anchors and dividers can't be quoted. Up to 32 quoted texts with total length up to 1024 characters can be specified. Only plain text, RichTextBold, RichTextItalic, RichTextUnderline, RichTextStrikethrough, RichTextSpoiler, RichTextSubscript, RichTextSuperscript, RichTextDateTime, RichTextCustomEmoji, RichTextMathematicalExpression, and arrays of them are kept in the quote; other rich text types are replaced with their text. If non-empty, then quote, quote_parse_mode and quote_entities are ignored.

1225: Optional. Position of the quote in the original message in UTF-16 code units. For quotes from rich messages, it is the position in the text formed by joining plain texts of all quotable texts of the message, separated by line feeds.

3183: Example: A poll bot for groups runs in privacy mode (only receives commands, replies to its messages and mentions). There could be two ways to create a new poll:
3184: Explain the user how to send a command with parameters (e.g. /newpoll question answer1 answer2). May be appealing for hardcore users but lacks modern day polish.

5351: Sending files
5352: There are three ways to send files (photos, stickers, audio, media, etc.):
5353: If the file is already stored somewhere on the Telegram servers, you don't need to reupload it: each file object has a file_id field, simply pass this file_id as a parameter instead of uploading. There are no limits for files sent this way.
5354: Provide Telegram with an HTTP URL for the file to be sent. Telegram will download and send the file. 5 MB max size for photos and 20 MB max for other types of content.
5355: Post the file using multipart/form-data in the usual way that files are uploaded via the browser. 10 MB max size for photos, 50 MB for other files.
5356: Sending by file_id
5357: It is not possible to change the file type when resending by file_id. I.e. a video can't be sent as a photo, a photo can't be sent as a document, etc.
5358: It is not possible to resend thumbnails.
5359: Resending a photo by file_id will send all of its sizes.
5360: file_id is unique for each individual bot and can't be transferred from one bot to another.
5361: file_id uniquely identifies a file, but a file can have different valid file_ids even for the same bot.
5362: Sending by URL
5363: When sending by URL the target file must have the correct MIME type (e.g., audio/mpeg for sendAudio, etc.).
5364: In sendDocument, sending by URL will currently only work for .PDF and .ZIP files.
5365: To use sendVoice, the file must have the type audio/ogg and be no more than 1MB in size. 1-20MB voice notes will be sent as files.
5366: Other configurations may work but we can't guarantee that they will.

5405: Available methods
5406: All methods in the Bot API are case-insensitive. We support GET and POST HTTP methods. Use either URL query string or application/json or application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data for passing parameters in Bot API requests.
5407: On successful call, a JSON-object containing the result will be returned.
5408: getMe
5409: A simple method for testing your bot's authentication token. Requires no parameters. Returns information about the bot in form of a BotFullInfo object.
5410: logOut
5411: Use this method to log out from the cloud Bot API server before launching the bot locally. You must log out the bot before running it locally, otherwise there is no guarantee that the bot will receive updates. After a successful call, you can immediately log in on a local server, but will not be able to log in back to the cloud Bot API server for 10 minutes. Returns True on success. Requires no parameters.
5412: close
5413: Use this method to close the bot instance before moving it from one local server to another. You need to delete the webhook before calling this method to ensure that the bot isn't launched again after server restart. The method will return error 429 in the first 10 minutes after the bot is launched. Returns True on success. Requires no parameters.

5484: Formatting options
5485: The Bot API supports basic formatting for messages. You can use bold, italic, underlined, strikethrough, spoiler text, block quotations as well as inline links and pre-formatted code in your bots' messages. Telegram clients will render them accordingly. You can specify text entities directly, or use markdown-style or HTML-style formatting.
5486: Note that Telegram clients will display an alert to the user before opening an inline link ('Open this link?' together with the full URL).
5487: Message entities can be nested, providing following restrictions are met:
5488: - If two entities have common characters, then one of them is fully contained inside another.
5489: - bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, and spoiler entities can contain and can be part of any other entities, except pre and code.
5490: - blockquote and expandable_blockquote entities can't be nested.
5491: - All other entities can't contain each other.
5492: Links tg://user?id=<user_id> can be used to mention a user by their identifier without using a username. Please note:
5493: These links will work only if they are used inside an inline link or in an inline keyboard button. For example, they will not work, when used in a message text.
5494: Unless the user is a member of the chat where they were mentioned, these mentions are only guaranteed to work if the user has contacted the bot in private in the past or has sent a callback query to the bot via an inline button and doesn't have Forwarded Messages privacy enabled for the bot.
5495: You can find the list of programming and markup languages for which syntax highlighting is supported at libprisma#supported-languages.
5496: Date-time entity formatting
5497: Date-time entity formatting is specified by a format string, which must adhere to the following regular expression: r|w?[dD]?[tT]?.
5498: If the format string is empty, the underlying text is displayed as-is; however, the user can still receive the underlying date in their local format. When populated, the format string determines the output based on the presence of the following control characters:
5499: r: Displays the time relative to the current time. Cannot be combined with any other control characters.
5500: w: Displays the day of the week in the user's localized language.
5501: d: Displays the date in short form (e.g., “17.03.22”).
5502: D: Displays the date in long form (e.g., “March 17, 2022”).
5503: t: Displays the time in short form (e.g., “22:45”).
5504: T: Displays the time in long form (e.g., “22:45:00”).

5602: Ephemeral Messages and Commands
5603: Ephemeral interactions allow a bot and an individual member of a group or supergroup chat to communicate privately on the public timeline without cluttering the chat for other members. They may disappear automatically after some time, or if the app is restarted.
5604: Ephemeral Commands (User to Bot)
5605: Bots can declare ephemeral commands by setting the is_ephemeral field to True in the BotCommand class. A user can then send an ephemeral command that is received by the target bot but remains invisible to all members of the chat, including both users and other bots.
5606: Ephemeral Messages
5607: Bots can send an ephemeral message response back to a specific user designated by the receiver_user_id parameter. Other members of the group or supergroup chat will not see the message.
5608: It is not guaranteed that the ephemeral message will be received, especially if the user is offline.
5609: Reply Targets and Conditions
5610: Any bot can send an ephemeral message to a user within 15 seconds of the incoming eligible action. The message will be sent to the exact client application that triggered the action. For this the bot must provide either:
5611: The callback_query_id from a received callback query, or
5612: The reply_parameters.ephemeral_message_id from an incoming ephemeral message.
5613: If the bot is a chat administrator, it can send an ephemeral message to any non-bot member of the chat at any time without needing to specify a callback_query_id or reply_parameters.ephemeral_message_id. In this case, the message may be delivered across multiple active client applications of the user, but is regardless not guaranteed to be delivered to any of them.
5614: Paid Broadcasts
5615: By default, all bots are able to broadcast up to 30 messages per second to their users. Developers can increase this limit by enabling Paid Broadcasts in @BotFather - allowing their bot to broadcast up to 1000 messages per second.
5616: Each message broadcasted over the free amount of 30 messages per second incurs a cost of 0.1 Stars per message, paid with Telegram Stars from the bot's balance. In order to use this feature, a bot must have at least 10,000 Stars on its balance.
5617: Bots with increased limits are only charged for messages that are broadcasted successfully.

9194: Methods and objects used in the inline mode are described in the Inline mode section.
9195: Updating messages
9196: The following methods allow you to change an existing message in the message history instead of sending a new one with a result of an action. 9197: Please note, that it is currently only possible to edit messages without reply_markup or with inline keyboards.

10175: Rich messages
10176: The following methods and objects allow your bot to handle and send rich messages.
10177: Rich Message Formatting Options
10178: Rich messages support advanced structured formatting options like headings, lists, tables, media, block quotations, collapsible blocks, footnotes, and formulas. Telegram clients will render them accordingly. You can specify rich message content using Markdown-style or HTML-style formatting, or explicit blocks.
10179: Plain URLs, e-mail addresses, username mentions, hashtags, cashtags, bot commands, phone numbers, and bank card numbers are detected automatically. To disable automatic entity detection, pass True in the skip_entity_detection field. Note that Telegram clients will display an alert to the user before opening an inline link ('Open this link?' together with the full URL).
10180: When Markdown-style or HTML-style formatting is used, you can use links in the form tg://photo?id=..., tg://video?id=..., tg://document?id=..., and tg://audio?id=... instead of an HTTP URL to reuse previously uploaded files or upload a new file.
10181: Rich Message Limits
10182: Rich messages are subject to the following limits:
10183: Up to 32768 UTF-8 characters in the rich message text, including custom emoji alternative text and formula source.
10184: Up to 500 blocks, including nested blocks, list items, ordered list items, table rows, quotation blocks, and details blocks.
10185: Up to 16 levels of nested formatting and blocks.
10186: Up to 50 media attachments in total.
10187: Up to 20 columns in a table.
10188: Rich Markdown style
10189: To use this mode, pass rich message content in the markdown field. Use the following syntax in your message:
10190: **bold text**
10191: __bold text__
10192: *italic text*
10193: _italic text_
10194: ~~strikethrough text~~
10195: `inline fixed-width code`
10196: ==marked text==
10197: ||spoiler||
10198: [inline URL](https://t.me/)
10199: [inline e-mail](mailto:user@example.com)
10200: [inline phone number](tel:+123456789)

11809: Inline mode
11810: The following methods and objects allow your bot to work in inline mode.
11811: Please see our Introduction to Inline bots for more details.
11812: To enable this option, send the /setinline command to @BotFather and provide the placeholder text that the user will see in the input field after typing your bot's name, or use the parameters supports_inline_queries and inline_query_placeholder of the method setMySettings.
11813: InlineQuery
11814: This object represents an incoming inline query. When the user sends an empty query, your bot could return some default or trending results.
11815: Field
11816: Type
11817: Description

11821: from
11822: User
11823: Sender

11825: String

11827: offset
11828: String
11829: Offset of the results to be returned, can be controlled by the bot
11830: chat_type
11831: String
11832: Optional. Type of the chat from which the inline query was sent. Can be either “sender” for a private chat with the inline query sender, “private”, “group”, “supergroup”, or “channel”. The chat type should be always known for requests sent from official clients and most third-party clients, unless the request was sent from a secret chat.
11833: location
11834: Location
11835: Optional. Sender location, only for bots that enabled user location requests via @BotFather or using the parameter needs_inline_query_location of the method setMySettings
11836: answerInlineQuery
11837: Use this method to send answers to an inline query. On success, True is returned.
11838: No more than 50 results per query are allowed.

11862: Pass the offset that a client should send in the next query with the same text to receive more results. Pass an empty string if there are no more results or if you don't support pagination. Offset length can't exceed 64 bytes.

11877: Optional. Description of the Web App that will be launched when the user presses the button. The Web App will be able to switch back to the inline mode using the method switchInlineQuery inside the Web App.
11878: start_parameter
11879: String
11880: Optional. Deep-linking parameter for the /start message sent to the bot when a user presses the button. 1-64 characters, only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and - are allowed.
11881: Example: An inline bot that sends YouTube videos can ask the user to connect the bot to their YouTube account to adapt search results accordingly. To do this, it displays a 'Connect your YouTube account' button above the results, or even before showing any. The user presses the button, switches to a private chat with the bot and, in doing so, passes a start parameter that instructs the bot to return an OAuth link. Once done, the bot can offer a switch_inline button so that the user can easily return to the chat where they wanted to use the bot's inline capabilities.

13891: Games
13892: Your bot can offer users HTML5 games to play solo or to compete against each other in groups and one-on-one chats. Create games via @BotFather using the /newgame command. Please note that this kind of power requires responsibility: you will need to accept the terms for each game that your bots will be offering.
13893: Games are a new type of content on Telegram, represented by the Game and InlineQueryResultGame objects.
13894: Once you've created a game via BotFather, you can send games to chats as regular messages using the sendGame method, or use inline mode with InlineQueryResultGame.
13895: If you send the game message without any buttons, it will automatically have a 'Play GameName' button. When this button is pressed, your bot gets a CallbackQuery with the game_short_name of the requested game. You provide the correct URL for this particular user and the app opens the game in the in-app browser.
13896: You can manually add multiple buttons to your game message. Please note that the first button in the first row must always launch the game, using the field callback_game in InlineKeyboardButton. You can add extra buttons according to taste: e.g., for a description of the rules, or to open the game's official community.
13897: To make your game more attractive, you can upload a GIF animation that demonstrates the game to the users via BotFather (see Lumberjack for example).
13898: A game message will also display high scores for the current chat. Use setGameScore to post high scores to the chat with the game, add the disable_edit_message parameter to disable automatic update of the message with the current scoreboard.
13899: Use getGameHighScores to get data for in-game high score tables.
13900: You can also add an extra sharing button for users to share their best score to different chats.
13901: For examples of what can be done using this new stuff, check the @gamebot and @gamee bots.

10: Telegram APIs
11: We offer three kinds of APIs for developers. The Bot API allows you to easily create programs that use Telegram messages for an interface. The Telegram API and TDLib allow you to build your own customized Telegram clients. You are welcome to use both APIs free of charge. Lastly, the Gateway API allows any business, app or website to send verification codes through Telegram instead of traditional SMS.
12: You can also add Telegram Widgets to your website.
13: Designers are welcome to create Animated Stickers and Emoji or Custom Themes for Telegram.
14: Bot API
15: This API allows you to connect bots to our system. Telegram Bots are special accounts that do not require an additional phone number to set up. These accounts serve as an interface for code running somewhere on your server.
16: To use this, you don't need to know anything about how our MTProto encryption protocol works — our intermediary server will handle all encryption and communication with the Telegram API for you. You communicate with this server via a simple HTTPS interface that offers a simplified version of the Telegram API.
17: Learn more about the Bot API here »
18: Bot developers can also make use of our Payments API to accept payments from Telegram users around the world.
19: TDLib – build your own Telegram
20: Even if you're looking for maximum customization, you don't have to create your app from scratch. Try our Telegram Database Library (or simply TDLib), a tool for third-party developers that makes it easy to build fast, secure and feature-rich Telegram apps.
21: TDLib takes care of all network implementation details, encryption and local data storage, so that you can dedicate more time to design, responsive interfaces and beautiful animations.
22: TDLib supports all Telegram features and makes developing Telegram apps a breeze on any platform. It can be used on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux and virtually any other system. The library is open source and compatible with virtually any programming language.
23: Learn more about TDLib here »
24: Gateway API
25: The Telegram Gateway API allows any business, app or website to send authorization codes through Telegram instead of traditional SMS – offering a powerful and convenient way to lower costs while increasing the security and delivery speed of your codes to Telegram’s 1 billion monthly active users. Users will instantly receive messages with codes in a special chat inside Telegram.
26: Telegram's Gateway API is completely free to test. Learn more here »
27: Telegram API
28: This API allows you to build your own customized Telegram clients. It is 100% open for all developers who wish to create Telegram applications on our platform. Feel free to study the open source code of existing Telegram applications for examples of how things work here. Don't forget to register your application in our system.

106: A bot API dialog ID is a single, unique 64-bit peer ID sequence derived from the user, chat, channel and secret chat ID sequences, maintaining uniqueness across all of them.
107: This page specifies how to convert MTProto peer IDs to bot API dialog IDs and vice versa.
108: Managed bots
109: Users can create managed bots (which are controlled by a specific manager bot) directly through the MTProto API, without interacting with @BotFather.
110: Commands
111: Bots offer a set of commands that can be used by users in private, or in a chat.
112: Buttons
113: Users can interact with your bot via buttons or even inline buttons, straight from inline messages in any chat.
114: Menu button
115: Bots can choose the behavior of the menu button shown next to the text input field.
116: Inline queries
117: Users can interact with your bot via inline queries, straight from the text input field in any chat.
118: Games
119: Bots can offer users HTML5 games to play solo or to compete against each other in groups and one-on-one chats; how to work with games in the MTProto API.
120: Mini apps
121: Bots can offer users interactive HTML5 mini apps to completely replace any website.
122: Affiliate programs
123: Developers can open affiliate programs for their mini app – allowing content creators, other mini app developers and any Telegram user to promote it and earn commissions on purchases made by people they referred.
124: Attachment menu
125: Bots can install attachment menu entries, offering conveniently accessible, versatile mini apps.
126: Editing bot info
127: Users can edit and localize the profile picture, name, about text and description of bots they own; the same can be done by the bots themselves.
128: AI bots
129: Telegram bots offer a number of features for AI chatbots.
130: Guest mode
131: Guest bots can be queried by username from any non-secret private chat, group and supergroup, posting their results directly into the chat, even if they're not a member.
132: Bot-to-bot communication »
133: Bots may receive and send messages to and from other bots in groups, private chats and chats, if Bot-to-Bot Communication Mode is enabled.
134: Stories
135: Telegram users and channels can easily post and view stories through the API.
136: Similar channels and bots
137: The API offers a method to obtain a list of similarly themed public channels and bots, selected based on similarities in their subscriber bases.
138: Accent colors
139: Telegram users and channels can change the accent color and background pattern of their profile page and their messages!
140: Privacy settings
141: Telegram allows users to specify granular privacy settings, choosing which users can or can't interact with them in certain ways.
142: Search & filters
143: Telegram allows applying detailed message filters while looking for messages in chats.
144: This allows the server to filter messages based on a text query, and even on their type, and this feature is often used by graphical clients to implement features like the chat gallery, chat profile pictures and more.
145: Polls
146: Telegram allows sending polls and quizzes, that can be voted on by thousands, if not millions of users in chats and channels.
147: Checklists
148: Premium users can now create collaborative checklists in any chat to track tasks and coordinate teams — or manage shopping and to-do lists.
149: Reactions
150: Telegram allows users to react to any message using specific emojis, triggering cute Lottie animations.
151: Animated message effects
152: Telegram allows adding spectacular animated effects to messages you send.
153: Emoji categories
154: Sticker, custom emoji and GIF selection UIs should offer a list of categories to quickly filter results by a (list of) emojis, or by some other criteria.
155: Emoji status
156: Telegram allows users to set an emoticon or a custom emoji as status, to show next to their name in chats and profiles.
157: Invite links and join requests
158: Channels, basic groups and supergroups may have a public username or a private invite link: private invite links may be further enhanced with per-user join requests.
159: Admin, banned and default rights for channels, supergroups and groups
160: How to handle admin permissions, granular bans and global permissions in channels, groups and supergroups.
161: Discussion groups
162: Groups can be associated with a channel as a discussion group, allowing users to discuss posts.
163: Channel comments and message threads
164: Telegram allows commenting on a channel post or on a generic group message, thanks to message threads.
165: Admin log
166: Both supergroups and channels offer a so-called admin log, a log of recent relevant supergroup and channel actions, like the modification of group/channel settings or information on behalf of an admin, user kicks and bans, and more.
167: Pinned messages
168: Telegram allows pinning multiple messages on top of a specific chat.
169: Group member/admin tags
170: Members in group chats (both basic groups and supergroups) can now add a tag next to their name — to show their role at work, what they study in school, and more.
171: Mentions
172: Telegram allows mentioning other users in case of urgent duckling matters, and quickly navigating to those mentions in order to read them as swiftly as possible.
173: Scheduled messages
174: Telegram allows scheduling messages.
175: Live geolocations
176: Telegram allows sending the live geolocation of a user in a chat, optionally setting a proximity alert.
177: Peer database
178: How to work with peer information in the API.
179: Min constructors
180: Sometimes, user and channel constructors encountered in group chat updates may not contain full info about the user: this page explains how to handle such constructors.
181: Account deletion
182: How to delete a Telegram account.
183: Imported messages
184: Telegram allows importing messages and media from foreign chat apps.
185: Telegram Passport
186: How to work with Telegram Passport directly using the MTProto API.
187: Telegram Payments
188: How to work with Telegram Payments directly using the MTProto API.
189: Third-party verification
190: To further improve transparency on Telegram, official third-party services are able to assign extra verification icons to user accounts and chats — in order to prevent scams and reduce misinformation.
191: Styled text with message entities
192: How to create styled text with message entities.
193: Working with GIFs
194: Telegram clients support displaying GIFs.
195: Working with stickers
196: Telegram clients support displaying animated, static and video stickers.
197: Working with custom emojis
198: Telegram allows including custom animated, static and video emojis directly inside of messages.
199: Working with animated emojis
200: Graphical Telegram clients should transform emojis into their respective animated versions.
201: Working with animated dice
202: Telegram supports sending animated dice emojis.
203: Message drafts
204: How to handle message drafts.
205: Folders
206: Working with folders.
207: Top peer rating
208: If enabled, the rating of top peers indicates the relevance of a frequently used peer in a certain category (frequently messaged users, frequently used bots, inline bots, frequently visited channels and so on).
209: Handling file references
210: How to handle file references.
211: Seamless Telegram Login
212: Handle Seamless Telegram Login URL authorization requests.
213: Wallpapers
214: How to work with chat backgrounds.
215: Notification sounds
216: How to work with chat notification sounds.
217: Message transcription
218: How to transcribe voice messages.
219: Message translation
220: Telegram allows translating chat messages, and Telegram Premium users may even enable real-time chat translation.
221: Native antispam system
222: Admins of supergroups with a certain number of members can choose to unleash the full proactive power of Telegram's own antispam algorithms – turning on the new Aggressive mode for the automated spam filters.
223: Collectibles
224: Telegram users can make it easy for others to contact them or find their public groups and channels via usernames: clients can also assign multiple Fragment » collectible usernames to accounts, supergroups and channels they own; Fragment » also allows purchasing phone number collectibles that can be used to register Telegram accounts.
225: Telegram Premium
226: Telegram Premium is an optional subscription service that unlocks additional exclusive client-side and API-side features, while helping support the development of the app. It is a part of Telegram’s sustainable monetization – driven by our users, rather than advertisers or shareholders. This way, Telegram can remain independent and prioritize its users first.
227: Telegram Business
228: Users can turn their Telegram account into a business account, gaining access to business features such as opening hours, location, quick replies, automated messages, custom start page, chatbot support, and more.
229: Most Telegram Business features are available to Telegram Premium » subscribers; connected business bots » are also available to non-Premium users.
230: Telegram Stars
231: Telegram Stars are virtual items that allow users to purchase digital goods and services from bots and mini apps inside the Telegram ecosystem, send gifts to content creators on the Telegram platform, and more.
232: Subscriptions
233: Bots and channels may create subscriptions, periodically charging users a certain amount of Telegram Stars in exchange for content and services.
234: Protected content
235: Users and bots who want to keep their messages private, as well as Group and Channel owners who want to keep their content members-only can restrict message forwarding from their chat, which also prevents screenshots, disables message forwards (attempting to forward protected messages will emit a CHAT_FORWARDS_RESTRICTED RPC error) and limits the ability to save media from posts.
236: Gifts
237: Users can send Gifts to their friends. The recipients of gifts can display them on their profile pages or turn them into Telegram Stars ». Telegram Stars can be used for many things, including supporting creators and buying services in mini apps.
238: Collectible gift auctions
239: To guarantee fair distribution of collectible gifts, new gift releases will be based on auctions — allowing users to place bids with Stars for new gifts over several rounds.
240: Paid media
241: Content creators can accept Stars by publishing paid photos or videos on their channels. Subscribers will be allowed to view such posts only after paying the author to unlock them.
242: Paid messages
243: Telegram Stars can be used to pay for sending messages to users, supergroups and channels that have configured Star Messages », requiring a payment for every message sent to them.
244: Suggested posts
245: Telegram offers a powerful monetization feature to channel administrators: suggested posts.
246: Channel and supergroup boosts
247: Telegram Premium users can grant their favorite channels additional features like the ability to post stories by giving them boosts.
248: Giveaways & gifts
249: Telegram channel administrators may launch giveaways to randomly distribute Telegram Premium subscriptions and other gifts among their followers, in exchange for boosts.
250: Action bar
251: Sometimes, when interacting with Telegram users via private or secret chats, an action bar must be shown on top of the chat, offering convenient action buttons or notices regarding the user.
252: Saved messages
253: The Saved Messages chat allows users to bookmark messages and media: it's a personal cloud storage for any messages or media you may want to send or forward there.
254: Profile
255: Telegram offers many customization options for your profile!
256: Themes
257: Telegram apps support generating, sharing and synchronizing app themes.
258: Sponsored messages
259: If your app allows accessing content from Telegram channels, you must include support for official sponsored messages in Telegram channels.
260: Channel and bot ad revenue
261: Telegram has one of the most generous reward systems in the history of social media. Telegram channel and bot owners can now receive 50% of the revenue from ads displayed in their channels and bots.
262: This page describes the methods used to withdraw channel and bot ad revenue, as well as view detailed revenue stats.
263: Fact-checks
264: Telegram clients support displaying fact-checks added to messages by independent fact-checkers.
265: Contacts
266: Working with contacts in the API.
267: Blocklist
268: Working with the blocklist.
269: Age verification
270: Some legislations require age verification to view restricted content: Telegram implements this through the Main Mini App of a special bot.
271: Web events
272: When interacting with HTML5 games and the websites of payment gateways, Telegram apps should expose the following JS APIs.
273: Deep links
274: Telegram clients must handle special tg:// and t.me deep links encountered in messages, link entities and in other apps by registering OS handlers.
275: Takeout
276: Telegram's API allows users to export all of their information through the takeout API.
277: Terms of Service
278: Terms of Service that all third-party client apps must comply with.
279: Telegram
280: Telegram is a cloud-based mobile and desktop messaging app with a focus on security and speed.

172: About
173: The server is a bridge between the Telegram API and the AI assistants and is based on the Model Context Protocol.
174: Important
175: Ensure that you have read and understood the Telegram API Terms of Service before using this server.
176: Any misuse of the Telegram API may result in the suspension of your account.
177: What is MCP?
178: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a system that lets AI apps, like Claude Desktop, connect to external tools and data sources. It gives a clear and safe way for AI assistants to work with local services and APIs while keeping the user in control.
179: What does this server do?
180: As of not, the server provides read-only access to the Telegram API.
181: Get the list of dialogs (chats, channels, groups)
182: Get the list of (unread) messages in the given dialog
183: Mark chanel as read
184: Retrieve messages by date and time
185: Download media files
186: Get the list of contacts
187: Draft a message
188: ...
189: Practical use cases
190: Create a summary of the unread messages
191: Find contacts with upcoming birthdays and schedule a greeting
192: Find discussions on a given topic, summarize them and provide a list of links
193: Prerequisites
194: uv tool
195: Installation
196: uv tool install git+https://github.com/sparfenyuk/mcp-telegram
197: Note
198: If you have already installed the server, you can update it using uv tool upgrade --reinstall command.
199: Note
200: If you want to delete the server, use the uv tool uninstall mcp-telegram command.
201: Configuration
202: Telegram API Configuration
203: Before you can use the server, you need to connect to the Telegram API.
204: Get the API ID and hash from Telegram API
205: Run the following command:
206: mcp-telegram sign-in --api-id <your-api-id> --api-hash <your-api-hash> --phone-number <your-phone-number>
207: Enter the code you received from Telegram to connect to the API.
208: The password may be required if you have two-factor authentication enabled.
209: Note
210: To log out from the Telegram API, use the mcp-telegram logout command.
211: Claude Desktop Configuration
212: Configure Claude Desktop to recognize the Exa MCP server.
213: Open the Claude Desktop configuration file:
214: in MacOS, the configuration file is located at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
215: in Windows, the configuration file is located at %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json
216: Note:
217: You can also find claude_desktop_config.json inside the settings of Claude Desktop app
218: Add the server configuration
219: {
220: "mcpServers": {
221: "mcp-telegram": {
222: "command": "mcp-server",
223: "env": {
224: "TELEGRAM_API_ID": "<your-api-id>",
225: "TELEGRAM_API_HASH": "<your-api-hash>",
226: },
227: }
228: }
229: }
230: }
231: Telegram Configuration
232: Before working with Telegram’s API, you need to get your own API ID and hash:
233: Login to your Telegram account with the phone number of the developer account to use.
234: Click under API Development tools.
235: A 'Create new application' window will appear. Fill in your application details. There is no need to enter any URL, and only the first two fields (App title and Short name) can currently be changed later.
236: Click on 'Create application' at the end. Remember that your API hash is secret and Telegram won’t let you revoke it. Don’t post it anywhere!
237: Development
238: Getting started
239: Clone the repository
240: Install the dependencies
241: uv sync
242: Run the server
243: uv run mcp-telegram --help
244: Tools can be added to the src/mcp_telegram/tools.py file.
245: How to add a new tool:
246: Create a new class that inherits from ToolArgs
247: class NewTool(ToolArgs):
248: """Description of the new tool."""
249: pass
250: Attributes of the class will be used as arguments for the tool.
251: The class docstring will be used as the tool description.
252: Implement the tool_runner function for the new class
253: @tool_runner.register
254: async def new_tool(args: NewTool) -> t.Sequence[TextContent | ImageContent | EmbeddedResource]:
255: pass
256: The function should return a sequence of TextContent, ImageContent or EmbeddedResource.
257: The function should be async and accept a single argument of the new class.
258: Done! Restart the client and the new tool should be available.
259: Validation can accomplished either through Claude Desktop or by running the tool directly.
260: Debugging the server in terminal
261: To run the tool directly, use the following command:
262: # List all available tools
263: uv run cli.py list-tools
264: # Run the concrete tool
265: uv run cli.py call-tool --name ListDialogs --arguments '{"unread": true}'
266: Debugging the server in the Inspector
267: The MCP inspector is a tool that helps to debug the server using fancy UI. To run it, use the following command:
268: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector uv run mcp-telegram
269: Warning
270: Do not forget to define Environment Variables TELEGRAM_API_ID and TELEGRAM_API_HASH in the inspector.
271: Troubleshooting
272: Message 'Could not connect to MCP server mcp-telegram'
273: If you see the message 'Could not connect to MCP server mcp-telegram' in Claude Desktop, it means that the server configuration is incorrect.
274: Try the following:
275: Use the full path to the uv binary in the configuration file
276: Check the path to the cloned repository in the configuration file
