10798: Retrieve an Analytics Report Export
10799: Returns the current state of an Analytics report export job. While the job is processing, the response carries status: PENDING. Once it has finished, the response includes the final status and — on success — a presigned downloadUrl you can use to fetch the generated file.
10800: Poll roughly every minute while status is PENDING. End-to-end completion typically takes seconds to a few minutes depending on the date range and report.
10801: The downloadUrl is presigned and time-limited (currently ~1 hour from completion; check downloadUrlExpiresAt for the exact expiry). Once it has passed, the link stops working — re-call this endpoint to mint a fresh URL while the export is still available on Aircall's storage.
10802: When status is FAILED, no data is generated and there is nothing to download. Read errorMessage before retrying — most failures are deterministic (invalid filters, unsupported combinations) and a retry with the same payload will fail again.
10803: Once the job has completed, the response carries the download URL:
10804: Response
10805: Status: 200 OK
10806: {
10807: "exportID": "9d3f2a1e-2b6c-4f0a-9c3e-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
10808: "createdAt": "2026-05-20T09:35:12.000Z",
10809: "status": "COMPLETED",
10810: "format": "CSV",
10811: "exportName": "calls-history-may-2026",
10812: "isZipCompressed": false,
10813: "downloadUrl": "https://aircall-analytics-exports.s3.amazonaws.com/...",
10814: "downloadUrlExpiresAt": "2026-05-20T10:35:12.000Z"
10815: }
10816: If the job failed, status is FAILED and errorMessage describes the reason:
10817: Response
10818: Status: 200 OK
10819: {
10820: "exportID": "9d3f2a1e-2b6c-4f0a-9c3e-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
10821: "createdAt": "2026-05-20T09:35:12.000Z",
10822: "status": "FAILED",
10823: "errorMessage": "Report generation failed: too many rows for the requested date range"
10824: }

10941: Register an endpoint
10942: The following steps describe how to register a server endpoint to start receiving Webhook events.
10943: Up to 100 Webhooks can be registered per account!
10944: Login on your Aircall account (sign up here if you don't have one).
10945: Go to the Integrations' page ( Integrations & API section in Aircall Dashboard)
10946: Search for “Webhook” and click on Integration “Webhook” in “All Integrations” section.
10947: Create a Webhook Integration by clicking on the “Install Integration” button.
10948: Provide a name and a valid URL and select all the events you want to subscribe to.
10949: Click on the green Add Webhook button and… that's it!
10950: Your Webhook URL must be behind a SSL certificate and start with https.
10951: Aircall will start sending events to your server right after the Webhook creation, make sure your server is up and running.
10952: Webhook usage
10953: Make sure your server can receive POST requests, reads JSON format and always answers a 200 HTTP Code!
10954: During development, you can create SSH tunnels to your local environment. At Aircall, we use and recommend ngrok which is free and open-source.
10955: Web server
10956: Once the endpoints are registered, a simple web server is needed in order to receive events.
10957: Then, Aircall will send a POST request to the Webhook's URL each time an event occurs with a JSON payload body.
10958: The Web server must be publicly available, Aircall does not provide a list of static IP addresses to whitelist.
10959: Please note an event will be delivered at least once, if generated, but events might not be delivered in a specific sequence/order
10960: Automatic deactivation
10961: If webhook delivery fails, Aircall will retry the event up to 50 times. If the issue persists after all retries, the webhook will be automatically disabled and no further events will be sent. A notification will also appear on the Aircall Dashboard indicating that the webhook has been disabled.
10962: Once disabled, Aircall will continue retrying the failed events for up to 12 hours. If a successful response is received for any of the failed events during this period, the webhook will be automatically re-enabled.
10963: Admin users can receive email notifications when a webhook is disabled or re-enabled by turning on email notifications in User Settings within the Aircall Dashboard.
10964: A request is considered failed if the server responds with an HTTP status code outside the 2xx range, or if the request times out. To prevent your webhook from being deactivated, ensure your server always returns a 200 HTTP status code.
10965: Aircall's HTTP requests sent to external web servers are set up to timeout after 5 seconds.
10966: Filtering by Numbers
10967: If the integration is built using the OAuth authentication method, Admins will be able to filter from which Numbers they want to receive Call events from on their Aircall Dashboard.
10968: If the integration is using the Basic Auth method, Call webhook events will be sent for all Numbers of a Company.
10969: Payload
10970: Webhook events are sent with a JSON payload attached.
10971: This payload mixes the JSON formatting of an Aircall's object (User, Number, Call, Contact) and some metadata like an absolute timestamp or the name of the event.

10973: resource
10974: String
10975: Name of the resource for this event.
10976: Can be number, user, contact or call.
10977: event
10978: String
10979: Event's name for this payload.
10980: See the complete list here.
10981: timestamp
10982: Integer
10983: UNIX timestamp for when the payload was built, in UTC.
10984: token
10985: String
10986: Token associated to the Webhook. Use it to identify from which Aircall account a Webhook event is sent from.
10987: data
10988: Object
10989: Modelization of the resource at the timestamp value.
10990: User, Number, Call or Contact for more info on the data structure.

11556: Conversation events
11557: Limited availability: The Conversations endpoints and events are being rolled out gradually and aren't available to all Aircall accounts yet. If your account doesn't have access, requests to these endpoints won't work and the related webhook events won't be sent. To ask for access, please contact the Aircall Support team. We'll make this feature available to all accounts soon.
11558: The following events refer to the Conversation object.
11559: The data of each event is a Conversation, with one more attribute: reason. It tells why the event was sent.
11560: Reason
11561: reason
11562: String
11563: The cause of the event.
11564: sms.received, sms.sent, mms.received, mms.sent, whatsapp.received, whatsapp.sent, whatsapp_username.received, whatsapp_username.sent, group_message.received, group_message.sent, call.received, call.sent, agent_request, api_request, bulk_api_request, support_bulk_close or auto_close_inactivity. It is null when the cause is unknown.
11565: The dates of the Conversation in data are ISO 8601 strings, while the timestamp of the event is a UNIX timestamp in seconds.
11566: Delivery
11567: Like every Aircall Webhook, Conversation events are delivered at least once. The same event can arrive more than once: Aircall can publish an event again after a timeout, and it can retry the delivery of an event to your server.
11568: Treat the events as idempotent. To spot a duplicate, compare the data.id, the event and the data.updated_at of the events you already processed. The events have no event id of their own.
11569: The events can also arrive out of order: a conversation.closed can reach your server before the conversation.reopened sent earlier for the same Conversation. Keep the event with the most recent data.updated_at, or call Retrieve a Conversation to read the current state.

11745: WhatsApp username message
11746: The whatsapp_username_message.* events describe WhatsApp conversations identified by a Business-Scoped User ID (BSUID).
11747: A BSUID identifies a WhatsApp user within a Meta business portfolio. It is not a phone number, username, or UUID.
11748: You receive these events when:
11749: You have created a webhook.
11750: Your webhook subscribes to the relevant whatsapp_username_message.* events.
11751: Aircall identifies the conversation by a BSUID because no phone number is available.
11752: This typically applies to new contacts with a WhatsApp username and no prior phone-based exchange with your business.
11753: Existing contacts can normally provide both a phone number and a BSUID, even with a WhatsApp username.
11754: If a phone number is available, Aircall uses it and the conversation sends message.* events.
11755: A subscription to username events does not change that routing.
11756: See Meta's phone-number rules and Twilio's WhatsApp identity documentation.
11757: Message
11758: id
11759: String
11760: Identifier of the message.
11761: Required.
11762: external_user_id
11763: String
11764: BSUID of the external WhatsApp user.
11765: Required.
11766: external_user_name
11767: String
11768: WhatsApp username.
11769: Optional.
11770: external_user_display_name
11771: String
11772: WhatsApp profile name, distinct from the username.
11773: Optional.
11774: external_number
11775: String
11776: External phone number, only when a separate phone number is available.
11777: Optional. Absent for BSUID-only identities.
11778: body
11779: String
11780: Text of the message.
11781: Optional. Sent and received events only. Can be absent for media-only or template messages.
11782: created_at
11783: String
11784: Creation time of the message in ISO 8601 format.
11785: Optional. Sent and received events only.
11786: status
11787: String
11788: Message status as a lowercase string.
11789: Required for received and status events. Absent from sent events.
11790: sub_status
11791: String
11792: Reason for the status, when available.
11793: Optional. Status events only.
11794: type
11795: String
11796: Type of the message, for example text, image, or template.
11797: Optional. Sent and received events only.
11798: parent_id
11799: String
11800: Identifier of the message that this message replies to.
11801: Optional. Sent and received events only.
11802: origin
11803: String
11804: Origin of the message, for example native.
11805: Optional.
11806: delivery_method
11807: String or null
11808: Delivery method, when available.
11809: Optional. Can be null.
11810: metadata
11811: Object
11812: JSON object with information specific to the message type.
11813: Optional. Not a JSON string.
11814: template_content
11815: Object
11816: JSON object with the template content of a sent message.
11817: Optional. Not a JSON string.
11818: media_details
11819: Array of Objects
11820: Attached media files, each with file_name, file_type, and presigned_url.
11821: Optional. file_type is a full MIME type, such as image/jpeg.
11822: whatsapp_service_window_closing_time
11823: String
11824: Closing time of the WhatsApp customer service window, in ISO 8601 format.
11825: Optional. Received events only.
11826: whatsapp_free_entry_point_opportunity_closing_time
11827: String
11828: Closing time of the opportunity to open a free-entry-point window, in ISO 8601 format.
11829: Optional. Received events only.
11830: whatsapp_free_entry_point_closing_time
11831: String
11832: Closing time of the free-entry-point window in ISO 8601 format.
11833: Optional. Status events only.
11834: whatsapp_message_category
11835: String
11836: WhatsApp template category: marketing, utility, or authentication.
11837: Optional. Status events only.
11838: whatsapp_message_type
11839: String
11840: WhatsApp billing type: service, regular, free_entry_point, or free_customer_service.
11841: Optional. Status events only. service identifies a free-form message without a template.
11842: recipient_country
11843: String
11844: Two-letter country code for the recipient, for example GB.
11845: Optional. Status events only.
11846: number
11847: Object
11848: Number object for the Aircall number.
11849: Optional.
11850: user
11851: Object
11852: User object for the Aircall agent.
11853: Optional. Sent and status events only.
11854: contact
11855: Object
11856: Contact object matched by a separate external phone number.
11857: Optional. No phone-based lookup occurs for a BSUID-only identity.
11858: Upstream serialization can omit default values.
11859: These events do not include channel, media counts, or media sizes, and do not provide a BSUID-to-phone lookup.
11860: The examples omit optional Number, User, and Contact objects.

11862: Sent when Aircall sends a WhatsApp message in a conversation identified by a BSUID.

12634: Mobile
12635: In this section, you will find documentation for integrating with the Aircall mobile applications on Android and iOS.
12636: URL Schemes
12637: The aircall:// URL scheme enables external applications to launch the Aircall mobile app. By using a formatted URL, any client application can hand off an action to Aircall by pre-filling the relevant information.
12638: Open app (iOS)
12639: Available since Aircall for iOS v9.9.0.
12640: The aircall:// URL scheme enables external applications to launch the Aircall iOS app directly. When triggered, it brings the Aircall app to the foreground, allowing users to quickly switch to Aircall from any third-party application without navigating through the home screen.
12641: This is useful for CRM or helpdesk integrations that need to bring the Aircall app into focus before or after performing other actions.
12642: Scheme Syntax
12643: Parameters
12644: This URL scheme does not accept any parameters. It simply opens the Aircall app.
12645: Example
12646: Opens the Aircall app:
12647: aircall://
12648: Behavior
12649: If the Aircall app is installed and the user is logged in, the app will be brought to the foreground.
12650: If the user is not authenticated, the app will open on the login screen.
12651: If the Aircall app is not installed, iOS will not be able to open the URL and UIApplication.shared.open will return false in its completion handler.
12652: Integration Example
12653: // Swift
12654: if let url = URL(string: "aircall://") {
12655: UIApplication.shared.open(url, options: [:]) { success in
12656: if !success {
12657: // Aircall app is not installed
12658: }
12659: }
12660: }
12661: You can check if the Aircall app is installed before attempting to open the URL by calling UIApplication.shared.canOpenURL(url). Note that this requires adding aircall to the LSApplicationQueriesSchemes array in your app's Info.plist.
12662: aircall://
12663: Call (Android & iOS)
12664: Available since Aircall for Android v8.2.0 and iOS v9.9.0.
12665: The aircall://call URL scheme allows external applications to trigger outbound calls from within the Aircall mobile app. By using a formatted URL, any client application can hand off a call to Aircall by pre-filling the dialpad.
12666: Scheme Syntax
12667: Parameters
12668: Parameter
12669: Required
12670: Format
12671: Description
12672: to
12673: Yes
12674: E.164
12675: The destination phone number to call (e.g., +14155552671).
12676: from
12677: No
12678: E.164
12679: The Aircall line to place the call from. Defaults to the user's current line.
12680: Phone numbers must be in E.164 format, which includes a leading + followed by the country code and subscriber number (e.g., +33612345678). See Dealing with phone numbers for more details.
12681: Examples
12682: Basic call (default line):
12683: Initiates a call to a US number using the user's default Aircall line:
12684: aircall://call?to=+14155552671
12685: Call with a specific line:
12686: Initiates a call to a French number, placing it from a specific Aircall line:
12687: aircall://call?to=+33612345678&from=+33140000001
12688: Behavior
12689: If the from parameter is provided, Aircall will attempt to place the call from that line. If the line does not belong to the authenticated user, the call falls back to the default line.
12690: If the from parameter is omitted, Aircall uses the user's currently selected default line.
12691: The app will prefill the Dialpad with the provided information.
12692: If the Aircall app is not installed, the operating system will not be able to handle the URL and it will have no effect.
12693: The user must be logged into the Aircall app and have an active session for the URL scheme to work. If the user is not authenticated, the app will prompt them to log in first.
12694: Integration Examples
12695: Android (Kotlin):
12696: // Kotlin
12697: val uri = Uri.parse("aircall://call?to=+33655445566&from=+33112233445")
12698: val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri)
12699: startActivity(intent)
12700: Android (Java):
12701: // Java
12702: Uri uri = Uri.parse("aircall://call?to=+33655445566&from=+33112233445");
12703: Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri);
12704: startActivity(intent);
12705: iOS (Swift):
12706: // Swift
12707: if let url = URL(string: "aircall://call?to=+33655445566&from=+33112233445") {
12708: UIApplication.shared.open(url, options: [:]) { success in
12709: if !success {
12710: // Aircall app is not installed
12711: }
12712: }
12713: }
12714: On iOS, you can check if the Aircall app is installed before attempting to open the URL by calling UIApplication.shared.canOpenURL(url). Note that this requires adding aircall to the LSApplicationQueriesSchemes array in your app's Info.plist.

13194: Extras
13195: In this section, we will describe a few non-essential things to know when working with Aircall Public API, like Timezones, Phone numbers formats and emojis.
13196: CTI - Aircall Everywhere SDK
13197: Looking to build a more advanced integration with Aircall? Aircall Everywhere is a JavaScript SDK that lets you embed and control the Workspace app in your website.
13198: The Workspace app will be loaded in a HTML iframe and will send events to your main page when incoming calls are ringing, when calls are answered, when agents log in... You can also send instructions to the Workspace app such as dial a number or exit the keyboard! The full list of events is available on GitHub.
13199: A demo website is available here and the full documentation of it is available on GitHub!
13200: import AircallWorkspace from 'aircall-everywhere';
13201: const aircallWorkspace = new AircallWorkspace({
13202: onLogin: settings => {
13203: console.log('phone loaded');
13204: doStuff();
13205: },
13206: onLogout: () => {},
13207: domToLoadWorkspace: '#workspace',
13208: integrationToLoad: 'zendesk',
13209: size: 'big'
13210: });
13211: Dealing with phone numbers
13212: Aircall uses international phone number formatting in its Public API.
13213: But dealing with phone number formatting can be complex and time consuming. We recommend using libphonenumber, built by Google, complete and up-to-date!
13214: It extracts useful information from any phone number, like the number's type (mobile, toll-free, landline...), the country, the international/national/e164 format...
13215: SIP trunking
13216: Aircall uses several providers under the hood to buy and configure phone numbers all around the World.
13217: As each provider is specific, Aircall does not offer SIP trunking capabilities or any advanced voice feature via its Public API yet!
13218: The best way to get access to the audio data is to get the recording mp3 file URL at the end of a Call.
13219: Timezones
13220: Aircall dates and times are rendered in UTC.
13221: Timezones listed in Aircall's products follow the tz database format.
13222: Emojis
13223: We love emojis, but they don't fit well everywhere in our products (yet!). You can display emojis in Insight Cards, to make caller insights displayed in Aircall Workspace more compelling 💅 . For the rest, the Public API will return an error if you try to update any string with an emoji 😱

348: FAQs
349: How much does Aircall cost?
350: Aircall offers three plans, Essentials, Professional and Enterprise, plus AI Voice Agents as a standalone product from $99 per month. The Essentials plan starts at $30/license/month (billed annually) and includes 250+ integrations, IVR, call recording, and SMS. The Professional plan starts at $50/license/month and adds advanced analytics, smart routing, Power Dialer, and AI conversation intelligence. Both require a minimum of 3 licenses. The Enterprise plan is available for teams of 25+ licenses with SLA, SSO, and dedicated onboarding. Pricing may vary; talk to our team for more information.
351: Does Aircall offer a free trial?
352: Yes. Aircall offers free access to test the platform before committing. New accounts receive 100 AI Voice Agents minutes at sign-ups in addition to the 50 free minutes all customers get every month. That way, teams can evaluate AI-powered call handling alongside core phone features.
353: What AI features are included in Aircall?
354: Aircall is the customer communications platform where both AI and your team handle every conversation. AI Voice Agents handle volume so your team handles the conversations only humans can win, with AI Assist helping your reps win every call.
355: Call recording, call transcription, and 50 AI Voice Agents minutes per month are included in every plan, from Essentials to Enterprise.
356: Conversational intelligence features such as call summary, sentiment analysis, and key topics are included in the Professional plan.
357: For real-time assistance during your call and post-call automation, AI Assist Pro is a standalone add-on available at $49/user/month.
358: Additional AI Voice Agent minutes can be added in two ways: Pay as you go: $0.29 per minute, with no commitment. Monthly bundle: 1,000 minutes for $250, 3,500 minutes for $805, or 10,000 minutes for $1,900.
359: How does Aircall pricing compare to Dialpad and RingCentral?
360: Aircall's Essentials plan starts at $30/license/month with unlimited inbound calls, 250+ integrations, and no hidden recovery fees. Dialpad's comparable Standard plan starts at $15/user/month but requires separate products for contact center ($80+/user/month) and sales features. RingCentral's entry pricing is competitive but AI and analytics features typically require higher-tier plans. Every plan includes 50 AI Voice Agents minutes per month. Professional adds conversation intelligence.
361: Can I use Aircall for both sales and customer support?
362: Yes. Aircall is built for both inbound support and outbound sales on the same platform. Support teams get IVR, smart routing, shared call inbox, and queue callback. Sales teams get Power Dialer, voicemail drop, and outbound campaigns. AI features like call summaries, call scoring, and everything syncs to your CRM or helpdesk through 250+ integrations.
363: Are there additional costs beyond the license fee?
364: Aircall includes one local or toll-free number per plan, with additional numbers available at $6/month each. Inbound and internal calls are unlimited (excluding toll-free). Outbound domestic calling is unlimited within the US and Canada; international rates vary by destination. AI Voice Agents usage is billed per minute in tiered bundles: 1,000 minutes for $250, 3,500 minutes for $805, or 10,000 minutes for $1,900 (about $0.19 per minute). Above 50,000 minutes, custom pricing is available at rates as low as $0.12 per minute. Pay as you go is $0.29 per minute. There are no administrative recovery fees or hidden surcharges.
365: What integrations does Aircall support?
366: Aircall integrates with 250+ tools including Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, Intercom, Pipedrive, Microsoft Dynamics, Shopify, and Monday.com. All plans include API access and 250+ integrations. Aircall also offers an open API and webhook framework for custom integrations.
367: Does Aircall offer annual and monthly billing?
368: Yes. Aircall offers both annual and monthly billing. Annual plans include a 25% discount compared to monthly pricing. All plans require a minimum of 3 licenses regardless of billing cycle.

57: 1 Messages supports both JWT and Basic authentication, however basic authentication does not support webhooks or advanced features such as ACLs. For most use-cases we recommend JWT Authentication. See Messages API Authentication

60: Contents
61: In this document you can learn about authentication via the following means:
62: API Key and Secret
63: Basic Authentication
64: Secret Rotation
65: JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
66: API Key and Secret
67: When you create a Vonage account, an API key and secret will be created for you. These are located in your account settings in the Vonage Dashboard. You should always keep these secure and never share these details: be careful when adding it to your codebase to make sure they are not shared with anyone who may use it maliciously. If you use message signatures, these are generated using the SIGNATURE_SECRET rather than the API_SECRET; both values can be found in your account settings.
68: Note: The secret should always be kept secure and never shared. Be careful when adding it to your codebase to make sure it is not shared with anyone who may use it maliciously. Read more about the Best Security Practices for your Vonage Account.
69: Vonage APIs may require your API Key and Secret in a number of different ways.
70: Basic Authentication
71: A number of newer Vonage APIs require authentication to be done using an API key and secret sent Base64 encoded in the Authorization header.
72: For these APIs, you send your API key and secret in the following way:
73: Copy
74: Authorization: Basic base64(API_KEY:API_SECRET)
75: If your API key were aaa012 and your API secret were abc123456789, you would concatenate the key and secret with a : (colon) symbol and then encode them using Base64 encoding to produce a value like this:
76: Copy
77: Authorization: Basic YWFhMDEyOmFiYzEyMzQ1Njc4OQ==
78: A website for generating Base64 encoded strings can be found here:
79: General: Base64 Encode and Decode
80: Details on how to encode Base64 strings in a variety of programming languages can be found at the following websites:
81: C#/.NET: How do I encode and decode a Base64 string? from StackOverflow
82: Go: Base64 Encoding from Go By Example
83: Java: Base64
84: JavaScript: Base64 encoding and decoding from MDN web docs
85: PHP: base64_encode
86: Python: Base64
87: Ruby: Base64
88: Swift: Base64 Encode and Decode in Swift from iOS Developer Tips
89: Secret Rotation
90: It is possible to have two API secrets to be used against one API key at the same time. This way you can create a second API secret and test it before revoking the existing API secret in your production network. The API secret rotation procedure consists of the following steps:
91: Create a second API secret in your account settings or by using the secret rotation API.
92: Update one or more of your servers to use the newly created API secret for making calls to Vonage APIs
93: Test that there are no connectivity issues and roll out the API secret update across the remaining servers
94: Delete the replaced API secret
95: JSON Web Tokens
96: JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) are a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. For a full list of the APIs that use JWTs, please see the table above.
97: Header and Payload
98: JWTs consist of a Header and a Payload. The values for the Header are:
99: Name
100: Description
101: Required
102: alg
103: The encryption algorithm used to generate the JWT. RS256 is supported.
104: typ
105: The token structure. Set to JWT.
106: The values for the payload claim are:
107: Name
108: Description
109: Required
110: application_id
111: The unique ID allocated to your application by Vonage.
112: iat
113: The UNIX timestamp at UTC + 0 indicating the moment the JWT was requested.
114: jti
115: A unique string identifier of the JWT.
116: nbf
117: The UNIX timestamp at UTC + 0 indicating the moment the JWT became valid.
118: exp
119: The UNIX timestamp at UTC + 0 indicating the moment the JWT is no longer valid. A minimum value of 30 seconds from the time the JWT is generated. A maximum value of 24 hours from the time the JWT is generated. A default value of 15 minutes from the time the JWT is generated.
120: Generating JWTs
121: Using the Vonage CLI to generate JWTs
122: The Vonage CLI provides a command for generating a JWT.
123: An example of generating a JWT for an application is as follows:
124: Copy

144: Copy
145: The private key in question is generated from the application dashboard or from vonage apps create. You can save this
146: information for the CLI by running vonage auth set. The contents of the private key will then be saved in either
147: the .vonagerc file or $HOME/.vonage/config.json.
148: Further information on the Vonage CLI can be found in its repository on GitHub.
149: Examples of using the Vonage libraries to generate JWTs can be found below. If you are not using a Vonage library you should refer to RFC 7519 to implement JWTs.
150: Vonage Client SDKs
151: The Vonage Client and Video SDKs use JWTs for authentication when a client connects to Vonage. These JWTs are generated using the application ID and private key that is provided when a new application is created.
152: Claims
153: Using that private.key and the application ID, you can mint a new JWT. In order to log a user into a Vonage client, the JWT will need the following claims:
154: Vonage Client SDK
155: Claim
156: Description
157: sub
158: The "subject". The subject, in this case, will be the name of the user created and associated with your Vonage Application.
159: acl
160: Access control list. The Client SDK uses this as a permission system for users. Read more about it in the ACL overview.
161: application_id
162: This is the ID of the Vonage Application you created.
163: iat
164: "Issued at time" This is the time the JWT was issued, in unix epoch time.
165: jti
166: "JWT ID". This is a unique string identifier for this JWT.
167: exp
168: "Expiration time" This is the time in the future that the JWT will expire, in unix epoch time.
169: The exp claim is optional. If the claim is not provided, then the JWT will expire by default in 15 minutes. The max expiration time for a JWT is 24 hours. JWTs should typically be short-lived, as it is trivial to create a new JWT and some JWTs can have multiple far-reaching permissions.
170: Sample Client SDK JWT Payload
171: Once all the claims have been provided, the resulting claims should appear like so:
172: Copy
173: {
174: "iat": 1532093588,
175: "jti": "705b6f50-8c21-11e8-9bcb-595326422d60",
176: "sub": "alice",
177: "exp": "1532179987",
178: "acl": {
179: "paths": {
180: ...
181: }
182: },
183: "application_id": "aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-0123456789ab"
184: }
185: ( ... snippet is truncated)
186: Vonage Video Client SDK
187: Claim
188: Description
189: sub
190: The "subject". The subject, in this case, should be the string video.
191: acl
192: Access control list. The Client SDK uses this as a permission system for users. Read more about it in the ACL overview.
193: application_id
194: This is the ID of the Vonage Application you created.
195: session_id
196: This is the ID of the Session you created.
197: scope
198: This is the scope of the token. It should be the string session.connect.
199: role
200: This is the role of the token. It can be a range of string values depending on what permissions you want to grant this token.
201: data
202: This custom metadata you can optionally add to describe the token. This is a string limited to 1000 characters.
203: initial_layout_class_list
204: This lets you optionally, when broadcasting, specify the initial layout class list for streams published by the client.
205: iat
206: "Issued at time" This is the time the JWT was issued, in unix epoch time.
207: jti
208: "JWT ID". This is a unique string identifier for this JWT.
209: exp
210: "Expiration time" This is the time in the future that the JWT will expire, in unix epoch time.
211: The exp claim is optional. If the claim is not provided, then the JWT will expire by default in 15 minutes. The max expiration time for a Video SDK JWT is 24 hours. JWTs should typically be short-lived, as it is trivial to create a new JWT and some JWTs can have multiple far-reaching permissions. Always make sure to try and set an exp time to the least amount of time that is feasible for your application.
212: Sample Video Client SDK JWT Payload
213: Copy
214: {
215: "scope": "session.connect",
216: "session_id": "1_MX44YjY4NTFmZS01NjdjLTRlODYtYWRmOC0zYmVhODM2MzNjNjB-fjE3NDIzMDY0ODY0NjZ-WS9FOHhybUdHV0JtTGZYTEV2aVlwV1N4fn5-",
217: "role": "moderator",
218: "initial_layout_class_list": "",
219: "sub": "video",
220: "acl": {
221: "paths": {
222: "/session/**": {}
223: }
224: },
225: "jti": "c04c96ba-3229-4fd4-9f55-406b6a6eb485",
226: "iat": 1742306486,
227: "exp": 1742307386,
228: "application_id": "8b6851fe-567c-4e86-adf8-3bea83633c60"
229: }
230: Access Control List (ACL)
231: In the sample JWT request payload above, notice how the acl claim has a paths object. The path object contains a list of endpoints that correspond to certain permissions a user has when using the Client SDK.
232: Below is the list of endpoints you can grant a user access to:
233: Endpoint
234: Description
235: Required for
236: /*/rtc/**
237: Create signalling session to receive events and send metrics
238: In-app calls/message
239: /*/sessions/**
240: Log in as an in-app voice or chat user
241: In-app calls/messages
242: /*/users/**
243: Getting user conversations, user sessions and user object
244: In-app calls/messages
245: /*/conversations/**
246: Create and manage conversations & send/receive messages
247: In-app calls/messages
248: /*/knocking/**
249: Start phone calls
250: In-app calls
251: /*/devices/**
252: Register device to receive push notifications
253: In-app calls/messages
254: /*/legs/**
255: Create and manage legs in a conversation
256: In-app calls
257: /*/session/**
258: Connect to a video session
259: Video
260: You should provide the user you are generating with permissions to access only the relevant paths. For instance, if the Voice Client SDK user is not going to need to fetch information about their User object or other Users, you should omit the users path. To further illustrate, if you add the /*/conversations/** path to a JWT's ACL, the user will be able to create and manage conversations. Also, if this is the only ACL set, the user will only have access to the /conversations endpoint.
261: Note: Using wildcards in your ACL paths (e.g. /*/conversations/**) will allow the JWT token to access all the operations for that endpoint. It is strongly recommended that you use more granular control of your ACL paths as illustrated below.
262: Granular ACL Paths
263: Above, we looked at how to grant users access to endpoints. You may also limit or grant access based on sub-paths and HTTP methods. This allows you to very granularly define what permissions a token should have. For example in your Voice Client SDK application you want users to be able to get information about a conversation:
264: Copy
265: {
266: "acl": {
267: "paths": {
268: "/*/conversations/**": {}
269: }
270: }
271: }
272: The above ACL paths allows anyone with this token to make requests to any Conversation API endpoint linked to your Vonage application. This will allow whoever holds this token get a list of ongoing Conversations in your application, create new Conversations, or more. To mitigate this, you can specify which paths specifically should be accessible and which HTTP methods are allowed to be used on those paths.
273: Copy
274: {
275: "acl": {
276: "paths": {
277: "/*/conversations/*": {
278: "methods": [
279: "GET"
280: ]
281: }
282: }
283: }
284: }
285: This new ACL paths allows anyone with this token to only make a GET request to a specific conversation and no further subpaths or operations. Which is far more restrictive than before.
286: Minimum ACL Paths for Client SDKs
287: Below are the minimum ACL paths needed to perform various actions in the Vonage Client SDKs. To add support for more endpoints based on your use case, refer to the ACL table above and add them as restrictively as possible.
288: This supports the basic use case of creating a session, using serverCall, reconnectCall, and being able to answer, reject, hangup a call.
289: Copy
290: {
291: "acl": {
292: "paths": {
293: "/*/sessions/**": { "methods": ["POST"] },
294: "/*/conversations/*": { "methods": ["GET"] },
295: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/answer": { "methods": ["POST"] },
296: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/offer/*": { "methods": ["POST"]},
297: "/*/conversations/*/members/*": { "methods": ["PUT", "DELETE"] },
298: "/*/knocking/**": { "methods": ["POST", "DELETE"] },
299: "/*/legs/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] },
300: "/*/v2/rtc/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] }
301: }
302: }
303: }
304: In addition to the base Calling case, this will allow you to use SDK functions such as mute, say, etc. This is needed for the Chat SDK.
305: Copy
306: {
307: "acl": {
308: "paths": {
309: "/*/sessions/**": { "methods": ["POST"] },
310: "/*/conversations/*": { "methods": ["GET"] },
311: "/*/conversations/*/events/*": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"]},
312: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/answer": { "methods": ["POST"] },
313: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/offer/*": { "methods": ["POST"]},
314: "/*/conversations/*/members/*": { "methods": ["PUT", "DELETE"] },
315: "/*/knocking/**": { "methods": ["POST", "DELETE"] },
316: "/*/legs/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] },
317: "/*/v2/rtc/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] }
318: }
319: }
320: }
321: In addition to the base Calling case, this will allow you to use SDK functions to manage push tokens. Add the device methods you want to support as needed.
322: Copy
323: {
324: "acl": {
325: "paths": {
326: "/*/sessions/**": { "methods": ["POST"] },
327: "/*/conversations/*": { "methods": ["GET"] },
328: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/answer": { "methods": ["POST"] },
329: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/offer/*": { "methods": ["POST"]},
330: "/*/conversations/*/members/*": { "methods": ["PUT", "DELETE"] },
331: "/*/knocking/**": { "methods": ["POST", "DELETE"] },
332: "/*/legs/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] },
333: "/*/v2/rtc/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] },
334: "/*/devices/**": { "methods": [] }
335: }
336: }
337: }
338: Devices methods:
339: POST - Register new user devices.
340: GET - Fetch registered devices for the user.
341: PUT - Update registered devices for the user.
342: DELETE - Delete registered devices for the user.
343: In addition to the base Calling case, this will allow you to use SDK functions to get information about a specific user.
344: Copy
345: {
346: "acl": {
347: "paths": {
348: "/*/sessions/**": { "methods": ["POST"] },
349: "/*/conversations/*": { "methods": ["GET"] },
350: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/answer": { "methods": ["POST"] },
351: "/*/conversations/*/rtc/*/offer/*": { "methods": ["POST"]},
352: "/*/conversations/*/members/*": { "methods": ["PUT", "DELETE"] },
353: "/*/knocking/**": { "methods": ["POST", "DELETE"] },
354: "/*/legs/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] },
355: "/*/v2/rtc/**": { "methods": ["POST", "GET"] },
356: "/*/users/*": { "methods": ["GET"] },
357: }
358: }
359: }
360: This supports connecting to a session with the Video SDK
361: Copy
362: {
363: "acl": {
364: "paths": {
365: "/*/session/**": {}
366: }
367: }
368: }
369: Generating JWTs using the Vonage CLI
370: The Server SDKs contain methods for generating JWT tokens. You may however use the Vonage CLI to do this as well.
371: This is particularly helpful during testing.
372: Copy
373: # A command with parameters
374: vonage jwt create `
375: --app-id='00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000' `
376: --private-key=./private.key `
377: --sub='Alice' `
378: --acl='{\"paths\":{\"\/*\/users\/**\":{},\"\/*\/conversations\/**\":{},\"\/*\/sessions\/**\":{},\"\/*\/devices\/**\":{},\"\/*\/push\/**\":{},\"\/*\/knocking\/**\":{},\"\/*\/legs\/**\":{}}}'
379: # Will produce a token
380: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..BscMdDXZ1-nuLtKyPJvw9tE8E8ZjJvTPJPMT9y0TjPz4Q7qqNaqxcjglc5QPtYEjh2YpZH6btSKbUF4XTClI026Hl5_QOBlnayYo7jXwhba16fa5PeyzSf30QFGFrHbANwrQJFVCjd329SZUpwK4GxgB1gf230NhbfmkhegKezqicru2WTGCKm8kQncYliFwIEYUlcRAb2c8xcaVrn_6QNNahyeJRwGFfWpIkX0Oe-S4RDlPjoq47_gYWac9MmaetB4Dd3Yp531AuniGV5JiIShkaEwuY4Zyov4Hcmajm4Lm_UFY119la7vzHis0P7cT9pPUDe5cyPj7eT8-VhitfQ

382: REM A command with parameters
383: vonage jwt create ^
384: --app-id='00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000' ^
385: --private-key=./private.key ^
386: --sub='Alice' ^

388: REM Will produce a token
389: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..BscMdDXZ1-nuLtKyPJvw9tE8E8ZjJvTPJPMT9y0TjPz4Q7qqNaqxcjglc5QPtYEjh2YpZH6btSKbUF4XTClI026Hl5_QOBlnayYo7jXwhba16fa5PeyzSf30QFGFrHbANwrQJFVCjd329SZUpwK4GxgB1gf230NhbfmkhegKezqicru2WTGCKm8kQncYliFwIEYUlcRAb2c8xcaVrn_6QNNahyeJRwGFfWpIkX0Oe-S4RDlPjoq47_gYWac9MmaetB4Dd3Yp531AuniGV5JiIShkaEwuY4Zyov4Hcmajm4Lm_UFY119la7vzHis0P7cT9pPUDe5cyPj7eT8-VhitfQ

399: Using the Server SDKs
400: It is expected that the accompanying server for your Vonage application will generate JWTs for the Client SDKs. Here are some examples using the Vonage Server SDKs:
401: Version 3 of the Vonage Node Server SDK includes a package for generating JWT tokens. It can also generate a JWT using the appropriate claims.
402: Copy
403: const { tokenGenerate } = require('@vonage/jwt');
404: const privateKey = readFileSync('path/to/private.key');
405: const aclPaths = {
406: "paths": {
407: ...
408: }
409: }
410: const token = tokenGenerate("aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-0123456789ab", privateKey, {
411: //expire in 24 hours
412: exp: Math.round(new Date().getTime()/1000)+86400,
413: sub: "Alice",
414: acl: aclPaths,
415: });
416: The Vonage JWT JDK library can be used to generate a signed JWT with claims.
417: Copy
418: val token : String = Jwt.builder()
419: .applicationId("aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-0123456789ab")
420: .privateKeyPath("/path/to/private.key")
421: .issuedAt(ZonedDateTime.now())
422: .subject("Alice")
423: .addClaim("acl", mapOf(
424: "paths" to mapOf(
425: ...
426: )
427: ))
428: .build()
429: .generate()
430: The Vonage JWT JDK library can be used to generate a signed JWT with claims.
431: Copy
432: String token = Jwt.builder()
433: .applicationId("aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-0123456789ab")
434: .privateKeyPath(Paths.get("/path/to/private.key"))
435: .subject("Alice")
436: .issuedAt(ZonedDateTime.now())
437: .expiresAt(ZonedDateTime.now().plusMinutes(20))
438: .addClaim("acl", Map.of(
439: "paths", Map.of(
440: ...
441: )
442: ))
443: .build()
444: .generate();
445: The Vonage .NET SDK can be used to generate a signed JWT with claims.
446: As an example, let's assume we want to add the following claims in the JWT:
447: Copy
448: var payload = new Dictionary<string, object>
449: {
450: {"sub", "Alice"},
451: {"exp", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddDays(1).ToUnixTimeSeconds().ToString()},
452: {
453: "acl", new Dictionary<string, object>
454: {
455: ["paths"] = new Dictionary<string, object>
456: {
457: ...
458: },
459: }
460: },
461: };
462: There are several ways to generate a JWT.
463: You can either use the static method CreateToken on the Jwt class:
464: Copy
465: var credentials = Credentials.FromAppIdAndPrivateKeyPath(VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID, VONAGE_APPLICATION_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH);
466: var token = Jwt.CreateToken(credentials.ApplicationId, credentials.ApplicationKey, payload);
467: Or use the method GenerateToken on a Jwt instance:
468: Copy
469: // Using the credentials instance
470: var result = tokenGenerator.GenerateToken(credentials, payload);
471: // Using ApplicationId and ApplicationKey values
472: var result = tokenGenerator.GenerateToken(credentials.ApplicationId, credentials.ApplicationKey, payload);
473: The current version of the Vonage PHP Server SDK can also create a JWT including the appropriate claims when using the Keypair authentication.
474: Copy
475: $keypair = new \Vonage\Client\Credentials\Keypair(
476: file_get_contents('/path/to/private.key'),
477: 'aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-0123456789ab'
478: );
479: $client = new \Vonage\Client($keypair);
480: $claims = [
481: 'acl' => [
482: 'paths' => [
483: ...
484: ]
485: ]
486: ];
487: $token = $client->generateJwt($claims);
488: $tokenString = $token->toString();
489: The Vonage Python JWT library can be used to generate a signed JWT with default or custom claims.
490: Copy
491: from vonage_jwt import JwtClient
492: jwt_client = JwtClient(application_id, private_key)
493: # The `claims` field is optional and can be omitted as defaults are set
494: paths = { ... }
495: claims = {'sub': 'Alice', 'paths': paths}
496: vonage_jwt = jwt_client.generate_application_jwt(claims)
497: The Vonage JWT JDK library can be used to generate a signed JWT with claims.
498: Copy
499: @builder = Vonage::JWTBuilder.new(application_id: YOUR_APPLICATION_ID, private_key: YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY)
500: @token = @builder.jwt.generate
501: ( ... snippet is truncated)
502: If you are not using a Vonage library you should refer to RFC 7519 to implement JWT. JWT.io has a selection of libraries for generating JWTs in multiple languages.

30: multiple messaging platforms through a single integration. This API is currently in Beta, so
31: expect some changes before it is production-ready.
32: Dispatch API
33: Use the Dispatch API for a multichannel messaging solution with failover.
34: SMS API
35: For applications that only need to send and/or receive SMS, the SMS API is our stable, recommended
36: solution. The SMS API has extensive support in all our client libraries and lots of code examples
37: and tutorials to help you along your way.
38: External Accounts API
39: Use this to manage accounts for the Messages and Dispatch APIs across all the various channels
40: that we support.
41: WhatsApp Provisioning API
42: Use this to manage allocate WhatsApp Numbers to your Vonage API account
43: Conversation API
44: Add text messaging (and voice, and video) features to your web and mobile applications.
45: Conversation API allows you to create real-time communications channels to use in your apps.
46: Alerts API - Subscription
47: For subscribing users to event-based alerts with US Short Codes
48: Alerts API - Sending
49: For sending event-based alerts to users with US Short Codes
50: 2FA
51: For verifying users with US Short Codes
52: Voice
53: Voice API
54: Make and receive telephone calls to or from anywhere in the world. The Voice API lets you dial
55: other phones, answer incoming calls, and control all aspects of the call including conferences,
56: recordings, capturing user input and sending various audio content.
57: NCCO: Nexmo Call Control Objects
58: Control all aspects of incoming and outgoing calls with NCCO in JSON format
59: Voice Webhooks
60: Details of the incoming webhooks sent by the Voice API. Learn how to respond to an incoming call
61: and react to events during a call.
62: Media API
63: Manage media items for use with Vonage APIs. This API allows you to handle media to send and to
64: download recordings.
65: Conversation API
66: Add voice communication (and video, and text messaging) features to your web and mobile
67: applications, connecting users anywhere in the world.
68: Network Features
69: Identity Insights API
70: Request real-time access to a broad range of attributes related to the carrier, subscriber, or device associated with a phone number.
71: Device Location Retrieval API
72: Retrieve the last known location of a SIM enabled device using cellular network positioning.
73: Core Services
74: Application API
75: Create and manage the applications you use across Vonage APIs. Create, manage and configure your
76: applications and authentication.
77: Conversation API
78: Create real-time communications channels for text, voice and video.
79: Reports API
80: Retrieve and search message, call, and conversation records in JSON format, by ID, or by time
81: period. Request a CSV report of activity for your account.
82: Numbers
83: Number Management API
84: Manage all the numbers you need for your applications. Search for numbers, list and configure your
85: purchased numbers, cancel any number you no longer need.
86: Number Pools API
87: Manage account-level number pools programmatically as a self-service.
88: US Number Deactivation API
89: Download number deactivations lists for US numbers.
90: Account
91: Account API
92: Configure account-level settings, check and manage your account balance, and manage your API
93: secrets using the Account API
94: External Accounts API
95: Use this to manage accounts for the Messages and Dispatch APIs across all the various channels
96: that we support.
97: Pricing API
98: Query the prices of Vonage services, either by country or by dialling prefix.
99: Verify
100: Verify API
101: Use both SMS and Voice calling to verify that a phone number belongs to a user that registers with
102: it. Helps to protect your organisation against spam and fraudulent registrations.
103: Verify API - Custom templates
104: You may optionally custom templates to modify the format and wording of messages sent by the
105: Verify API.
106: Security and Compliance
107: Redact API
108: Ensure your organization is compliant with data regulations such as GDPR by redacting individual's
109: data from the Vonage platform.
110: Audit API
111: Get an audit trail of changes to your account for security and compliance purposes.

991: Simplify record retrieval for Vonage SMS, Messages, Voice, Video, Verify, and Identity Insights APIs in one powerful API. Enjoy automated discounts as your usage scales – no negotiation necessary.

994: Maximize your communications investment with API management services from our experts. We offer flexible Service and Support plans to get you started and help you grow.
995: See API service and support plan details
996: API Pricing Models: Understanding Approaches to API Charges
997: With Vonage as your provider, API costs are generally straightforward and simple to understand. They’re all based on a pay as you go API pricing model, meaning you’re charged based on usage. Pay as you go isn’t the only API pricing model, however. Let’s take a quick look at the four most common:
998: The Pay as You Go API Pricing Model
999: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1000: This is probably the most popular API pricing model. Here, API users pay according to their actual usage of the API. There’s no set or fixed fee. This makes this model attractive as if the API is only occasionally used, it doesn’t cost as much.
1001: Pay-per-use and pay-per-call are prime examples of the pay as you go API pricing model. In the case of the latter, the user is charged whenever an API gets a request and retrieves the corresponding data.
1002: The Fixed API Pricing Model
1003: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1004: The fixed API pricing model is also sometimes known as a subscription-based model. It’s adopted by some software as a service (SaaS) companies that provide APIs.
1005: Under this model, API users are charged a flat fee, usually on a monthly or annual basis. That fee doesn’t change, regardless of API usage. However, sometimes, API providers will place restrictions or caps on usage.
1006: When these kinds of quotas are part of an API pricing arrangement, once a user has reached the limit of their API use for a month or year, they can’t carry on using it until the next billing period.
1007: Fixed API pricing is generally attractive to users who expect to get heavy usage out of APIs. It also has the advantage of giving both users and providers greater clarity on what they’ll spend or be paid.
1008: The Tiered or Overage API Pricing Model
1009: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1010: The tiered or overage API pricing model is in many ways an evolution of the fixed API pricing model.
1011: Users are still charged a monthly or annual fee, and this time, usage quotas are applied as standard. In this case, however, users don’t have to wait until the next billing period to keep operating the APIs once they reach their quota. Instead, they’re then charged on a pay as you go basis for any usage beyond the initial limit.
1012: The tiered element of this model comes from the fact that API providers will typically offer a range of pricing tiers. Each will come with a different monthly or annual fee and a varying usage quota. The higher the fee, the higher the quota. It’s then up to each user to determine which tier best suits their needs.
1013: The Free Trial API Pricing Model
1014: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1015: This is perhaps better described as a possible addendum to any of the above API pricing models, rather than a model in of itself. It’s worth discussing briefly, however, due to its inherent benefits for both users and providers.
1016: When API providers offer a free trial, prospective users get to directly experience the APIs and their potential benefits. That works well to convince them that they’re worth the investment—arguably more so than any sales call or demo ever could.
1017: In general, free trials will last for a set period of time or give a certain amount of usage. After which, the trial user will need to switch to an offered pay as you go, fixed price, or tiered pricing plan.
1018: Try it free
1019: Start developing now with free credit. No credit card required.
1020: Start coding
1021: API Pricing FAQs
1022: What Is an API?
1023: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1024: API stands for Application Programming Interface. An API is a connection mechanism which allows two software components or applications to work together. It defines and manages how the applications communicate with one another in terms of requests and responses. For an end user, APIs work to combine the functionalities of otherwise distinct applications.
1025: How Much Does an API Cost to Build?
1026: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1027: Pricing API development and creation is tricky. There are many factors that can determine the exact costs involved in the process. Things such as the complexity involved and, therefore, the level of expertise necessary, security considerations, and the volume of data involved. In general, however, you’re looking at thousands rather than hundreds of dollars to build an API from scratch.
1028: Are Any APIs Free?
1029: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1030: Yes, there are free APIs that developers can use without any charge within their projects. These are sometimes known as public or open-source APIs. Some API providers also offer free trials of APIs, such as Vonage’s Communication APIs to let prospective users experience the benefits of the APIs first hand, for no charge.
1031: How Much Do Vonage Communications APIs Cost?
1032: Select to expand or collapse this FAQ answer.
1033: Vonage’s API pricing differs depending on the API in question, but is based on usage. Meaning, you only pay for what use you get from the API. In the case of the Voice API, for example, that means you pay per minute for the calls made and received via the API. The exact amount depends on the nature of the call; whether it’s domestic or international, PSTN or VoIP, etc.

245: Set up the MCP server
246: VS Code
247: Cursor
248: Windsurf
249: Claude Desktop
250: The details of the MCP server should look like this.
251: "vonage-mcp-server-api-bindings": {
252: "type": "stdio",
253: "command": "npx",
254: "args": [
255: "-y",
256: "@vonage/vonage-mcp-server-api-bindings"
257: ],
258: "env": {
259: "VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID": "<YOUR_VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID>",
260: "VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64": "<YOUR_VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64>",
261: "VONAGE_API_KEY": "<YOUR_VONAGE_API_KEY>",
262: "VONAGE_API_SECRET": "<YOUR_VONAGE_API_SECRET>",
263: "VONAGE_VIRTUAL_NUMBER": "<YOUR_VONAGE_VIRTUAL_NUMBER>",
264: "VONAGE_WHATSAPP_NUMBER": "<YOUR_VONAGE_WHATSAPP_NUMBER>",
265: "RCS_SENDER_ID": "<YOUR_RCS_SENDER_ID>"
266: }
267: }
268: Encoding your private key
269: VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64 must be your application's private key file, base64 encoded on a single line.
270: Run one of these commands locally, replacing private.key with the path to your key file, and paste
271: the output into your config:
272: macOS:
273: base64 -i private.key
274: Linux:
275: base64 -w 0 private.key
276: Windows PowerShell:
277: [Convert]::ToBase64String([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes((Resolve-Path .\private.key)))
278: Security
279: STDIO transport
280: This server runs locally and talks to your MCP client (VS Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop, etc.) over
281: STDIO. Tool calls and their responses travel between the two processes as plaintext JSON-RPC. There
282: is no transport-layer encryption or authentication on this channel, which is how local MCP servers
283: are designed to work.
284: That is safe on a single-user machine you trust, which is the intended way to run this server. Keep
285: in mind that:
286: Any process with enough privilege on the same machine can read or tamper with the STDIO stream. If
287: the machine is compromised, the server cannot protect the data passing through it.
288: In shared, multi-user, or containerised environments, other users or workloads may be able to
289: observe the process. Only run the server where you trust everything else running alongside it.
290: Storing credentials
291: The setup above puts your Vonage credentials, including VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64, into your MCP
292: client's config file (for example claude_desktop_config.json or .cursor/mcp.json) as plaintext.
293: Any process running as your user can read that file, and it is easy to leak by accident.
294: Treat VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64 like a private SSH key. Anyone who has it can act as your Vonage
295: application.
296: If the config file lives inside a project, such as .cursor/mcp.json or .vscode/mcp.json, add
297: it to that project's .gitignore so it is never committed.
298: Cloud sync services (iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive) can silently upload config
299: directories. Exclude those directories from sync, or keep credential-bearing config files outside
300: synced folders.
301: For stronger protection, keep the secrets out of the config file entirely. The options are below.
302: Keeping secrets out of the config file
303: The server only reads credentials from its environment, so the goal is to have your MCP client
304: supply VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64 and VONAGE_API_SECRET at launch without writing them into a file.
305: This protects the credentials at rest. Once the server is running, they are still in its
306: environment.
307: macOS (Keychain)
308: Store the secrets in your login Keychain. The private key is too long to paste at a terminal prompt,
309: so the first command reads it straight from the key file. The second command ends with -w, which
310: makes security prompt for the API secret so it doesn't end up in your shell history:
311: security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s vonage-mcp-private-key64 -w "$(base64 -i private.key)"
312: security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s vonage-mcp-api-secret -w
313: Then launch the server through a shell that reads them from Keychain, and keep only the non-secret
314: values in env:
315: "vonage-mcp-server-api-bindings": {
316: "type": "stdio",
317: "command": "/bin/sh",
318: "args": [
319: "-c",
320: "VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64=$(security find-generic-password -s vonage-mcp-private-key64 -w) || exit 1; VONAGE_API_SECRET=$(security find-generic-password -s vonage-mcp-api-secret -w) || exit 1; export VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64 VONAGE_API_SECRET; exec npx -y @vonage/vonage-mcp-server-api-bindings"
321: ],
322: "env": {
323: "VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID": "<YOUR_VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID>",
324: "VONAGE_API_KEY": "<YOUR_VONAGE_API_KEY>",
325: "VONAGE_VIRTUAL_NUMBER": "<YOUR_VONAGE_VIRTUAL_NUMBER>",
326: "VONAGE_WHATSAPP_NUMBER": "<YOUR_VONAGE_WHATSAPP_NUMBER>",
327: "RCS_SENDER_ID": "<YOUR_RCS_SENDER_ID>"
328: }
329: }
330: The first time the server starts, macOS may ask whether security can access the items. Choose
331: Always Allow so later launches don't prompt.
332: VS Code (input variables)
333: VS Code can prompt for a secret the first time the server starts and store it securely, using input
334: variables in .vscode/mcp.json or your user-profile mcp.json:
335: {
336: "inputs": [
337: {
338: "type": "promptString",
339: "id": "vonage-private-key64",
340: "description": "Vonage private key (base64)",
341: "password": true
342: },
343: {
344: "type": "promptString",
345: "id": "vonage-api-secret",
346: "description": "Vonage API secret",
347: "password": true
348: }
349: ],
350: "servers": {
351: "vonage-mcp-server-api-bindings": {
352: "type": "stdio",
353: "command": "npx",
354: "args": ["-y", "@vonage/vonage-mcp-server-api-bindings"],
355: "env": {
356: "VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID": "<YOUR_VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID>",
357: "VONAGE_API_KEY": "<YOUR_VONAGE_API_KEY>",
358: "VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64": "${input:vonage-private-key64}",
359: "VONAGE_API_SECRET": "${input:vonage-api-secret}"
360: }
361: }
362: }
363: }
364: Add the remaining non-secret variables from the setup example to env as needed. VS Code doesn't
365: forward servers that use input variables to Copilot harness sessions. See the
366: VS Code MCP configuration reference
367: for details.
368: Linux and Windows
369: Neither has a secret store with a command-line client that is installed and working by default. If
370: you already use one, such as secret-tool with GNOME Keyring or PowerShell SecretManagement, you
371: can apply the same pattern as the macOS example: launch the server through a shell that reads the
372: secrets and exports them before starting it. Otherwise, follow the file-handling guidance above.

151: Feishu OpenPlatform Server SDK for Python
152: 商店应用 ClientAssertion 认证
153: 中文
154: The Feishu Open Platform provides server-side APIs for messaging, contacts,
155: approval, sheets, Base, and many other product capabilities. This SDK wraps the
156: repeated platform work around API calls, including token management, request
157: signing, encryption/decryption, event dispatching, and typed request/response
158: models.
159: Documentation
160: Preparations before development
161: Calling server-side APIs
162: Handle events
163: Handle card callbacks
164: SDK FAQs
165: Installation
166: pip install lark-oapi
167: Python 3.8 or later is required.
168: Basic Usage
169: import lark_oapi as lark
170: from lark_oapi.api.im.v1 import *
171: client = lark.Client.builder() \
172: .app_id("cli_xxx") \
173: .app_secret("your_app_secret") \
174: .build()
175: request = CreateMessageRequest.builder() \
176: .receive_id_type("chat_id") \
177: .request_body(CreateMessageRequestBody.builder()
178: .receive_id("oc_xxx")
179: .msg_type("text")
180: .content("{\"text\":\"hello world\"}")
181: .build()) \
182: .build()
183: response = client.im.v1.message.create(request)
184: ClientAssertion Keyless Mode
185: For self-built apps and eligible ISV apps that use an external signing service, the SDK can fetch
186: tenant tokens with client_assertion instead of app_secret. The SDK does not
187: generate, parse, sign, or store JWT private keys; your provider supplies the
188: final assertion string.
189: import os
190: import lark_oapi as lark
191: from lark_oapi.core.client_assertion import ClientAssertionToken
192: class EnvClientAssertionProvider:
193: def retrieve_token(self, aud: str) -> ClientAssertionToken:
194: return ClientAssertionToken(os.environ["LARK_CLIENT_ASSERTION"])
195: client = lark.Client.builder() \
196: .app_id(os.environ["LARK_APP_ID"]) \
197: .client_assertion_provider(EnvClientAssertionProvider()) \
198: .build()
199: If you use a custom OpenAPI domain, also configure oauth_base_url(...) so the
200: SDK can derive the OAuth audience correctly. Eligible ISV apps also set
201: app_type(lark.AppType.ISV) and pass tenant_key for tenant API calls.
202: Keyless mode does not support AppAccessToken-only APIs.
203: One-Click App Registration
204: lark_oapi.register_app creates an app through the OAuth device flow. It
205: returns a verification URL in on_qr_code; render the URL as a QR code or show
206: it as a link for the user to open in Feishu/Lark.
207: import lark_oapi as lark
208: def on_qr_code(info):
209: print(info["url"])
210: result = lark.register_app(
211: on_qr_code=on_qr_code,
212: app_preset={
213: "avatar": [
214: "https://example.com/a.png",
215: "https://example.com/b.webp",
216: ],
217: "name": "{user}'s app",
218: "desc": "Created by the business platform",
219: },
220: )
221: print(result["client_id"])
222: Custom scopes/events/callbacks and updating an existing app
223: When creating an app, use addons to incrementally request scopes, event subscriptions,
224: and callbacks on top of the platform base template. They are pre-filled into the
225: confirm page shown after the user scans the QR code, and take effect once the user
226: confirms:
227: result = lark.register_app(
228: on_qr_code=on_qr_code,
229: addons={
230: "scopes": {
231: "tenant": ["im:message:send_as_bot"],
232: "user": ["calendar:calendar:read"],
233: },
234: "events": {"items": {"tenant": ["im.message.receive_v1"]}},
235: "callbacks": {"items": ["card.action.trigger"]},
236: },
237: create_only=True,
238: )
239: lark.register_app(
240: on_qr_code=on_qr_code,
241: app_id="cli_xxx",
242: addons={"scopes": {"tenant": ["drive:drive.metadata:readonly"]}},
243: )
244: Notes:
245: addons is additive only: items are merged on top of the base template; base permissions can never be removed.
246: addons.preset picks the base template: omitted or True keeps the default base template, while False switches to the minimal base template so the final config only contains what addons declares. With "preset": False, an addons without any incremental item is also valid.
247: Only the 5 public config types are supported: tenant/user scopes, tenant/user events, and callbacks. Sensitive config such as event request URLs, security.*, or encrypt keys cannot travel through addons.
248: The SDK validates the shape, not the item names; names unknown to the platform catalog are ignored by the confirm page.
249: For a real manual E2E run without mocked registration responses:
250: python3 samples/registration/app_preset_live_e2e.py --open

401: Webhook authentication
402: When no EncryptKey is configured and a nonempty VerificationToken is explicitly supplied, the SDK validates the token before invoking event or callback handlers: top-level token for v1 and header.token for v2. Missing, null, empty, non-string, or mismatched tokens are rejected. Challenge responses also validate explicitly configured verification tokens.
403: Leaving both credentials empty retains the previous behavior. Encrypted events retain existing decryption and signature checks, and WebSocket clients continue using trusted internal dispatch.
404: Rollback: reverting this change restores the validation gap for explicitly configured VerificationTokens. Keep independent webhook authentication in place before rolling back.
405: Runtime webhook credentials
406: Register a combined provider while building the handler:
407: handler = (lark.EventDispatcherHandler.builder("", "")
408: .webhook_credentials_provider(credential_store.get_webhook_credentials)
409: .build())
410: The provider is called once per HTTP webhook (events, callbacks, and challenge), before decryption and validation. It is not called while building the handler or by trusted WebSocket dispatch. The returned pair overrides static credentials for that request only; the next request sees updates. The example store method returns a lark.WebhookCredentials value and reads the complete pair atomically from a thread-safe local cache. Providers must return promptly, with caller-owned timeouts for any I/O. Empty strings retain legacy empty-configuration behavior. Invalid results and exceptions reject the request without static fallback, and original exception details are not logged or returned. Provider registration is initialization-only. Monitor acquisition latency and failures in the provider. Remove the provider registration to return to static credentials.
411: WebSocket connection host and handshake headers
412: domain controls HTTP endpoint discovery. The optional connection host replaces only the WebSocket URL host[:port], preserving scheme, path and query. Default DNS and TLS/SNI follow the resulting hostname; existing custom transport settings still apply. Domains below are placeholders.
413: client = lark.ws.Client(
414: os.environ["APP_ID"], os.environ["APP_SECRET"],
415: domain="https://bootstrap.example.com",
416: connection_host="websocket.example.com:443",
417: connection_headers={"X-Route": "events"},
418: event_handler=event_handler,
419: )
420: Handshake headers are copied at initialization and for each handshake, including reconnects, and are never forwarded to endpoint discovery. Omitting both settings preserves existing behavior. Host, Connection, Upgrade and Sec-WebSocket-* cannot be overridden through headers. Basic host checks reject empty values, schemes/paths and query parameters; other address and header settings are passed to the underlying libraries without additional SDK format checks. These basic host and reserved-header checks run before network I/O (Start returns an error in Go; construction/build throws in other SDKs). Use trusted developer configuration, not headers/hosts supplied by an end-user request.

186: Overview
187: Feishu Open Platform provides a series of atomic APIs on the server side to realize diversified functions, but the actual coding process is not very smooth: when using these APIs to complete operation, a lot of extra work needs to be considered, such as token acquisition and maintenance, data encryption and decryption, request signature verification, etc.; in the actual coding process, the semantics of function calls are missing, cause mental burden.
188: All of these make the overall development experience poor. In order to make the open capability easy to use, we have written this SDK, which integrates all the verbose logic into built-in processing, provides a complete type hints, and provides external semantics. Programming interface to improve coding experience.

199: Enterprise self-built Application: The application can only be installed and used within the enterprise, more introduction.
200: ISV Application: The app will be listed in the ISV Application

207: How to use
208: Provides two versions of ECMAScript and CommonJS, and supports the use of native Javascript and Typescript. The examples are all taking Typescript as an example.
209: Typescript
210: import * as lark from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
211: CommonJS
212: const lark = require('@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk');

214: import * as lark from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
215: API Call
216: The list of all APIs on Feishu Open Platform: click here.
217: The SDK provides a semantic calling method. You only need to construct a client instance according to the relevant parameters, and then use the semantic method (client.business domain.resource.method) on it to complete the API call, the calling process and the calling result. There are complete types for prompting, such as sending a message to a group chat:
218: import * as lark from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
219: const client = new lark.Client({
220: appId: 'app id',
221: appSecret: 'app secret',
222: appType: lark.AppType.SelfBuild,
223: domain: lark.Domain.Feishu,
224: });
225: const res = await client.im.message.create({
226: params: {
227: receive_id_type: 'chat_id',
228: },
229: data: {
230: receive_id: 'receive_id',
231: content: JSON.stringify({text: 'hello world'}),
232: msg_type: 'text',
233: },
234: });

239: For self-built applications, you can use the following code to create a client:
240: import * as lark from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
241: const client = new lark. Client({
242: appId: 'app id',
243: appSecret: 'app secret'
244: });
245: For store apps, the specified appType that needs to be displayed is lark.AppType.ISV:
246: import * as lark from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
247: const client = new lark.Client({
248: appId: 'app id',
249: appSecret: 'app secret',
250: appType: lark.AppType.ISV,
251: });
252: When using the client of the created store application to initiate an API call, you need to manually pass the tenant_key, you can Use lark.withTenantKey to do it:

325: For the interface whose return value is presented in the form of pagination, it provides iterator encapsulation (the method name suffix is ​​WithIterator), which improves the usability and eliminates the tedious operation of repeatedly obtaining data according to page_token, such as obtaining the user list:
326: // Process 20 pieces of data each time
327: for await (const items of await client.contact.user.listWithIterator({
328: params: {
329: department_id: '0',
330: page_size: 20,
331: },
332: })) {
333: console.log(items);
334: }
335: // You can also use next to manually control the iteration, fetching 20 pieces of data each time
336: const listIterator = await SDKClient.contact.user.listWithIterator({
337: params: {
338: department_id: '0',
339: page_size: 20,
340: },
341: });
342: const { value } = await listIterator[Symbol.asyncIterator]().next();
343: console.log(value);
344: Of course, you can also use the version without iterator encapsulation. In this case, you need to manually perform paging calls each time according to the returned page_token. *

355: The returned binary stream is encapsulated, eliminating the processing of the stream itself, just call the writeFile method to write the data to the file, such as:

357: path: {
358: file_key: 'file key',
359: },

362: If you want to customize the processing of the stream, you can call the getReadableStream method to obtain the stream, such as writing the stream to a file:
363: import * as fs from 'fs';
364: const resp = await client.im.file.get({
365: path: {
366: file_key: 'file key',
367: },
368: });
369: const readableStream = resp.getReadableStream();
370: const writableStream = fs.createWriteStream('file url');
371: readableStream.pipe(writableStream);

499: Events handling
500: For a list of all events opened on Feishu Open Platform, please click here.
501: For the event processing scenario, we care about is only what kind of events to listen for, and what we do after the event occurs. other work such as data decryption we don't want to care about. The SDK provides an intuitive way to describe this part of the logic:
502: Construct an instance of the event handler EventDispatcher;
503: Register the events to be monitored and their handler functions on the instance;
504: Bind the instance to the service;

557: unregister(...keys) removes the handler registered for each of the given event keys. It accepts one or more event keys, returns the dispatcher itself so that calls can be chained, and does nothing for a key that has no handler.

684: Subscribing to Events Using Long Connection Mode
685: Official Documentation：Documentation：
686: Developers establish a WebSocket full-duplex channel with the open platform by integrating the Lark SDK. When an event callback occurs, the open platform will send messages to the developer through this channel.Compared with the traditional Webhook mode, the long connection mode significantly reduces the access cost, reducing the original development cycle of about 1 week to 5 minutes. The specific advantages are as follows:
687: There is no need to use intranet penetration tools during the testing phase. Event callbacks can be received in the local development environment through the long connection mode.
688: Authentication is only performed when the connection is established. Subsequent event pushes are all plaintext data, and developers do not need to handle decryption and signature verification logic.
689: Only need to ensure that the running environment has the ability to access the public network, no need to provide public IP or domain name.
690: There is no need to deploy a firewall and configure a whitelist.
691: Points to Note
692: Similar to Webhook, under the long connection mode, developers need to complete processing within 3 seconds after receiving a message, otherwise, a timeout re-push will be triggered.
693: Message pushing is in cluster mode, it does not support broadcasting, that is, if multiple clients are deployed for the same application, only one random client will receive the message.
694: Currently, the long connection mode only supports event subscriptions and does not support callback subscriptions
695: SDK supports this function integration,1.24.0 and later versions are available, sample code:
696: import * as Lark from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
697: const baseConfig = {
698: appId: 'xxx',
699: appSecret: 'xxx'
700: }
701: const client = new Lark.Client(baseConfig);
702: const wsClient = new Lark.WSClient({...baseConfig, loggerLevel: Lark.LoggerLevel.info});
703: wsClient.start({
704: eventDispatcher: new Lark.EventDispatcher({}).register({
705: 'im.message.receive_v1': async (data) => {
706: const {
707: message: { chat_id, content}
708: } = data;
709: await client.im.v1.message.create({
710: params: {
711: receive_id_type: "chat_id"
712: },
713: data: {
714: receive_id: chat_id,
715: content: Lark.messageCard.defaultCard({
716: title: `reply： ${JSON.parse(content).text}`,
717: content: 'hello'
718: }),
719: msg_type: 'interactive'
720: }
721: });
722: }
723: })
724: });
725: Channel module
726: Channel is a high-level module built on top of WSClient / Client that bundles transport, message normalization, safety policy, outbound sending, streaming replies, media upload, and card interactions into a single abstraction. It is the recommended entry point for conversational bots (AI chat, streaming replies, interactive card buttons, etc.).

728: const channel = createLarkChannel({ appId, appSecret });

730: await channel.send(
731: msg.chatId,
732: { markdown: `received: ${msg.content}` },
733: { replyTo: msg.messageId },
734: );
735: });
736: await channel.connect();
