817: Custom scopes/events/callbacks (addons) and updating an existing app
818: When creating an app, use addons to incrementally request scopes, event subscriptions and callbacks on top of the platform base template. They are pre-filled into the confirm page shown after the user scans the QR code, and take effect once the user confirms:
819: // Create: incrementally request scopes/events/callbacks, and only allow
820: // creating a new app (selecting an existing app is disabled)
821: const result = await lark.registerApp({
822: addons: {
823: scopes: { tenant: ['im:message:send_as_bot'], user: ['calendar:calendar:read'] },
824: events: { items: { tenant: ['im.message.receive_v1'] } },
825: callbacks: { items: ['card.action.trigger'] },
826: },
827: createOnly: true,
828: onQRCodeReady(info) { /* ... */ },
829: });
830: // Update: pass the appId of an existing app to let the user re-scan and
831: // confirm, incrementally granting scopes to that app
832: await lark.registerApp({
833: appId: 'cli_xxx',
834: addons: { scopes: { tenant: ['drive:drive.metadata:readonly'] } },
835: onQRCodeReady(info) { /* ... */ },
836: });
837: // Minimal base: drop the default template (bot capability only, no business
838: // scopes) and show only the explicitly declared items. With `preset: false`
839: // an otherwise-empty addons is valid.
840: await lark.registerApp({
841: addons: {
842: preset: false,
843: scopes: { tenant: ['im:message:send_as_bot'] },
844: },
845: onQRCodeReady(info) { /* ... */ },
846: });
847: Notes:
848: addons.preset selects the template base: true / omitted keeps the platform default template and layers the declared items on top (additive — the default behavior); false drops the default template and starts from the minimal base (bot capability only, no business scopes), showing only the explicitly declared items. Only with preset: false may addons be otherwise empty (minimal base, zero increments); otherwise at least one scope, event or callback is required.
849: addons is additive only: items are merged on top of the base template; base permissions can never be removed.
850: Only the 5 public config types (tenant/user scopes, tenant/user events, callbacks) are supported. Sensitive config (event subscription type and request URLs, security.*, encrypt keys, etc.) cannot travel via addons — use the update application config OpenAPI instead.
851: The SDK only validates the shape, not the item names; names unknown to the platform catalog are silently ignored by the confirm page.

995: Webhook authentication
996: When no EncryptKey is configured and a nonempty VerificationToken is explicitly supplied, the SDK validates the token before invoking event or callback handlers: top-level token for v1 and header.token for v2. Missing, null, empty, non-string, or mismatched tokens are rejected. Challenge responses also validate explicitly configured verification tokens.
997: Leaving both credentials empty retains the previous behavior. Encrypted events retain existing decryption and signature checks, and WebSocket clients continue using trusted internal dispatch.
998: Rollback: reverting this change restores the validation gap for explicitly configured VerificationTokens. Keep independent webhook authentication in place before rolling back.
999: Runtime webhook credentials
1000: Both EventDispatcher and CardActionHandler accept an optional webhookCredentialsProvider:
1001: import { EventDispatcher, WebhookCredentials } from '@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk';
1002: // Application-owned local cache, populated by your configuration/KMS integration.
1003: const readCachedCredentials: () => WebhookCredentials = () => credentialCache.read();
1004: const dispatcher = new EventDispatcher({
1005: webhookCredentialsProvider: readCachedCredentials,
1006: });
1007: The provider can return WebhookCredentials directly or a Promise. Construction does not call it. Each validated direct invocation or HTTP adapter request calls it once before crypto; automatic challenge and ordinary dispatch share that copied snapshot. Subsequent requests see updated values, while in-flight requests retain their snapshot. Trusted WebSocket dispatch (needCheck: false) does not call the provider.
1008: When configured, the provider replaces both static credentials. Both fields must be strings; two empty strings retain credential-free legacy behavior. Throws, Promise rejections, and malformed results fail before handlers, without static fallback or exposing provider error details. Direct invoke rejects with a sanitized error; adapters return HTTP 403. Keep providers thread safe and prompt; read a local cache and enforce any external I/O timeout/cancellation inside the provider. Remove the provider option to roll back to static configuration without reverting the token validation fix.
1009: WebSocket connection host and handshake headers
1010: domain controls HTTP endpoint discovery. The optional connection host replaces only the WebSocket URL host[:port], preserving scheme, path and query. Default DNS and TLS/SNI follow the resulting hostname; existing custom transport settings still apply. Domains below are placeholders.
1011: const client = new Lark.WSClient({
1012: appId: process.env.APP_ID!,
1013: appSecret: process.env.APP_SECRET!,
1014: domain: 'https://bootstrap.example.com',
1015: connectionHost: 'websocket.example.com:443',
1016: connectionHeaders: { 'X-Route': 'events' },
1017: });
1018: Handshake headers are copied at initialization and for each handshake, including reconnects, and are never forwarded to endpoint discovery. Omitting both settings preserves existing behavior. Host, Connection, Upgrade and Sec-WebSocket-* cannot be overridden through headers. Basic host checks reject empty values, schemes/paths and query parameters; other address and header settings are passed to the underlying libraries without additional SDK format checks. These basic host and reserved-header checks run when constructing WSClient; invalid settings throw an error before any network request. Use trusted developer configuration, not headers/hosts supplied by an end-user request.

143: Pumble SDK
144: This repository contains the tools to create Pumble apps.
145: Pumble SDK - A javascript framework to quickly build Pumble apps.
146: Pumble CLI - A cli tool to generate and run Pumble apps from your local environment.
147: Read the full documentation to get started.
148: Quick Start
149: npm i -g pumble-cli
150: After successfully installing pumble-cli use the command below to log in to your workspace
151: pumble-cli login
152: You will be asked to input your email address and you will receive a code in your inbox.
153: After logging in you can proceed to create your first Pumble App.
154: pumble-cli create
155: This command will ask you to type a name and description and will generate the project.
156: After this command has completed you can then cd into the generated directory and start the addon.
157: cd my_app
158: npm run dev
159: If you login into Pumble you will see your App is installed and ready to use.
160: Tip
161: You can also skip installing pumble-cli and use npx pumble-cli create instead

1: # Access Tokens Guide
2: The platform supports the following access token types. The type you use depends on who uses your application, and whether you are a [partner](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/solution-providers/overview).
3: * If you are a **direct developer**, meaning only you or your business accesses your own data, use a [System User access token](#system-user-access-tokens).
4: * If you are a **Tech Provider**, use a [Business Integration System User access token](#business-integration-system-user-access-tokens).
5: * If you are a **solution partner**, use [System User access tokens](#system-user-access-tokens) to share your line of credit with newly onboarded customers, and [Business Integration System User access tokens](#business-integration-system-user-access-tokens) for everything else.
6: ## System user access tokens
7: System user access tokens ("system tokens") represent you, your business, organization, or people within your business or organization. The main advantage of these tokens is that they are long-lived and can represent automated services within your business that don't require any user input.
8: System tokens rely on system users. Most endpoints check if the user identified by the token has access to the queried resource. If the user doesn't have access to the resource, the system rejects the request with [error code `200`](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/support/error-codes) (not to be confused with HTTP status code `200`).
9: System users can be [admins](#admin-system-users) or [employees](#employee-system-users).
10: ### Admin system users {#admin-system-users}
11: By default, admin system users have full access to all WhatsApp accounts (WAACs), Messaging accounts, and their assets owned by or shared with you or your business portfolio.
12: Admin system users are useful if your app needs access to all of the business portfolio's assets, without having to manually grant business asset access to each asset whenever it is created, or shared with your business portfolio.
13: You can override an admin system user's default business asset access by granting partial access per account. Grant it separately for each WhatsApp account and each Messaging account. See [Business Asset Access](#business-asset-access) to learn how to set and override access.
14: ### Employee system users {#employee-system-users}
15: Employee system users must be granted access to the individual WhatsApp accounts and Messaging accounts that are owned by, or shared with, your business portfolio. If your app only needs access to a few accounts that you own, an employee system user should be sufficient.
16: Once created, you must grant **Partial** or **Full** [business asset access](#business-asset-access) for **both** accounts the system user needs to work with: the **WhatsApp account** and the **Messaging account**. Access to the Messaging account alone is not sufficient.
17: How the grant is applied differs by surface:
18: - **API.** Granting business asset access on a Messaging account also applies that grant to the WhatsApp account it is linked to. This cascade exists because the WhatsApp account has no Graph API endpoints of its own yet. Treat it as interim behavior rather than something to depend on.
19: - **Meta Business Suite.** The panel does not cascade. Assign the system user to the WhatsApp account and to the Messaging account explicitly.
20: ### Generate system user access tokens {#generating-system-user-access-tokens}
21: To generate a system token, access the [**Business settings**](https://business.facebook.com/settings/) panel and then click **System Users**:
22: Click the **+Add** button, and in the **Create system user** window that appears, enter a system user name and assign it an **Admin** or **Employee** role:
23: Once you create the admin system user, it appears in the list of system users. Click the system user's name to display the asset assignment overlay:
24: Click the **Assign assets** button to display the **Select assets and assign permissions** window:
25: Select your app and grant your system user the **Manage app** permission, then click the **Assign assets** button to confirm and dismiss the window.
26: Back in the **System Users** panel, reload the page to confirm that your system user has been granted **Full control** of your app. Granting the permissions may take a few minutes, so reload the page if your app doesn't appear as an assigned asset. Once the asset has been assigned, it should look like this:
27: Once you see that your system user has been granted full control of your app, in the asset assignment overlay, click the **Generate token** button. In the window that appears, select your app, choose a token expiration preference, and assign your app these three Graph API permissions:
28: - `business_management`
29: - `whatsapp_business_management`
30: - `whatsapp_business_messaging`
31: You can search for `business` to find these permissions quickly:
32: Click the **Generate token** button and copy the token when it appears.
33: ## Business integration system user access tokens
34: Business Integration System User access tokens ("business tokens") are scoped to individual onboarded customers and should be used by Tech Providers and solution partners when accessing onboarded customer data.
35: These tokens are useful for apps that perform programmatic, automated actions on customer Messaging accounts, without having to rely on input from an app user, or requiring future re-authentication.
36: To generate a Business Integration System User access token, you must implement Embedded Signup (configured with Facebook Login for Businesses) and exchange the code returned to you when a customer completes the flow.
37: See [Embedded Signup](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/embedded-signup/overview) and [Business Integration System User access tokens](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/facebook-login/facebook-login-for-business#business-integration-system-user-access-tokens) to learn more about these tokens and how to generate them.
38: ## User access tokens
39: Although User access tokens are supported and can be used by all app developers, you typically only use them when you first use the App Dashboard to [send your first test message](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/get-started). As you develop your app, however, you switch to a System User access token (and eventually a Business Integration System User access token, if you are a Tech Provider or a partner). This is because user access tokens expire quickly, so you have to keep generating a new one every few hours.
40: There are several ways to generate a User access token:
41: * Access the **App Dashboard** > **WhatsApp** > **API setup** panel. This panel always generates a new User access token whenever you visit it. The token is automatically scoped to your user, since you are signed into your developer account when you access the panel.
42: * Use [Graph API Explorer](https://developers.facebook.com/tools/explorer).
43: * Implement [Facebook Login](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/facebook-login).
44: ## Use tokens in requests
45: When making API requests, include your token in an authorization request header, preceded by `Bearer`. For example:
46: ```html
47: curl 'https://graph.facebook.com/v27.0/102290129340398/message_templates' \
48: -H 'Authorization: Bearer EAAJB...'
49: ```
50: ## Token format
51: Access tokens are opaque strings. A full token looks like this:
52: ```
53: EAAJBsbCmS80BO4hZBf5xYKFaFW7kVMNxAWzIInZB7q1PuZCLiEqKh3gZDZD
54: ```
55: Tokens can vary in length, and their internal structure and characteristics can change over time. Do not parse, decode, or make assumptions about the format of an access token — treat it as an opaque string. Use a variable-length data type without a specific maximum size to store access tokens.
56: ## Business asset access
57: After creating a system user, you must set business asset access levels. Many endpoints require the system user whose token is included in API requests to have either **Partial** or **Full** business asset access to both the **WhatsApp account** and the **Messaging account** being queried (or their assets). If the system user doesn't have this access, these endpoints return [error code `200`](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/support/error-codes) (not to be confused with HTTP status code `200`).
58: Granting access on a Messaging account through the API also applies the grant to the WhatsApp account linked to it. Meta Business Suite does not do this — there, assign the system user to each account explicitly. The cascade is interim behavior that exists only until the WhatsApp account has API endpoints of its own, so do not build on it.
59: If you set a system user's business asset access on a WhatsApp account or Messaging account to **Partial** access, you can further restrict access to certain assets or actions on that account. For example, if you have a large business and want a certain department to only have read access to a Messaging account's template data and a WhatsApp account's business phone number data, you could create a system user for that department and set granular access to view only for that data.
60: To set business asset access, follow these steps for the WhatsApp account, then repeat them for the Messaging account:
61: 1. Sign into [Meta Business Suite](https://business.facebook.com).
62: 1. Locate your business portfolio in the dropdown menu at the top of the page and click its **Settings** (gear) icon.
63: 1. Navigate to **Accounts** > **WhatsApp accounts**, or **Accounts** > **Messaging accounts**.
64: 1. Select the appropriate account.
65: 1. Select the **People** subtab.
66: 1. Click the **+Add people** button.
67: 1. Select the appropriate system user and assign appropriate access levels on the account.
68: ---
69: Full documentation index for this product: https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/llms.txt

162: Vonage CPaaS Power for Kiro
163: A Kiro Power that brings the Vonage Communications Platform directly into your AI-assisted development workflow. Go from zero to a working Vonage integration in minutes with guided, conversational workflows.

175: What Is This?
176: This Power connects Kiro to the Vonage CPaaS platform via two MCP servers:
177: Server
178: Description
179: vonage-api
180: Live API bindings for account management, phone numbers, applications, and activity reports
181: vonage-docs
182: Vonage developer documentation, SDK references, and code examples
183: Combined with steering files that encode best-practice workflows, Kiro can guide you through tasks like setting up a new Vonage application, purchasing a phone number, and pulling activity reports — all through natural conversation.
184: Prerequisites
185: Kiro installed and running
186: A Vonage API account (free to create)
187: Your Vonage API Key and Secret from the Vonage Dashboard
188: Installation
189: Clone this repository:
190: git clone https://github.com/Vonage/vonage-kiro-power.git
191: Set your Vonage credentials as environment variables before launching Kiro. The quickest way is a .env file in your project root:
192: VONAGE_API_KEY=your_api_key_here
193: VONAGE_API_SECRET=your_api_secret_here
194: Find both values at Vonage Dashboard → API Settings. See Configuration for the full list of variables.
195: Open the directory in Kiro — the Power is detected automatically from POWER.md. Kiro reads your environment variables and passes them to the MCP server on startup.
196: Credentials not set? When you trigger a workflow, the Power will detect missing credentials and walk you through the setup before proceeding.
197: Configuration
198: Set the following environment variables in your shell, a .env file, or directly in mcp.json.
199: Required for all workflows
200: Variable
201: Description
202: Where to find
203: VONAGE_API_KEY
204: Your Vonage account API key
205: Dashboard → API Settings
206: VONAGE_API_SECRET
207: Your Vonage account API secret
208: Dashboard → API Settings
209: Required for messaging and voice
210: Variable
211: Description
212: Where to find
213: VONAGE_APPLICATION_ID
214: UUID of your Vonage Application
215: Dashboard → Applications
216: VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY64
217: Base64-encoded RSA private key
218: Downloaded when creating an application; encode with base64 -i private.key (macOS) or base64 -w 0 private.key (Linux)
219: Optional, channel-specific
220: Variable
221: Description
222: VONAGE_VIRTUAL_NUMBER
223: Your purchased Vonage number in E.164 format (e.g. +12015550100)
224: VONAGE_WHATSAPP_NUMBER
225: Your WhatsApp Business number
226: RCS_SENDER_ID
227: Your RCS agent/sender identifier
228: Workflows
229: Get Started
230: Goes from credentials to a fully configured Vonage Application with a linked phone number.
231: Trigger phrases: "Set up Vonage", "Help me get started with Vonage", "Create a Vonage app", "Buy a number"
232: Steps:
233: Validates your API credentials against the live API
234: Creates a Vonage Application with your chosen capabilities (Messages, Voice, or both)
235: Searches for available phone numbers in your chosen country
236: Purchases and links the number to your application
237: Outputs all environment variables you need to continue building
238: Reports & Monitoring
239: Pulls activity records, visualizes data, and checks account balance.
240: Trigger phrases: "Show my reports", "Check message delivery", "Monitor usage", "Check my balance"
241: Steps:
242: Retrieves message and call records for a date range you specify (up to 30 days)
243: Filters by channel, destination number, status, or direction
244: Generates charts to visualize message volume, delivery rates, and channel distribution
245: Reports your current account balance with optional low-balance warnings

1: # WhatsApp app review
2: App Review is part of [app development](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/development) that enables us to verify that your app uses our Products and APIs in an approved manner. Meta needs to validate how you intend to use the requested permissions to make sure it is compliant with our requirements and policies.
3: Businesses first need to develop a prototype of their product so they can demonstrate their use case with a video recording for the App Review submission. To pass App Review, it is important that you ask for only the permissions your app needs; **requesting unnecessary permissions is a common reason for rejection** during App Review.
4: The following video provides a brief overview of the App Review process:
5: Business apps are automatically approved for [Standard Access](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api/overview/access-levels#standard-access) for all Permissions and Features available to the Business app type, so you can test your app while you are in this access level. Make sure your test users have a `developer` or `admin` role in the Meta app being used to implement Embedded Signup. **This means that if you are using the API for yourself as a Direct Developer, you do not need Advanced access or app review.**
6: **If you are building an app that other businesses will be using, you must request Advanced access for any permissions your app needs.**
7: You can request [Advanced access](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api/overview/access-levels#advanced-access) by submitting your app to App Review.
8: ## Permissions
9: Commonly requested permissions and what to include to get approval for **Advanced access**:
10: | Permission | Description | What to include in your submission |
11: | --- | --- | --- |
12: | [whatsapp_business_management](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/permissions#w) | The **whatsapp_business_management** permission allows your app to read and/or manage WhatsApp business assets you own or have been granted access to by other businesses through this permission. These business assets include WhatsApp accounts and Messaging accounts, business phone numbers, message templates, QR codes and their associated messages, and webhook subscriptions. Access to a WhatsApp account does not grant access to its Messaging account, and access to a Messaging account does not grant access to its WhatsApp account — you must be granted access to both.<br><br>If your app uses this permission to access WhatsApp accounts or Messaging accounts not owned by your business, you must have **Advanced access**. Without it, API calls return error code `200`. | **Written:** Explain how you will use this permission to access the business assets of clients who you have onboarded onto the platform.<br><br>**Video:** Record a video of your app, or WhatsApp Manager, being used to create a message template. |
13: | [whatsapp_business_messaging](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/permissions#w) | The **whatsapp_business_messaging** permission allows an app to send WhatsApp messages and make calls to a specific phone number, upload and retrieve media from messages, manage and get WhatsApp business profile information, and to register those phone numbers with Meta. | **Written:** Explain what messaging functionality your app offers to clients who you have onboarded onto the platform, and how they perform those functions.<br><br>**Video:** Record a video showing your app being used to send a message to a WhatsApp number, and the WhatsApp client (either web or mobile app) receiving and displaying the sent message. If you wish, you can use the **App Dashboard** > **WhatsApp** > **API Setup** panel to generate a cURL request that you can integrate into your app to send the message.<br><br>If you are partnering with a Solution Partner and plan to use their API, ask the Solution Partner to share a video with you that you can submit as part of your submission. |
14: | [whatsapp_business_manage_events](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/permissions#w)<br><br>Only request this permission if you are using the [Marketing Messages API for WhatsApp](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/marketing-messages/overview) with [Conversions API](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/ads-commerce/conversions-api). | The **whatsapp_business_manage_events** permission allows an app to log events, such as purchase, add-to-cart, leads, and more, on behalf of a WhatsApp account or Messaging account administered by an app user. The allowed usage for this permission is to log events on WhatsApp accounts and Messaging accounts, and send this activity data to Meta for ads targeting, optimization, and reporting. | This permission is automatically approved if you already have **Advanced access** for `whatsapp_business_messaging` permission. |
15: The average turnaround time for App Review is about 24 hours. Start the App Review process as soon as possible. You don't need to wait for Embedded Signup to be fully implemented to start this process.
16: ## Reducing chances of App Review rejection
17: You must request **Advanced access** for the permissions above.
18: You can request these permissions in a single bulk submission, or as separate submissions. For each permission, an explanation and screen recording specific to the permission being requested is required.
19: As part of your submission, you must include separate screen recordings that show how your app uses each permission in your submission. The video can be a screen recording directly from your computer, or a recording using a digital camera or camera phone. You will need to attach this file to your App Review submission.
20: Do not submit a video that includes multiple permissions supporting different use cases. You must submit a different video clip for each permission. Your submission may be rejected if you highlight multiple permissions being used as part of the same video.
21: Both written descriptions and screen recordings are required for each permission. If you include a screen recording that shows how your app uses a permission, but fail to include a description of how it uses it, your submission will be rejected.
22: Submissions in draft mode will not be reviewed, so don't forget to **submit your App Review submission!**
23: ## Examples
24: This is an example of a screen recording showing your app being used to submit a template for approval. This demonstrates your app using the **whatsapp_business_management** permission, which you requested in your App Review submission.
25: This is a screenshot from an example screen recording showing your app being used to send and receive a message to and from a WhatsApp user number (right-click and open in a new tab to see a larger version). This demonstrates your app using the **whatsapp_business_messaging** permission, which you requested in your App Review submission.
26: Note that **you cannot submit a screenshot**, you must submit a screen recording.
27: ---
28: Full documentation index for this product: https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/llms.txt

155: WhatsApp Business MCP Server
156: A security-hardened Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for the official WhatsApp Business Cloud API. Connect AI assistants like Claude, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client to WhatsApp Business.
157: Features
158: 50+ tools across 8 modules — messaging, templates, media, analytics, flows, webhooks, business profile, account management
159: Security-first — API key auth, rate limiting, input validation, webhook signature verification, error sanitization, path traversal protection
160: Official Meta API only — all calls go to graph.facebook.com, no unofficial/third-party APIs
161: Two transport modes — stdio (for MCP clients like Claude Desktop) and HTTP (for REST API access)
162: Production-ready — CORS controls, security headers, configurable via environment variables
163: Tools Overview

167: Messaging
168: Send text, media, interactive, location, contact, reaction, reply
169: All WhatsApp message types

173: Media

191: Quick Start
192: 1. Clone and install
193: git clone https://github.com/tkhattar14/whatsapp-business-mcp.git
194: cd whatsapp-business-mcp
195: python -m venv venv
196: source venv/bin/activate # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
197: pip install -r requirements.txt
198: 2. Configure
199: cp .env.example .env
200: # Edit .env with your Meta WhatsApp Business API credentials
201: # Get them from: https://developers.facebook.com/
202: 3. Run (stdio mode — for MCP clients)
203: source .env && python main.py
204: 4. Run (HTTP mode — for REST API)
205: source .env && python main_http.py

256: Security
257: This server is security-hardened with:
258: API key authentication on HTTP endpoints (X-API-Key header)
259: Rate limiting (10 req/sec per IP, in-memory token bucket)
260: Webhook signature verification (HMAC-SHA256 via META_APP_SECRET)
261: Input validation — phone number format, message length limits
262: Error sanitization — tokens and sensitive URLs stripped from error responses
263: Path traversal protection — media uploads restricted to allowed directory
264: Security headers — X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Cache-Control
265: No wildcard CORS — explicit origin allowlist only
266: See SECURITY.md for full details.
267: API Version
268: Uses WhatsApp Cloud API v22.0 (latest stable, March 2026). Configurable via WHATSAPP_API_VERSION env var.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Slack apps are installed with a v2 OAuth 2.0 flow. Your app can act with its own identity instead of acting on behalf of users, without requesting excessive permissions that could cause installations to be rejected.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: OAuth 2.0 refers to the 2.0 version of the OAuth spec, and this is our second version of OAuth 2.0. For the rest of this guide, we'll just refer to it as "OAuth".

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: OAuth allows a user in any Slack workspace to install your app. At the end of the OAuth flow, your app gains an access token. Your app's access token allows your app to open doors to the Slack platform. During the OAuth flow, you specify which scopes your app needs. Those scopes determine exactly which doors your app can open.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Implementing an OAuth flow can feel hard because there are a lot of steps, but your app really only has to worry about three steps to make OAuth work: requesting scopes, waiting for a user to give their approval, and exchanging a temporary authorization code for an access token. Redirecting a user to Slack can be done with a single link. For example:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: [Add to Slack](https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&client_id=33336676.569200954261)

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Obtaining access tokens with OAuth​

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Why is there a third exchanging step in OAuth at all? Why doesn't Slack send your app an access token directly after the user okays your app? The reason is two-factor authentication. You have to prove both that you have the right temporary authorization code, and that you have your app's client secret.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: To request scopes, redirect Slack users to https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize. If you're developing a GovSlack app for use by public sector customers, redirect users to https://slack-gov.com/oauth/v2/authorize.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: A scope conflict occurs when attempting to combine Sign in with Slack (SIWS) user scopes with non-Sign in with Slack scopes in the same OAuth flow

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Each set of scopes must be requested in a separate OAuth flow.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook,commands&client_id=3336676.569200954261

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When requesting scopes, you also need to tell Slack where to send your temporary authorization code afterward. Include a redirect_uri parameter in the URL above. The redirect_uri is where Slack will send the user back to, along with the temporary authorization code, once the user okays your app. The redirect_uri must use HTTPS. Alternatively, you can configure a Redirect URL in the App Management page under OAuth & Permissions. A Redirect URL must also use HTTPS.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Authorize: You direct the user to the corresponding /oauth/v2/authorize path (this can be done with a link or button, for example). Send the redirect_uri in this step.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Access: Your server retrieves the verification code from the previous step and sends it to the oauth.v2.access API endpoint to exchange that code for an access token. If you sent a redirect_uri field in the first step, you must send that same field with the same value in this step.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: If there are multiple Redirect URL values configured, but no redirect_uri parameter is sent, the OAuth flow will use the first Redirect URL listed on the App Management page. You can use the redirect_uri parameter in your oauth/v2/authorize redirect as mentioned above and configure a Redirect URL in the App Management page. Your redirect_uri must match or be a subdirectory of a Redirect URL configured under App Management. A Redirect URL can not contain an anchor (#).

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: BAD: http://oauth.example.com:8080/path

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The user is signed in to Slack, but not to the workspace you named.team is dropped without an error, and the user authorizes against a workspace they already have a session on. Your app isn't told that this happened, so confirm the result in the oauth.v2.access response, as described below.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Both of the last two situations can end with the team parameter being dropped, so don't assume the value you sent is where the app ended up. The oauth.v2.access response is the source of truth:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: App manifest: Add optional scopes to the bot_optional or user_optional fields within the oauth_config.scopes object. Optional scopes must also be listed in the corresponding bot or user fields.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: oauth_config:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Now, you just need to exchange the code for an access token. You'll do this by calling the oauth.v2.access method as follows:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: curl -F code=1234 -F client_id=3336676.569200954261 -F client_secret=ABCDEFGH https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.access

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: One more suggestion: show the user a nice message once they are redirected and you successfully gain an access token — or, if there's been an error, report that error to the user. The reason the user is redirected back to your app at the end of OAuth is for transparency purposes: the user deserves to know the end of the story, whether your app was installed successfully or not.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Graceful degradation: Handle missing_scope API errors when optional scopes aren't granted.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Token scope storage: Store the granted scopes from the oauth.v2.access response to proactively show or hide features based on what the user has authorized.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The user-centric flow: the oauth.v2.user.access method​

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: In addition to the standard workspace installation flow, Slack provides a dedicated flow for obtaining user-specific access tokens. To initiate a user-specific flow, redirect users to the v2_user authorization endpoint:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: https://slack.com/oauth/v2_user/authorize?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&scope=chat:write,channels:history

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Unlike the the standard v2/authorize endpoint, this flow focuses exclusively on the user's identity and personal permissions. After approval, Slack redirects back to your redirect_uri with a temporary code, just like the standard flow.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Exchanging the code with oauth.v2.user.access​

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Once you have the temporary authorization code, you must exchange it using the oauth.v2.user.access API method. This method is compliant to the OAuth 2.0 RFC.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Comparing oauth.v2.access and oauth.v2.user.access endpoints​

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The oauth.v2.access API method supports generating either a bot token or user token or both.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The oauth.v2.user.access API method generates a user token by default following the standard OAuth spec and works out-of-the-box with MCP authorization flows.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The oauth.v2.user.access endpoint should be used in scenarios where:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: You're building MCP integrations with desktop IDE clients like Cursor or Claude Code

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Use the oauth.v2.access API method unless your client cannot support passing scope and scope_user in the same request.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When you initially send a user through the OAuth flow, you receive a token that has the set of scopes you requested. Any subsequent time(s) you send that same user through the OAuth flow, any new scopes you request will be added to that initial set.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: For example, if you initially request channels:read and channels:write from a user, the initial token will only be scoped to channels:read channels:write (plus identify, which is automatically included in any OAuth grant for a classic app). If you send that same user through a second OAuth flow, this time requesting files:write, the resulting token will have the new scope added to the previous set: channels:read channels:write files:write identify.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: As you make Web API requests, a x-oauth-scopes HTTP header will be returned with every response indicating which scopes the calling token currently has:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: x-oauth-scopes: identity.basic,reactions:read

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Securing OAuth connections for enterprise customers​

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When your app completes the OAuth flow with a Slack workspace, we strongly recommend verifying that the connecting user's account matches the enterprise customer's expected domain.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Call the team.info and users.info API methods to retrieve the workspace's domain configuration.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Enterprise administrators expect that when they install your app on their workspace, employees will connect using corporate-managed accounts. Implementing this check at the end of your OAuth flow helps protect your enterprise customers' data and demonstrates that your integration meets the security expectations of organizations using Slack.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The best way to communicate your access tokens — also known as bearer tokens — to Slack is by presenting them in a request's Authorization HTTP header where the full value, including "Bearer", is case-sensitive. evidence.observation: quote: Before we dive into the semantics of the different OAuth2 grants, we should stop and discuss security, specifically the use of the state parameter. Cross-site request forgery, or CSRF, and Clickjacking are security vulnerabilities that must be addressed by individuals implementing OAuth. This is typically accomplished using the state parameter. state is sent in the authorization request and returned back in the response and should be a value that binds the user’s request to their authenticated state. For example, state could be a hash of the user’s session cookie, or some other nonce that can be linked to the user’s session.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When a user begins an authorization flow on the client, a state is generated that is unique to that user’s request. This value is stored somewhere only accessible to the client and the user, i.e. protected by the same-origin policy. When the user is redirected, the state parameter is returned. The client validates the request by checking that the state returned matches the stored value. If they match, it is a valid authorization request. If they do not match, it’s possible that someone intercepted the request or otherwise falsely authorized themselves to another user’s resources, and the request should be denied.

The concept of archiving a call is deprecated for Aircall Workspace users.

evidence.observation: quote: API Pricing Models: Understanding Approaches to API Charges

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: With Vonage as your provider, API costs are generally straightforward and simple to understand. They’re all based on a pay as you go API pricing model, meaning you’re charged based on usage. Pay as you go isn’t the only API pricing model, however. Let’s take a quick look at the four most common:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The Pay as You Go API Pricing Model

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: This is probably the most popular API pricing model. Here, API users pay according to their actual usage of the API. There’s no set or fixed fee. This makes this model attractive as if the API is only occasionally used, it doesn’t cost as much.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Pay-per-use and pay-per-call are prime examples of the pay as you go API pricing model. In the case of the latter, the user is charged whenever an API gets a request and retrieves the corresponding data.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The Fixed API Pricing Model

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The fixed API pricing model is also sometimes known as a subscription-based model. It’s adopted by some software as a service (SaaS) companies that provide APIs.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Under this model, API users are charged a flat fee, usually on a monthly or annual basis. That fee doesn’t change, regardless of API usage. However, sometimes, API providers will place restrictions or caps on usage.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When these kinds of quotas are part of an API pricing arrangement, once a user has reached the limit of their API use for a month or year, they can’t carry on using it until the next billing period.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Fixed API pricing is generally attractive to users who expect to get heavy usage out of APIs. It also has the advantage of giving both users and providers greater clarity on what they’ll spend or be paid.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The Tiered or Overage API Pricing Model

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The tiered or overage API pricing model is in many ways an evolution of the fixed API pricing model.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The tiered element of this model comes from the fact that API providers will typically offer a range of pricing tiers. Each will come with a different monthly or annual fee and a varying usage quota. The higher the fee, the higher the quota. It’s then up to each user to determine which tier best suits their needs.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The Free Trial API Pricing Model

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: This is perhaps better described as a possible addendum to any of the above API pricing models, rather than a model in of itself. It’s worth discussing briefly, however, due to its inherent benefits for both users and providers.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When API providers offer a free trial, prospective users get to directly experience the APIs and their potential benefits. That works well to convince them that they’re worth the investment—arguably more so than any sales call or demo ever could.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: In general, free trials will last for a set period of time or give a certain amount of usage. After which, the trial user will need to switch to an offered pay as you go, fixed price, or tiered pricing plan.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: What Is an API?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: API stands for Application Programming Interface. An API is a connection mechanism which allows two software components or applications to work together. It defines and manages how the applications communicate with one another in terms of requests and responses. For an end user, APIs work to combine the functionalities of otherwise distinct applications.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: How Much Does an API Cost to Build?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Pricing API development and creation is tricky. There are many factors that can determine the exact costs involved in the process. Things such as the complexity involved and, therefore, the level of expertise necessary, security considerations, and the volume of data involved. In general, however, you’re looking at thousands rather than hundreds of dollars to build an API from scratch.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Yes, there are free APIs that developers can use without any charge within their projects. These are sometimes known as public or open-source APIs. Some API providers also offer free trials of APIs, such as Vonage’s Communication APIs to let prospective users experience the benefits of the APIs first hand, for no charge.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Vonage’s API pricing differs depending on the API in question, but is based on usage. Meaning, you only pay for what use you get from the API. In the case of the Voice API, for example, that means you pay per minute for the calls made and received via the API. The exact amount depends on the nature of the call; whether it’s domestic or international, PSTN or VoIP, etc.

evidence.observation: quote: The provider is called once per HTTP webhook (events, callbacks, and challenge), before decryption and validation. It is not called while building the handler or by trusted WebSocket dispatch. The returned pair overrides static credentials for that request only; the next request sees updates. The example store method returns a lark.WebhookCredentials value and reads the complete pair atomically from a thread-safe local cache. Providers must return promptly, with caller-owned timeouts for any I/O. Empty strings retain legacy empty-configuration behavior. Invalid results and exceptions reject the request without static fallback, and original exception details are not logged or returned. Provider registration is initialization-only. Monitor acquisition latency and failures in the provider. Remove the provider registration to return to static credentials.

evidence.observation: quote: Handshake headers are copied at initialization and for each handshake, including reconnects, and are never forwarded to endpoint discovery. Omitting both settings preserves existing behavior. Host, Connection, Upgrade and Sec-WebSocket-* cannot be overridden through headers. Basic host checks reject empty values, schemes/paths and query parameters; other address and header settings are passed to the underlying libraries without additional SDK format checks. These basic host and reserved-header checks run before network I/O (Start returns an error in Go; construction/build throws in other SDKs). Use trusted developer configuration, not headers/hosts supplied by an end-user request.

evidence_rules:
# Research format and evidence rules

Contract version 1.1, 2026-11-23 (updated in Task 06 from v1.0 based on verified Task 05 pilot findings; sealed v1.0 runs retain their frozen contract snapshots).

### Changelog (v1.0 → v1.1)
- Added `vendor_approval_required` to `credential_eligibility.{testing,production}` to separate platform/vendor API-access review (e.g., Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard application) from commercial/agency `partner_approval_required`.
- Clarified edition-matching for `mcp.discovery`: a community MCP targeting a different product edition (e.g., personal web/cookie scraping vs. Enterprise REST API) must not assert `found` for the Enterprise scope without explicit edition alignment.
- Reinforced per-claim attachment: every material detail in a claim (including `purpose` and MCP tool-list observations) must be anchored inside that claim's own attached evidence array and locator line range.

## Files and migration

- `data/apps.json` is the 100-app identity roster, in assignment order. Its provenance identifies the original conversation and user turn. Original app/hint Markdown is retained verbatim, including link targets and parenthetical hints. Categories and normalized names match the audited roster.
- `legacy_candidate_doc_urls` preserves the scaffold's URL leads with their separate provenance. Neither these URLs nor assignment hints establish auth, access, API or MCP findings. Do not inherit the old OAUTH/APIKEY/GATED/MCP lists, generic descriptions, breadth placeholders or buildability labels.
- `schemas/record.json` is a Draft 2020-12 schema for one app in one immutable run. `examples/unresearched-record.json` is a format example, excluded from research and accuracy totals.
- Initialize substantive claims as `not_researched`, with null values and empty evidence. Keep prior artifacts intact as legacy material; a migration must not relabel their guesses as documentary observations. Existing scripts do not yet consume or enforce this contract.
- Paygent Connect (84) is unresolved. Preserve the original `paygent (NMI-powered)` hint. The legacy paygentglobal.com lead has no established identity match. Resolve vendor/product/edition with primary evidence before attaching that domain's facts; do not substitute a similarly named payment company. The example intentionally leaves this unresolved.

## Claim states and evidence

Each scalar claim has a stable `claim_id`, `status`, `value`, `context`, `evidence`, `supporting_claim_refs` and `rationale`. Context names the edition, API version, account type, region and environment where relevant; say which details remain unknown. IDs remain stable across revisions for the same question. Split materially different scopes into distinct method/entry claims rather than merging them.

| Status | Meaning and counting |
| --- | --- |
| `observed` | Explicitly supported by captured source content; non-null value and evidence required. This means documentary observation, not verified truth or a successful API call. |
| `inferred` | Reasoned conclusion; non-null value, evidence, rationale and supporting claim references required. Report separately from documentary observations. |
| `unknown` | Attempted investigation did not resolve the question. Null value; explain the gap. |
| `disputed` | Conflicting content has not been reconciled. Null value; at least two evidence observations and an explanation required. |
| `not_researched` | No investigation yet. Null value; never count as a finding. |
| `not_applicable` | Evidence explains why the question does not apply to the stated scope. Null value; not a negative result or a correct auth/access claim. |
| `not_found_in_checked_sources` | A bounded search found no supported result. Null value and evidence identifying checked content/search scope required. Use for MCP discovery; never translate to 'no MCP exists'. |

`coverage_status` on auth/protocol/resource collections is workflow metadata: `not_researched`, `partial`, or `checked_sources`. `checked_sources` means only the listed sources were examined, never exhaustive coverage of the vendor. Empty arrays do not prove absence. Record unresolved questions in `notes`; a researched collection can still be incomplete.

For each evidence observation record:

- The actual source URL, source kind, exact heading/anchor, page/line range, or repository path plus commit and line range in `locator`.
- A short captured observation or faithful paraphrase supporting this specific claim. A homepage URL, search-result snippet, or a whole-page citation without a locator is a lead, not substantive evidence.
- `captured_on` (ISO date), capture method, and document date/version when known. Null document metadata means unknown, not current. Capture dates must reflect actual reading, not run creation.
- SHA-256 of the captured content and a relative `snapshot_ref` where feasible. Hash normalized/extracted content only if the snapshot is exactly that content and the extraction method is recorded. If no content snapshot/hash is available, use null and a specific `hash_unavailable_reason`; do not fabricate a digest. A hash proves content identity, not correctness. Never store credentials in snapshots.

For actual operational tests, use `source_kind: execution_receipt` and `capture_method: execution_log`. These require a real local receipt/log in `snapshot_ref` and its SHA-256; `source_url` may be null for a local log. Its locator identifies the run/tool call and relevant log lines; observation states the actual result. This is the only source kind that allows a null source URL. This format permits future receipts; it implements no execution functionality and the Task 02 example has no operational findings.

Prefer vendor developer/auth/pricing/access docs and official repositories. Community repositories support their own implementation claims, not vendor endorsement. Assignment text supports identity/category/hints only. Cite approval and pricing sources for eligibility claims; an API reference alone need not establish a free credential path. If official sources conflict, preserve both observations and their time, version and scope; do not silently pick one. `conflicts` links the affected claim IDs and explains the discrepancy; `disputed` claims may also hold both observations directly.

Evidence is attached per claim. Each auth method, API protocol, resource group and MCP entry has its own claim and evidence. A shared page may be cited repeatedly with the appropriate locator. One citation must not silently support other array members or scopes. When one claim necessarily includes several details (e.g. an auth method plus documented scopes), its evidence must support every detail; otherwise split the claim or omit unestablished optional details. For review, any unsupported material detail makes that whole claim unsupported; do not inflate the denominator by splitting punctuation into claims.

## Field rules

**Identity and purpose.** `identity.id`, `app` and `category` come from the roster; resolve product identity in `identity.resolution` using a cited product/edition description. Category is assignment metadata, not a researched auth claim. `purpose` is a short, single-line, cited description. Do not put placeholder prose in an observed value.

**Auth.** `auth.items` contains a separate claim per method and scope. Preserve OAuth2, API key, Basic and tokens separately; don't choose a single winner. `context` and `details` explain API/edition/actor, OAuth grant or signing scheme; `scopes` lists only documented scopes relevant to the described use. An empty scopes list means no scopes captured, not unrestricted permissions. For CLI/local software, only assert `none` or `not_applicable` when supported for that interface; lack of a REST API does not settle CLI buildability.

**Credentials.** `credential_eligibility.testing` and `.production` each contain independent boolean claims:

- `free_access`, `trial_access`, `sandbox_access`: true means a documented credential/use path is available for this environment; false requires evidence of its absence or inapplicability. Unknown stays null.
- `paid_required`, `admin_approval_required`, `vendor_approval_required`, `partner_approval_required`, `contact_sales_required`: true means this condition is required for the stated path/scope. False needs explicit support for proceeding without it; silence is unknown. Distinguish `vendor_approval_required` (vendor/platform API-access review or application, such as Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard) from `partner_approval_required` (commercial, agency, or technology partnership program gating) and `admin_approval_required` (customer tenant/organization admin role or approval).
- `self_serve`: a documented path allows the intended developer to obtain the relevant credentials without vendor/partner intervention. A paid path may be self-serve; an existing tenant's admin can still be required. State actor/plan/prerequisites in each claim's context. Never derive this by default or from 'Sign up'.

These conditions can coexist. A free sandbox can require admin approval; production may require a paid account and partner approval. For alternative credential paths, the context of each claim must identify exactly which path it describes. Do not collapse conflicting paths to one app-wide boolean: use unknown/disputed with explanatory evidence until a scoped answer is possible. A paid product does not automatically mean API access is gated, and a free trial does not establish production access.

**API surface.** Protocols, public documentation, resource groups and breadth are independent claims. A known REST protocol must survive even when breadth and resource groups are unknown. Record each documented protocol and resource group separately with supporting sections; a source can establish 'contacts' while leaving 'billing' unresearched. `public_documentation` refers to documentation visibility for this API scope, not credential eligibility or public data access. Public documentation does not mean anonymous API access.

`breadth` is an inference supported by resource-group claim IDs: `narrow` = one focused workflow/group; `moderate` = multiple related groups; `broad` = multiple distinct business domains. Explain the classification and captured examples in context/rationale. This is qualitative scope, not a fabricated endpoint inventory or a guarantee of completeness. Leave unknown if not enough resource documentation was read. REST/GraphQL/SDK/CLI can coexist; include other interfaces when relevant to agent-callable tools.

**MCP.** `mcp.discovery` is `observed` with value `found` only when at least one supported entry matching the record's declared product edition/scope is recorded. A community MCP targeting a separate consumer/personal edition (e.g., undocumented web-cookie scraping) does not establish `found` for an Enterprise API scope unless tested and documented for that edition; preserve such community entries only with explicit edition separation or leave Enterprise MCP discovery `not_found_in_checked_sources`/`unknown`. Otherwise use the appropriate null state. Each `mcp.entries` item is its own claim with `official`/`community`, source URL, scope, and repository/server URL where established (null otherwise). A server URL may be a hosted endpoint, while a local stdio server may have only a repository URL. No guessed URL. Vendor endorsement must be supported to call it official. Entries for outgoing MCP clients do not establish an app's callable server; record tool direction/scope. `operational_check` remains `not_researched` unless actual execution logs support the result. Docs, a server listing, or a GitHub README cannot establish successful connection, tool calls, or production readiness. This task runs no operational checks.

**Buildability.** This is an explicit inference for a stated agent workflow: `build_now`, `conditional`, `outreach_required` or `not_buildable_for_stated_scope`. Cite supported identity/auth/access/API/MCP or CLI claims through `supporting_claim_refs`, include relevant source evidence, explain the conclusion, list blockers and next steps. A public API can still require outreach; no MCP alone is not a blocker to building an API wrapper. Unknown identity/access/API details can leave buildability unknown. `build_now` is feasibility from evidence, not an implemented or tested integration. Blocker statements also require support; do not label an app unbuildable because a fetch failed.

## Fetch telemetry is separate

`fetches` records URL, attempt date, status, HTTP status, resolved URL, error and optional content digest. It never supplies claim truth. DNS/HTTP errors, login walls, robots blocks and timeouts do not establish no API, paid access, partner gating or nonexistent MCP. A 200 response does not establish a cited claim. Fetch outcomes can prompt follow-up but cannot promote research states automatically.

## Review, runs and accuracy

1. Every saved run gets a unique `run_id`, creation date and producer identity/type. Persist the run input roster hash, schema/rules versions, tool/model versions and configuration alongside that run in a run manifest. Never reuse a run ID or overwrite original records, evidence snapshots, logs or adjudications. The example's run ID is illustrative only.
2. Corrections create a new run with `parent_run_id` and `correction_refs` naming original run/claim IDs plus reasons. Keep the original value/evidence unchanged in the parent; revised claims reuse the same question ID where scope is unchanged. Record added/removed/split claims explicitly in the correction log. New evidence does not retroactively become first-pass evidence.
3. `review` is pending until actual claim adjudications exist. Completed means the listed adjudications are completed, not that every field/app was reviewed. Capture reviewer ID, `ai` or `human`, date, original run ID, each claim ID, judgment, rationale and review evidence. A tool/browser action or another AI is still AI review; only an actual identified person can sign human review. Producer and reviewer identities must be distinct for independent review; disclose shared model/context. Do not copy pending entries over completed reviews.

   An `unresolved` judgment may have an empty evidence array when no source content could be captured. Its required reason must name the actual fetch attempt (for example `fetches[0]` and its date/URL) or an existing failure-log path and describe why adjudication could not finish. Runtime review must resolve that reference. Do not fabricate a source observation for a DNS/access failure. `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported` and `not_applicable` judgments still require captured evidence; a failure-only review cannot establish any of them. A completed review containing unresolved judgments does not mean those claims have been verified and contributes no accuracy denominator for those judgments.
4. Before full-run verification, freeze a sampling manifest: manifest ID/path, target run, roster SHA-256, selection date, method/algorithm/version, seed, selected IDs, category counts, reviewer assignments and claim rubric. Use a deterministic seeded selection of two apps per category (20 total), without replacement; report all ten categories including Support and Helpdesk. Preserve pilot/targeted reviews separately from this sample. A seed alone does not reproduce an unspecified algorithm. Do not select actual sample IDs in Task 02.
5. Freeze the claim inventory and scoring rubric before review. Unit = each non-null `observed` or `inferred` claim object, identified by `(run_id, app_id, claim_id)`. Count auth methods, protocols, groups and MCP entries separately; nested operational checks are separate claims only if asserted. Score a compound claim correct only if all material details hold for its scope. Report documentary and inference results separately. Category/roster metadata, example fixtures, collection metadata, null states and bare URLs are not scored findings.
6. Each adjudication is `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported`, `unresolved`, or `not_applicable`. Unsupported is a failure to substantiate, not proof of factual falsity. Let C/I/U be completed correct/incorrect/unsupported judgments for asserted claims. Evidence-backed accuracy = C / (C + I + U); print those counts, with unresolved/pending/excluded totals alongside. If the denominator is zero, accuracy is null ('unmeasured'), not 0% or 100%. Exclude null-state claims and not-applicable judgments from this accuracy denominator; report any invalid applicability claims as audit issues. Do not drop incorrect or unsupported results after correction.
7. Report review coverage = completed C/I/U judgments / eligible asserted claims in the frozen sample, with unresolved and pending counts. Separately report research coverage across all 100: counts of observed, inferred and each null state for the six required research areas (purpose, auth, credentials, API, MCP, buildability), plus identity resolution. A collection is not covered just because it exists; distinguish partial protocol knowledge from missing breadth. Report area completion criteria and every denominator. Unknowns do not count as correct findings. No one overall 'accuracy' number should conceal missing research or missing review.
8. First-pass and corrected scores refer to immutable runs, the same sample and the frozen claim questions. Link changed/removed/split/new questions; publish paired results on comparable questions and the changed inventory separately. Do not claim improvement by deleting hard claims, changing denominators or relabeling a failure unknown. A corrected/previously reviewed sample is not an unbiased held-out estimate; disclose reuse. Report no accuracy or improvement until actual adjudication exists. Prepare a human checklist if no person has reviewed yet; do not claim human checks were performed.

## Publication contract (later tasks only)

A hosting config, Site registration, expected URL, local Git directory or ZIP is not proof of publication. Save a repository creation/write receipt, actual repository URL, commit SHA, source/README existence and readback evidence. Save the deployment ID/status, actual live URL, deployed commit or artifact SHA-256, date, and an independent fetch/browser result demonstrating the page is accessible to the intended reviewer. Record real errors/blockers when unsuccessful. No publication is attempted in Task 02.

## Validation and Task 03 handoff

No dependencies were installed. From the workspace root, the available PowerShell validates the example:

```powershell
Test-Json -Path examples/unresearched-record.json -SchemaFile schemas/record.json
$roster = Get-Content -Raw data/apps.json | ConvertFrom-Json
if ($roster.apps.Count -ne 100) { throw 'Expected 100 apps' }
if (($roster.apps.id -join ',') -ne ((1..100) -join ',')) { throw 'IDs/order changed' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category).Count -ne 10) { throw 'Expected 10 categories' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category | Where-Object Count -ne 10).Count) { throw 'Expected 10 apps per category' }
```

If `jsonschema` is already installed in another environment, this optional check verifies both the schema and example (do not install it for this task):

```console
python -c "import json,jsonschema; s=json.load(open('schemas/record.json')); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator.check_schema(s); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(s, format_checker=jsonschema.FormatChecker()).validate(json.load(open('examples/unresearched-record.json'))); print('valid')"
```

Schema validation enforces required fields, value types, explicit states, local evidence minimums for assertions, reference presence for inferences, and pending/completed review shape. It cannot establish source truth, identity, evidence relevance, all reference integrity, actual human activity, or immutable run history. Validators may treat `format` as annotation: Task 03 must explicitly validate URLs/date values.

Runtime/reviewer checks to implement in Task 03 (not implemented here):

- Match IDs/names/categories to the roster; unresolved identity blocks promotion of product-specific claims.
- Ensure unique claim IDs (including nested checks), resolve all support/conflict/adjudication/correction references, reject self/circular support, and ensure buildability/breadth dependencies are supported and scoped consistently. Referenced IDs are claim IDs within this app/run unless explicitly paired with an original run ID.
- Require each asserted method/group/server and every material detail to be supported by its own evidence; inspect the actual cited content. Do not accept assignment hints or legacy leads as product evidence. `breadth` must use `inferred` and reference resource claims; `not_found_in_checked_sources` is restricted to MCP discovery.
- Require no asserted items under `not_researched` collection status; track partial knowledge and source scope. MCP `found` needs at least one supported entry and source-backed origin; operational success needs execution receipts. No nonempty MCP entries under an unknown/negative discovery state.
- Verify valid dates/URLs, content hashes/snapshot paths, document versions, primary/community attribution and conflicts. Keep fetch failures separate and ensure captures correspond to real reads.
- Enforce append-only runs/reviews and snapshot storage, parent/correction linkage, review identity/type, sample reproducibility/category coverage, frozen claim denominators and metric arithmetic. Retain unsupported results.
- Require publication receipts/readback before reporting repo/live-page success.

Coordinator acceptance should cover: honest unknown example passes; multi-auth and REST-only partial knowledge pass; evidence-free observed auth/purpose and unsupported inferred buildability fail; malformed dates/refs are flagged by runtime if the validator does not reject them; completed review with no reviewer/judgments fails. Passing a schema is not evidence that Task 03 or the assignment research is complete.
